lessons.title: Higher-Order Functions
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Define what makes a function 'higher-order', (2) Pass functions as arguments and return them from other functions, (3) Compose small helpers into bigger behaviours.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on higher-order functions — functions that take or return other functions.
Why it matters: HOFs compared to LEGO bricks — knowing them unlocks composition that turns 50 lines of code into 5.
Core terms you will use: `higher-order function`, `first-class function`, `function as argument`, `function as return value`, `composition`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `arr.map(fn)`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: A function as an argument" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the calling-vs-passing bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You see callbacks as just values, not as something magical.

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: First-class functions
parts.description: In JavaScript, functions are values. They can be stored in variables, put in arrays, passed as arguments, and returned from other functions.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Take a function as input
parts.description: A higher-order function accepts another function (a callback) and calls it with arguments of its own choosing.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Return a function
parts.description: A higher-order function can also produce a new function — useful for partially applying arguments or building configurable helpers.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Naming patterns
parts.description: Callbacks are often named `fn`, `cb`, `predicate`, `mapper`. Inner factories are often named `make<Thing>` or `<verb>By`.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Built-in HOFs
parts.description: Array.prototype.map, filter, reduce, sort, forEach, find — all classics. They are the easiest way to feel HOFs in action.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Composition
parts.description: Chain small functions into a pipeline: arr.filter(isAdult).map(toName) — each line says exactly what it does.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Why this matters
parts.description: HOFs replace boilerplate loops with declarative one-liners. The intent stays visible; the mechanics shrink to a name.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Watch the parentheses
parts.description: Passing `fn` and calling `fn()` are different. fn passes the function; fn() invokes it and passes whatever it returns.

analogy.subject: Higher-order functions compared to LEGO bricks
analogy.comparison: Each small function is a brick with a defined shape. A higher-order function is a build instruction that says 'snap this brick into that one'. You compose small pieces into larger structures without redesigning the bricks.

quiz.question: Why is composing filter then map preferable to a hand-written for loop?

quiz.explanation: The returned function closes over n. Each call to multiplyBy creates a brand-new pair (n, returned-function).

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How Redux keeps state changes pure
realWorldStory.storyText: Redux's `createStore` and `applyMiddleware` are both higher-order functions. Each middleware is a function that takes the next dispatch function and returns a new one, letting teams chain logging, async, and analytics in any order. That HOF architecture is why the same Redux core has survived for almost a decade without breaking changes.

keyTakeaways: A higher-order function takes another function as an argument, returns a function, or both.
JavaScript functions are first-class: store, pass, and return them like any other value.
Built-in HOFs — map, filter, reduce, forEach, sort — turn boilerplate loops into one-line pipelines.
Returning a function gives you parameterised helpers: multiplyBy(3), repeatString(5), logger('INFO').
⚠️ Common Mistake: Writing `setTimeout(fn(), 1000)` instead of `setTimeout(fn, 1000)` — the first calls fn immediately.
💡 Pro Tip: Whenever you spot 'almost-identical' loops, factor the difference into a callback and pass it to a single HOF.

lessons.title: Callback Functions
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Identify the callback inside any higher-order function call, (2) Write synchronous and asynchronous callbacks, (3) Recognise the callback-hell pattern and the way out of it.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on callbacks — functions passed into other functions to be called later.
Why it matters: Callbacks compared to a doorbell — knowing when they ring unlocks async control flow.
Core terms you will use: `callback`, `synchronous callback`, `asynchronous callback`, `error-first callback`, `callback hell`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `setTimeout(() => doThing(), 1000)`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: A synchronous callback" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the pyramid-of-doom bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You can predict whether a given callback runs immediately or later.

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: What a callback is
parts.description: Any function passed to another function so it can be invoked later. The 'callback' name comes from the idea of 'call me back when done'.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Synchronous callback
parts.description: Runs during the call: arr.forEach(cb) calls cb once per element before forEach returns.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Asynchronous callback
parts.description: Runs after the current call stack finishes: setTimeout, fetch, fs.readFile schedule the callback for later.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Error-first pattern (Node)
parts.description: Older Node callbacks take (err, result). If err is truthy, handle the failure; otherwise use result.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Anonymous vs named
parts.description: Inline arrows are convenient. Naming the callback gives clearer stack traces and lets you reuse or unregister it.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Callback hell
parts.description: Deeply nested callbacks form a 'pyramid of doom' that becomes unreadable. Flatten by giving each callback a name or switching to promises/async-await.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Don't double-invoke
parts.description: Once a callback fires for a given operation, it should not fire again. Many libraries enforce this; if you write your own, ensure single-call semantics.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Modern alternatives
parts.description: Promises and async/await wrap most callback APIs. You will still meet plain callbacks in DOM events and older Node APIs.

analogy.subject: Callbacks compared to a doorbell
analogy.comparison: When you install a doorbell, you do not stand at the door waiting. You give the doorbell a job ('ring this chime when pressed') and walk away. A callback is the chime — code you hand over to be invoked when an event occurs.

example.title: Example 1: A synchronous callback
example.code: [1, 2, 3].forEach(n => console.log(n * 2));
example.explanation: forEach calls the callback once per element. By the time forEach returns, every call has happened.

example.title: Example 2: An asynchronous callback
example.explanation: Output: first, second, later. The callback waits in the queue until the synchronous code finishes — even with delay 0.

example.title: Example 3: Named callback for clarity
example.explanation: Naming the callback lets us pass it to addEventListener AND removeEventListener later — anonymous arrows cannot be unregistered.

example.title: Example 4: Error-first pattern (Node-style)
example.explanation: The callback receives (err, data). Always check err first. This convention dominates older Node APIs.

example.title: Example 5: A whiff of callback hell
example.explanation: Each step nests inside the next. With three levels it is manageable; with seven it becomes a pyramid. Promises and async/await are the fix.

quiz.question: What is a callback function?
options: A function passed to another function to be invoked later
A function attached to a class
A function defined inside a try-catch
quiz.explanation: A callback is any function passed as an argument to another function so the receiver can invoke it.

quiz.question: Is arr.forEach(cb) synchronous or asynchronous?
options: Synchronous — runs the callback before forEach returns
Asynchronous — schedules the callback for later
quiz.explanation: Array iteration callbacks run synchronously, one per element, before the array method returns.

quiz.question: What does setTimeout(cb, 0) do?
options: Schedules cb to run after the current call stack clears, with at least 0 ms wait
quiz.explanation: Even with 0 delay, the callback is queued. The current synchronous code finishes first.

quiz.question: What is the convention for an error-first callback?
quiz.explanation: Node-style callbacks take (err, result). err is null on success; truthy on failure.

quiz.question: Why prefer a NAMED callback when adding a DOM event listener?
options: Anonymous arrows cannot be unregistered with removeEventListener
Anonymous arrows are blocked in modern browsers
quiz.explanation: removeEventListener requires the same function reference you passed to addEventListener. Anonymous inline arrows produce a new reference each time.

quiz.question: What is 'callback hell'?
options: Callbacks running on the wrong thread
Deeply nested callbacks producing an unreadable pyramid
quiz.explanation: Stacking many nested callbacks creates a pyramid-shaped indent that becomes hard to follow. Promises and async/await flatten it.

quiz.question: Which built-in API uses callbacks for completion?
quiz.explanation: setTimeout takes a callback. fetch returns a promise; the other two are synchronous and have no callback contract.

quiz.question: What happens if a callback throws an error?
options: Propagates synchronously to the caller in sync cases; lost from the stack in async cases unless caught
quiz.explanation: Sync errors bubble up immediately. Async errors that escape can become unhandled — wrap with try/catch or use error-first callbacks.

quiz.question: Which pattern flattens deeply nested callbacks?
options: Using promises with .then chains or async/await
quiz.explanation: Promises and async/await are the modern, linear way to express what nested callbacks expressed before.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Callback Functions"?
quiz.explanation: The async callback — runs later when the runtime is ready — is the headline new idea of this lesson.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How Node escaped callback hell
realWorldStory.storyText: Node.js shipped in 2009 with an error-first callback API for everything I/O — fs.readFile, http.request, the works. Within a few years, the deepest production codebases were drowning in nested callbacks, prompting the community to invent Promises and eventually async/await. Today the same Node APIs offer `fs.promises` versions, but the original callback contracts are still respected for backwards compatibility.

keyTakeaways: A callback is a function passed to another function to be invoked at a later, library-decided moment.
Synchronous callbacks (map, filter, forEach) run before the outer call returns. Asynchronous callbacks (setTimeout, fetch, event listeners) wait in a queue.
Node-style error-first callbacks pass (err, result). Always handle err before reaching for result.
For DOM listeners, give the callback a name so removeEventListener can find the same reference.
⚠️ Common Mistake: `setTimeout(fn(), 1000)` runs fn immediately and passes undefined — drop the parentheses.
💡 Pro Tip: When you see three callbacks nested, refactor to named functions or promises before it grows to six.

lessons.title: Pure Functions and Side Effects
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Identify whether a function is pure, (2) List the common side effects to look for, (3) Refactor an impure helper into a pure version.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on the discipline of pure functions — same inputs, same outputs, no surprises.
Why it matters: Purity compared to a vending machine — knowing the contract unlocks predictable code and trivial tests.
Core terms you will use: `pure function`, `side effect`, `referential transparency`, `mutation`, `immutability`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `return [...arr, item]` (a pure append). Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: A textbook pure function" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the silent-mutation bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You can spot a side effect within five seconds of reading a function.

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: Determinism
parts.description: Same arguments produce the same return value, every single time. Date.now() and Math.random() break this rule.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: No side effects
parts.description: The function reads and returns; it does not write to disks, the DOM, the network, the console, or its arguments.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Side-effect sources to watch
parts.description: console.log, mutating an array passed in, assigning to a global, fetch, document.querySelector, throwing — all impurities.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Referential transparency
parts.description: Anywhere you see add(2,3), you could replace it with 5 without changing the program. Only pure functions earn this privilege.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Pure refactoring
parts.description: Instead of mutating the input array, return a NEW array. [...arr, item] beats arr.push(item).

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Pure functions test themselves
parts.description: No mocks, no setup, no teardown. expect(add(2,3)).toBe(5). Easy tests beget more tests beget more confidence.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Side effects belong at the edge
parts.description: Push I/O and mutation to the outer layers; keep the core pure. Functional cores, imperative shells is a popular architecture rule.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Pragmatism wins
parts.description: 100% pure code is impractical. Aim for pure helpers and a thin impure shell that wires them together.

analogy.subject: Purity compared to a vending machine
analogy.comparison: A vending machine takes a coin and returns the same snack every time — its behaviour depends only on inputs. An impure function is the cashier who occasionally chats with friends, accepts IOUs, and sometimes hands you a different drink. Predictability is the prize.

mapping.to: No external state read or written

quiz.question: What two properties define a pure function?
options: It returns a Promise; it uses async
Deterministic (same input -> same output) and no side effects
It is exported; it has no parameters
It uses const; it is shorter than 10 lines
quiz.explanation: Pure functions are deterministic and free of side effects — these two together make them safely replaceable by their result.

quiz.question: Which of these is a SIDE EFFECT?
quiz.explanation: console.log writes to standard output — observable from outside. The other actions are internal.

quiz.question: Why is Math.random() impure?
options: Same call returns different values, so the function is not deterministic
It mutates the global Math object
It runs in a separate thread
quiz.explanation: Math.random returns a different value each call, breaking the same-input-same-output rule.

quiz.question: Which append implementation is PURE?
quiz.explanation: [...arr, item] returns a new array. The other forms mutate the caller's array.

quiz.question: What is 'referential transparency'?
options: Anywhere a pure call appears, it can be replaced by its result without changing the program
A new operator introduced in ES2020
quiz.explanation: Pure calls earn referential transparency: f(2, 3) and 5 are interchangeable wherever f is pure.

quiz.question: Which of these is generally a GOOD design rule?
options: Keep a pure core and a thin impure shell
Use globals so functions stay short
quiz.explanation: Pure cores are testable; thin impure shells handle I/O. This separation scales much better than scattering effects everywhere.

quiz.question: What is the downside of pure code?
options: Cannot interact with the outside world by itself — you still need an impure layer for I/O
quiz.explanation: Pure functions cannot read user input, write to the DOM, or call a network. A program needs SOME impure code at the edges.

quiz.question: Which is true of pure functions and testing?
options: They are trivially testable with assertions over inputs and outputs
quiz.explanation: No mocks, no setup. Pass arguments, assert the return value. That simplicity is one of purity's biggest wins.

quiz.question: Does throwing an error make a function impure?
options: Yes — throws are observable side effects that break referential transparency
Only if the message is a string
quiz.explanation: A throw is a control-flow side effect: the caller observes a different execution path depending on inputs. Most functional definitions consider this impure.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Pure Functions and Side Effects"?
quiz.explanation: Immutability — avoiding mutation by returning new values — is the practical companion to function purity.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How React's StrictMode catches impure renders
realWorldStory.storyText: React's StrictMode wrapper deliberately invokes every render function twice in development. If a component is pure, both renders produce the same output and nothing user-visible changes. If a component sneaks in a side effect — incrementing a global, logging a request, mutating props — the doubled invocation makes the bug obvious immediately. That tool exists precisely because pure render functions are the contract React assumes.

keyTakeaways: A pure function is deterministic (same input -> same output) AND free of side effects.
Side effects include I/O, mutation, console.log, network calls, throwing, and reading non-deterministic sources like Date.now.
Pure functions are trivially testable — no mocks, no setup, just inputs and outputs.
Keep a pure core and a thin impure shell so the bulk of your code is easy to reason about.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Mutating an argument and assuming the caller will not notice — they will.
💡 Pro Tip: When refactoring, isolate side effects to the outermost layer and let the inner helpers remain pure.

lessons.title: Recursion Basics
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Identify the base case and recursive case of a function, (2) Trace a recursive call by hand, (3) Avoid infinite recursion that blows the stack.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on recursion — a function calling itself with smaller inputs.
Why it matters: Recursion compared to a set of Russian nesting dolls — knowing the pattern unlocks tree, graph, and divide-and-conquer code.
Core terms you will use: `recursion`, `base case`, `recursive case`, `call stack`, `stack overflow`, `tail call`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `if (n === 0) return 1; return n * factorial(n - 1);`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: Factorial" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the missing-base-case bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You can write a recursive function with a clear base case and a smaller recursive call.

hooklineimage.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["factorial(3)"] --> B["3 * factorial(2)"]
    B --> C["2 * factorial(1)"]
    C --> D["1 * factorial(0)"]
    D --> E["return 1 (base case)"]
```
hooklineimage.alt: Recursion unwinding to a base case

hooklines.text: Every recursion needs two pieces: a base case (when to stop) and a recursive case (where to shrink).

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["call"] --> B{"Base case?"}
    B -- yes --> C["return small answer"]
    B -- no --> D["call self with smaller input"]
    D --> A
```

hooklines.text: Each recursive call pushes a frame onto the call stack — too many frames and you crash with stack overflow.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["frame 1"] --> B["frame 2"]
    B --> C["frame 3"]
    C --> D["... 10000 frames"]
    D --> E["RangeError: stack overflow"]
```
image.alt: Too many recursive frames overflow the stack

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: Base case
parts.description: The exit condition. Without it, the function keeps calling itself forever. For factorial, n === 0 returns 1.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Recursive case
parts.description: The function calls itself with a smaller version of the problem. n - 1 in factorial, arr.slice(1) in list recursion.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Progress toward the base case
parts.description: Every recursive step must move closer to the base case. Calling the same arguments again is the classic infinite-loop trap.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Call stack
parts.description: Each call pushes a frame. The frames pile up; when the base case returns, frames unwind one by one.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Stack overflow
parts.description: Browsers cap the stack around 10,000-30,000 frames. Recursion deeper than that throws RangeError. Use iteration or trampolining.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Tail call
parts.description: When the recursive call is the LAST thing the function does, some engines reuse the frame. Useful pattern, but most JS engines do not implement it yet.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: When to choose recursion
parts.description: Problems that are naturally tree-shaped — file systems, DOM, JSON, parsing — read clearly as recursion. Flat lists are usually clearer as loops.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Iteration alternatives
parts.description: Any recursion can be rewritten as a loop with an explicit stack. Reach for it when depth or performance demands it.

analogy.subject: Recursion compared to Russian nesting dolls
analogy.comparison: Opening a Russian doll reveals a smaller version of itself. You keep opening until you reach the tiniest doll that does not open (base case). Each step is the same action on a slightly smaller object. Recursion is exactly that pattern in code.

mapping.from: Stacking opened dolls on the table

example.title: Example 1: Factorial
example.explanation: Base case n === 0 returns 1. Each step multiplies n by factorial(n - 1). Output: 120.

example.title: Example 2: Sum a list
example.explanation: Base case: empty array sums to 0. Otherwise add the head to the sum of the tail. Output: 10.

example.title: Example 3: Count down

// evil(0); // RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
example.explanation: Never reaches a base case, so the stack grows without bound. JavaScript runtimes raise RangeError once the limit is hit.

quiz.question: What is the base case in a recursive function?
options: The first call from the outside
The condition that returns without further recursion
quiz.explanation: The base case is what stops the recursion. Without it, the function calls itself forever.

quiz.question: What happens if a recursive function has no base case?
options: It loops at constant memory cost
It eventually throws RangeError due to stack overflow
quiz.explanation: Each call pushes a stack frame. With no base case, the stack grows until the engine refuses to push more and throws RangeError.

quiz.question: What does factorial(0) return in the textbook definition?
quiz.explanation: By convention, 0! = 1. This is the base case that makes factorial(n) terminate.

quiz.question: Which is true about tail-call recursion?
options: When the recursive call is the LAST action, some engines reuse the current frame, but most JS engines do not yet
It is forbidden in strict mode
quiz.explanation: Tail-call optimisation is in the ES2015 spec but most engines have not implemented it. Do not rely on it in JavaScript.

quiz.question: How do you convert deep recursion into an iterative loop?
options: Use an explicit stack array and a while loop
quiz.explanation: Maintain your own stack as an array and push/pop the work items inside a while loop — this gives you iteration with the same semantics.

quiz.question: Why does each recursive call need to make progress?
options: Otherwise it never reaches the base case and overflows the stack
Otherwise it loses access to closures
quiz.explanation: Progress is what guarantees termination. Calling yourself with the same argument is the classic infinite recursion.

quiz.question: Which problem feels MORE natural as recursion than as a loop?
options: Walk a JSON tree and collect all leaf values
Find the maximum of an array
quiz.explanation: Tree shapes — JSON, DOM, file systems — match the recursive call structure. Flat list problems usually read better as loops.

quiz.question: What is the call stack in this context?
options: The structure that tracks pending function calls and their local state
A list of registered event listeners
quiz.explanation: Each call pushes a frame holding parameters and locals. When a function returns, its frame is popped.

quiz.question: What does function bad(n) { return bad(n); } do?
options: Recurses with the same n forever and throws RangeError
quiz.explanation: No base case, no progress. Each call pushes another frame until the engine raises RangeError.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Recursion Basics"?
quiz.explanation: The base case is the most important new idea — without it, recursion runs forever.

useCaseCards.useCase: Walks abstract syntax trees recursively, since each node has a list of children of the same shape — a perfect recursion target.
Recursively traverses local folders to compare against the cloud snapshot, calling the same function on every subdirectory.
Implements minimax for board games as a recursive function that evaluates the game tree to a fixed depth.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: Why the React reconciler chose iteration over recursion
realWorldStory.storyText: The original React reconciler walked the component tree recursively, which fit the tree shape perfectly. But on very deep trees (such as wide forms generated on the fly), the call stack could overflow. The team rewrote the reconciler in Fiber to use an explicit stack and chunked work — preserving the tree-walking shape but avoiding the recursion-depth ceiling.

keyTakeaways: Every recursion needs a base case (when to stop) and a recursive case (how to shrink the input).
Each recursive call pushes a stack frame; too many frames (10k-30k typically) throw RangeError.
Recursion shines on tree-shaped problems: JSON, DOM, file systems, ASTs.
For very deep recursion, convert to an iterative loop with an explicit stack.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Forgetting the base case — the function calls itself until the runtime gives up.
💡 Pro Tip: When stuck, trace one tiny example by hand on paper before running code. Recursion clears up fast that way.

lessons.title: Function Scope and Closures (Intro)
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Distinguish global, function, and block scope, (2) Define what a closure is, (3) Use a closure to keep private state alive across calls.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on lexical scope and the closures that fall out of it.
Why it matters: Closures compared to a backpack a function carries — knowing them unlocks private state, factories, and modules.
Core terms you will use: `scope`, `lexical scope`, `closure`, `inner function`, `private variable`, `counter factory`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `return () => count++;`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: A basic closure" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the loop-with-var-closure bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You can build a counter factory that hides its state.

hooklines.text: A closure is a function that remembers where it was born.

hooklines.text: Closures let functions hide private data the caller cannot reach.

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: Scope
parts.description: The region of code where a name (variable or function) is reachable. Three flavours: global, function, block.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Lexical scope
parts.description: JavaScript decides what names are visible based on where the code is written, NOT where it is called. Same code, different call site, same scope.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Closure (one-sentence definition)
parts.description: A function bundled together with the variables it captured from its enclosing scope. The captured variables live as long as the function does.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Counter factory
parts.description: The classic demo: outer function declares count, inner function increments and returns it. Each call to the factory creates an independent counter.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Private variables
parts.description: Closures hide variables from outside callers. No one but the returned function can read or write count — true encapsulation.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Module pattern
parts.description: Return an object with multiple inner functions all sharing a closure: { next, reset } both touch the same hidden count.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Closure pitfalls in loops
parts.description: Using var in a for-loop captures the same variable across iterations. Use let inside the loop or wrap the body in an IIFE to capture per-iteration values.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Where closures are used
parts.description: Event listeners, setTimeout callbacks, memoisation caches, currying, hooks like React's useState — closures are everywhere.

analogy.subject: Closures compared to a backpack a function carries
analogy.comparison: When a function is created, it packs every outer variable it references into a backpack. Wherever it travels (returned, passed, stored), the backpack travels with it. The variables inside the backpack stay alive as long as the function holds the bag.

example.title: Example 1: A basic closure
example.explanation: outer returns an inner function that captures name. Even after outer has finished, greet can still print 'Hello, Ada'.

example.title: Example 2: Counter factory
example.explanation: Each call to c() increments and returns the SAME captured count. Output: 1, 2.

example.title: Example 3: Two independent counters
example.explanation: Each call to makeCounter creates a fresh closure with its own count. Output: 1 2 1.

example.title: Example 4: Module pattern
example.explanation: deposit and balance share the same hidden balance variable. No outside code can directly read or write balance. Output: 150.

example.title: Example 5: The loop-closure pitfall
example.explanation: Using let creates a fresh binding per iteration. Output: [0, 1, 2]. Try with var and you get [3, 3, 3].

quiz.question: What is a closure?
options: A function defined inside a class
A function bundled with the variables it captured from its enclosing scope
A function that always returns undefined
A try-catch with a finally block
quiz.explanation: A closure is the function plus the lexical environment it carries with it — the captured variables stay alive as long as the function does.

quiz.question: What is 'lexical scope'?
options: Scope decided at runtime by the caller
Scope decided by where the code is written in the source
quiz.explanation: JavaScript uses lexical (static) scope: nesting in source code determines what each name sees, not the call site.

quiz.question: What does this print? function out() { const x = 1; return () => x; } const f = out(); console.log(f());
quiz.explanation: The returned arrow captures x. Even after out() returns, f() still sees x = 1.

quiz.question: When are the variables captured by a closure released from memory?
options: Immediately after the outer function returns
When the inner function (and all references to it) are gone
quiz.explanation: As long as the closure is reachable, its captured variables are reachable. Drop the last reference and the garbage collector can free them.

quiz.question: Two calls to makeCounter give counters c1 and c2. Are their counts shared?
options: No — each call creates a fresh closure with its own variable
Only when run in strict mode
quiz.explanation: Each invocation of makeCounter creates a new scope and a new count. c1 and c2 are independent.

quiz.question: Which loop output uses CORRECT per-iteration closures?
options: for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) fns.push(() => i);
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) fns.push(() => i);
Both options 1 and 2 behave the same
quiz.explanation: let creates a new binding per iteration; var would share one i across the whole loop, giving [3, 3, 3].

quiz.question: What does the 'module pattern' use closures for?
options: Hiding private state behind a returned object of methods
quiz.explanation: Return an object with methods that share a closure. The methods can read or write the hidden variable; outside callers cannot.

quiz.question: How many scopes does block-scoped JavaScript distinguish?
quiz.explanation: ES6 introduced block scope (let/const). Combined with the older global and function scopes, modern JS has all three.

quiz.question: Inside an arrow function, where does `this` come from?
options: From the enclosing lexical scope (the place it was written)
quiz.explanation: Arrow functions inherit `this` lexically — the same closure-style scope that captures regular variables.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Function Scope and Closures (Intro)"?
quiz.explanation: Lexical scope — names resolved by source-code nesting — is the foundation that makes closures possible.

useCaseCards.useCase: Implements useState by returning a closure over the current state value, so each component instance keeps its own state across re-renders.
Uses a closure to hide the analytics endpoint URL and API key so consumers cannot accidentally overwrite or read them.
Wraps debounced validation callbacks in a closure so each form field has its own timer without sharing state across the page.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How React's useState works under the hood
realWorldStory.storyText: When you write useState in a React component, the hook stores your state in a closure attached to the component instance. The returned setter function captures references to that state slot; calling setter does not assign to a global, it nudges the component to re-render with the updated closure. That pattern would be impossible without JavaScript's lexical scope, and it is why closures are the single most important concept underneath modern frameworks.

keyTakeaways: JavaScript has global, function, and block scopes. let and const are block-scoped; var is function-scoped.
Lexical scope means a function sees what was around it WHERE IT WAS WRITTEN, regardless of where it is later called.
A closure is a function plus the captured environment from its enclosing scope. The captured variables outlive the outer call.
Closures power module patterns, private state, factories, currying, and most framework hooks.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Using var in a for-loop with closures — all callbacks share the same i. Use let.
💡 Pro Tip: When you need 'private' state in JavaScript, reach for a closure long before reaching for a class.

modules.title: Control Flow
modules.description: Direct the path of execution through your program. Make decisions with if and switch, repeat work with loops, and learn the patterns that read clearly six months from now.

points: This module covers Control Flow across 3 focused lessons, building from the basic if statement to switch and the modern loop family.
You will start with conditional statements — the foundation that every later lesson in the course quietly relies on.
By the end you will be comfortable with the vocabulary used everywhere in JavaScript: `if`, `else`, `ternary`, `switch`, `case`, `break`, `for`, `while`, `for-of`.
The lessons progress as: 1) Conditional Statements: if, else, and ternary; 2) Switch Statements; 3) Loops: for, while, and for-of. Each one builds on the last, so work through them in order.
Statements and keywords you will meet here: `if`, `else if`, `?:`, `switch`, `case`, `default`, `break`, `continue`, `for`, `while`, `for-of`.
Each lesson exposes one realistic beginner trap (e.g. "forgetting break in a switch case falls through") and shows the fix — by the end you will recognise mistakes before they happen.
Every lesson ships with a live "Try it" exercise, a graded mini challenge, drag-and-drop sorting, card-matching pairs, and a bug-hunt fix-it task — so practice is built into the flow.
After completing the final lesson on "Loops", you will have a working mental model for control flow that holds up against the next module's harder topics.

lessons.title: Conditional Statements: if, else, and ternary
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Write if / else if / else chains, (2) Use the ternary operator for short conditional expressions, (3) Avoid common comparison pitfalls.

lessonExplanation.topic: Conditional Statements: if, else, and ternary
points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on the conditional statements at the heart of every program.
Why it matters: Conditionals compared to traffic lights at a junction — knowing which branch to take unlocks intentional, readable logic.
Core terms you will use: `if`, `else if`, `else`, `condition`, `truthy`, `falsy`, `ternary operator`, `logical operators`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `if (score >= 90) { ... }`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: A single if" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the assignment-vs-comparison bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You can express a decision with if/else and rewrite it as a ternary when it is short enough.

hooklineimage.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Decision needed"] --> B{"Single condition?"}
    B -- yes --> C["if (cond) {} else {}"]
    B -- chain --> D["if / else if / else"]
    A --> E{"Tiny expression?"}
    E -- yes --> F["cond ? a : b (ternary)"]
```
hooklineimage.alt: Decision flow for picking conditional shape

hooklines.text: if is how a program disagrees with itself — same code, different paths depending on the data.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["score"] --> B{">= 90?"}
    B -- yes --> C["'A'"]
    B -- no --> D["'B or below'"]
```
image.alt: Two branches selected by a condition

hooklines.text: Ternary is if's tidy little sibling for one-line decisions inside expressions.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["isLoggedIn ? 'Welcome' : 'Sign in'"] --> B["One value"]
```
image.alt: Ternary produces a single value inline

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: if
parts.description: if (condition) { body } runs the body when the condition is truthy. The condition is coerced to a boolean.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: else
parts.description: else { body } runs when the if condition was falsy. Pair if with else when you genuinely have a fallback.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: else if chains
parts.description: Chain conditions with else if to express mutually exclusive cases — only the first matching branch runs.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Ternary
parts.description: condition ? a : b is an expression that yields a when the condition is truthy and b otherwise. Great for single-value decisions.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Logical AND (&&)
parts.description: Returns the first falsy operand, or the last operand if all are truthy. Idiom: cond && action() runs action only when cond is true.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Logical OR (||)
parts.description: Returns the first truthy operand. Idiom: name || 'Guest' falls back to 'Guest' when name is falsy.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Nullish coalescing (??)
parts.description: Only falls back when the left side is null or undefined. value ?? 0 keeps 0 and '' as valid inputs, unlike ||.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Avoid deep nesting
parts.description: When ifs nest more than three deep, refactor — early returns, lookup tables, or splitting into helpers all flatten the logic.

analogy.subject: Conditionals compared to a traffic junction
analogy.comparison: Every if is a traffic light at a junction. The condition picks a lane: green for the if body, red for the else. else if adds extra lanes for in-between cases. Ternary is the bicycle lane next to the road — same idea, just narrower and quicker.

example.title: Example 1: A single if
example.explanation: When score >= 90 is truthy, the body runs. Otherwise the program continues silently.

example.title: Example 2: if / else
example.explanation: Two mutually exclusive branches. Exactly one runs every time.

example.title: Example 3: else if chain
example.explanation: Branches are tested top to bottom. The first match wins; the rest are skipped.

example.title: Example 4: Ternary
example.explanation: A ternary is an expression with a value. Perfect for picking between two strings or numbers without four lines of if/else.

example.title: Example 5: Nullish coalescing
example.explanation: || treats 0 as falsy and falls back to 8080. ?? only falls back for null/undefined, so it correctly keeps port = 0.

flowchart.title: Picking the right conditional
flowchart.code:
flowchart TD
    A["Decision in code"] --> B{"Branches share a single value?"}
    B -- yes --> C["Use a ternary (cond ? a : b)"]
    B -- no --> D{"More than two branches?"}
    D -- yes --> E["if / else if / else"]
    D -- no --> F["if / else"]
    C --> G["Ship it"]
    E --> G
    F --> G

quiz.question: Which value would NOT enter an if block?
quiz.explanation: 0 is falsy. The other three values are all truthy and would run the body.

quiz.question: What does the ternary operator look like?
quiz.explanation: JavaScript ternary is condition ? ifTrue : ifFalse — three parts separated by ? and :.

quiz.question: How does an else if chain decide which branch to run?
options: All matching branches run in order
Only the first branch whose condition is truthy runs; the rest are skipped
Only the last matching branch runs
quiz.explanation: JavaScript evaluates conditions top to bottom and runs only the first truthy one. The else acts as the default.

quiz.question: What is the result of console.log(0 || 'fallback')?
quiz.explanation: || returns the first truthy operand. 0 is falsy, so the next operand 'fallback' is returned.

quiz.question: What is the result of console.log(0 ?? 'fallback')?
quiz.explanation: ?? only falls back for null and undefined. 0 is preserved because it is a real value.

quiz.question: Which operator returns the first FALSY operand?
quiz.explanation: && short-circuits on the first falsy operand — that operand is the returned value. Otherwise it returns the last operand.

quiz.question: What is wrong with: if (user.age = 18) { ... }?
options: It assigns 18 to user.age instead of comparing — the condition is then truthy unconditionally
quiz.explanation: A single = is assignment. The condition silently sets user.age to 18 and then evaluates 18 (truthy). Use === to compare.

quiz.question: Which check correctly handles 'name is truthy AND age is at least 18'?
quiz.explanation: && is JavaScript's logical AND. & is bitwise AND, and the word 'and' is not valid syntax.

quiz.question: What does the following return? const label = score >= 50 ? 'pass' : 'fail';
options: 'pass' when score is at least 50, otherwise 'fail'
TypeError because ternaries cannot use strings
quiz.explanation: A ternary evaluates the condition and picks one of the two values. label receives 'pass' or 'fail' accordingly.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Conditional Statements"?
quiz.explanation: The ternary operator is the compact decision tool introduced in this lesson and used everywhere in real code.

codereordering.title: Reorder: evaluating an else-if chain
codereordering.instruction: Drag the steps into the order JavaScript follows when running an if/else if/else for score = 78.
codelines: // 4. Match found — body runs and prints 'C'
// 1. The engine reaches the if statement
// 5. The remaining branches are skipped
// 3. score >= 80 is checked next; that is also false
// 6. Execution resumes after the chain
// 2. score >= 90 is checked first; it is false

dragandropp.instruction: Drag each condition into the right bucket: would it enter an if block?

cardmatching.title: Match the conditional construct with its purpose
cardmatching.instruction: Match each conditional concept on the left with its description on the right.

cards.content: Runs a block when the condition is truthy
Default branch when no earlier condition matched
Ternary expression that yields one of two values
Returns first falsy operand or the last operand
Returns first truthy operand or the last operand
Falls back only when a is null or undefined

bugHunt.title: Find and fix the bug
bugHunt.instruction: An access-control check should run only when the user has admin role, but it runs for everyone. Find the bug and fix it.
bugHunt.bug: The condition uses a single = (assignment) instead of === (comparison). This assigns 'admin' to user.role and evaluates that string — a non-empty string is truthy, so the body always runs. Use === to compare.
bugHunt.hint: Use === for comparisons; a single = is assignment.

useCaseCards.useCase: Uses if/else if chains to map a patient's vital signs into triage categories (green, yellow, red) shown on the floor dashboard.
Picks the right player UI with a ternary based on whether the user is logged in, keeping the JSX compact and readable.
Falls back to a default price label with ?? so listings displaying 0 (free trial month) keep showing the real number instead of an em-dash.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How Netflix avoids 'undefined episode' bugs
realWorldStory.storyText: When Netflix renders the resume-watching row, it picks the next-up episode with a small ternary that defaults to the first episode when no progress exists. They moved from || to ?? after one too many incidents where a position of exactly 0 seconds got coerced to falsy and silently jumped users to the next show. One operator change, hundreds of avoided 'why did my place change?' tickets.

keyTakeaways: if runs a block when its condition is truthy; else acts as the default; else if chains express mutually exclusive cases.
The ternary operator is an expression — it yields a value. Reach for it when an if/else just picks between two values.
Logical operators short-circuit: && stops at the first falsy operand, || stops at the first truthy one, ?? only falls back for null/undefined.
Avoid deep nesting. Early returns, lookup objects, or extracting a helper almost always read better than three levels of if.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Writing if (user.age = 18) — a single = assigns 18 and the condition is always truthy. Use ===.
💡 Pro Tip: Replace || with ?? whenever a valid value of 0, '' or false should not trigger the fallback.

lessons.title: Switch Statements
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Write a switch with case and default, (2) Use break to stop fall-through, (3) Group cases intentionally when fall-through is what you want.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on the switch statement as a clean alternative to long else-if chains.
Why it matters: Switch compared to a railway station's track switcher — knowing it unlocks readable multi-branch logic.
Core terms you will use: `switch`, `case`, `break`, `default`, `fall-through`, `strict equality matching`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `switch (value) { case 1: ...; break; }`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: A basic switch" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the missing-break fall-through bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You can choose between switch and if/else based on the shape of the comparison.

hooklineimage.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["value"] --> B["switch(value)"]
    B --> C{"case 'a'"}
    B --> D{"case 'b'"}
    B --> E{"case 'c'"}
    B --> F["default"]
    C --> X["runs and breaks"]
    D --> X
    E --> X
    F --> X
```
hooklineimage.alt: switch dispatches to a matching case

hooklines.text: switch turns a long ladder of else-ifs into a single neat dispatch table.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["if (x === 1) ... else if (x === 2) ... else if (x === 3) ..."] --> B["switch (x) { case 1: ... case 2: ... case 3: ... }"]
```

hooklines.text: Forget break and the next case runs too — fall-through is a feature, not a bug.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["case 'sat':"] --> B["falls through (no break)"]
    B --> C["case 'sun': weekend = true"]
    C --> D["break"]
```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: switch
parts.description: switch (expression) { ... } evaluates the expression once and jumps to a matching case label.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: case
parts.description: case value: starts a branch. Comparisons use strict equality (===) — '1' and 1 are different cases.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: break
parts.description: break ends the switch. Without it, execution falls through into the next case — a frequent source of bugs.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: default
parts.description: default: is the catch-all branch. It can be placed anywhere but is conventionally last.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Grouped cases
parts.description: Stack case labels with no body between them to share a body: case 'sat': case 'sun': isWeekend = true; break;

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Returning from inside switch
parts.description: Inside a function, return naturally exits the switch (and the function). No need for break before return.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: When NOT to use switch
parts.description: If you need range checks (>, <, between), use if/else. Switch only matches exact equality.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Lookup-object alternative
parts.description: For mapping a key to a value, a plain object is often clearer: const labels = { mon: 'start' }; labels[day].

analogy.subject: Switch compared to a railway station's track switcher
analogy.comparison: A switch statement is the lever at a junction. The incoming train (the value) is shown to the lever, the lever lines up with the matching track (case), and the train rolls down that track. If you forget the buffer (break), the train rolls onto the next track too — fall-through.

mapping.from: Buffer at the end of a track

example.title: Example 1: A basic switch
example.explanation: The engine compares day against each case using ===. 'mon' matches the first case; break exits the switch.

example.title: Example 2: Grouped cases
example.explanation: Stacking case labels with no body in between means both share the body underneath. 'sat' and 'sun' both print 'Weekend'.

example.title: Example 3: Forgotten break (fall-through bug)
example.explanation: No breaks means once a case matches it falls through all later ones. With role='admin', all three lines print. Always add break — or be sure fall-through is what you want.

example.title: Example 4: switch inside a function (early return)
example.explanation: switch(true) lets each case be a boolean expression. return naturally exits the switch — no break needed.

example.title: Example 5: Lookup object beats switch
example.explanation: When a switch only maps one value to another, an object literal is shorter and easier to update.

flowchart.title: When to reach for switch
flowchart.code:
flowchart TD
    A["Multi-branch decision"] --> B{"Comparing exact values?"}
    B -- yes --> C{"3+ branches?"}
    B -- no --> D["Use if / else if"]
    C -- yes --> E["Use switch"]
    C -- no --> F["if / else is fine"]
    E --> G["Add break or return for each case"]
    D --> G
    F --> G

interactiveExercise.title: Try It Yourself
interactiveExercise.instruction: Write a function dayType(day) that returns 'weekend' for 'sat' and 'sun', otherwise 'weekday'. Use a switch with grouped cases. Call it for every short day name ('mon' through 'sun') and log each result.
interactiveExercise.expectebehavior: Seven lines: weekday, weekday, weekday, weekday, weekday, weekend, weekend.

quiz.question: Which keyword exits a switch case?
quiz.explanation: break ends the switch. Inside a function, return also works because it exits the function entirely.

quiz.question: How does switch compare a value to a case label?
quiz.explanation: switch uses strict equality, so '1' and 1 do not match the same case.

quiz.question: What happens if a case body is missing break (and not a return)?
options: Execution jumps out of the switch
Execution falls through into the next case
quiz.explanation: Without break or return, execution continues into the next case. This fall-through is sometimes intentional but usually a bug.

quiz.question: Where can the default branch appear in a switch?
options: It must be after at least one case
quiz.explanation: default can be placed anywhere, though conventionally it is the last branch.

quiz.question: Why might switch (true) be useful?
options: It enables boolean expressions per case, like switch(true) { case x > 5: ... }
It is the only way to use case in JavaScript
quiz.explanation: switch(true) lets each case be any boolean expression — handy for range checks. The first matching case runs.

quiz.question: How do you group two cases that should run the same body?
options: Stack the labels with no body between: case 'a': case 'b': body; break;
quiz.explanation: Stack the case labels with nothing between them. Both labels share the body that follows.

quiz.question: Which alternative is often cleaner than a switch that only maps one value to another?
options: A lookup object: const map = { a: 1 }; map[key]
quiz.explanation: Mapping one value to another is exactly what an object literal does. It is shorter and easier to extend.

quiz.question: Inside a function, can return replace break in a switch?
options: No, return is not allowed inside switch
Yes, return exits the switch (and the function) cleanly
quiz.explanation: return exits the function, which also exits the switch. It often produces clearer code than break + variable assignment.

quiz.question: What value matches case '1': when the expression is the number 1?
options: No — strict equality means '1' (string) and 1 (number) are different
quiz.explanation: switch comparison is strict, so '1' === 1 is false and the case does not match.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Switch Statements"?
quiz.explanation: Fall-through is the behaviour unique to switch and the topic you must master to avoid the most common switch bugs.

codereordering.title: Reorder: how switch picks a case
codereordering.instruction: Drag the steps into the order JavaScript follows when running switch(day) for day = 'fri'.
codelines: // 4. The matching case body runs and prints
// 1. The expression day is evaluated to 'fri'
// 5. break exits the switch
// 3. 'fri' is compared with 'fri' using ===; matches
// 6. Execution resumes after the switch block
// 2. 'fri' is compared with 'mon' using ===; no match

bugHunt.bug: There are no break statements, so once a case matches, execution falls through to every later case. Add break after each console.log (or refactor to return).
bugHunt.hint: Every case body needs a break (or a return) unless you specifically want fall-through.

useCaseCards.useCase: Routes each Kubernetes event type ('Added', 'Modified', 'Deleted') to its handler with a switch, keeping the controller's dispatch table at the top of the file.
Uses switch on payment method ('card', 'upi', 'cod', 'wallet') to render the right form fields without nested ternaries blowing up the JSX.
Switches on robot state ('idle', 'running', 'error', 'charging') in the dashboard to swap status icons and disable controls per state.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How VS Code handles its command palette
realWorldStory.storyText: VS Code's command palette dispatches every command id to a handler via what is effectively one giant switch (extracted into a registry). When a new feature lands, its team adds exactly one case and one handler — nothing else can break, because the rest of the cases are untouched. That separation is why extensions feel safe to install.

keyTakeaways: switch dispatches on the value of an expression using strict equality (===). It shines when you have three or more exact-value branches.
break ends the switch. Forget it and execution falls through into the next case — fall-through is a feature, not a hidden bug.
default is the catch-all branch; convention places it last. Grouped case labels share one body without any duplication.
Inside a function, return cleanly exits both the case and the function — no break needed.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Omitting break in a multi-branch switch and getting unexpected extra output.
💡 Pro Tip: For pure key-to-value mappings, prefer a plain object — it is shorter, easier to extend, and harder to break.

lessons.title: Loops: for, while, and for-of
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Write a classic for loop, (2) Pick between while, do-while, for, and for-of based on the situation, (3) Use break and continue intentionally.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on the loop family every JavaScript program uses.
Why it matters: Loops compared to a metronome — knowing how to start, step, and stop unlocks every repetitive task.
Core terms you will use: `for`, `while`, `do-while`, `for-of`, `break`, `continue`, `iterable`, `iterator`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {}`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: A classic counter" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the off-by-one bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You can pick a loop style based on whether you know how many iterations you need.

hooklineimage.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Need to repeat?"] --> B{"Know count up front?"}
    B -- yes --> C["for (let i=0; i<n; i++)"]
    B -- no --> D{"Iterating an array/string?"}
    D -- yes --> E["for (const x of items)"]
    D -- no --> F["while (cond) {}"]
```
hooklineimage.alt: Decision flow for which loop to pick

hooklines.text: A loop is how a program does the same thing many times without you typing it many times.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["i = 0"] --> B["i < 3?"]
    B -- yes --> C["body runs"]
    C --> D["i++"]
    D --> B
    B -- no --> E["done"]
```

hooklines.text: for-of is the modern way to walk an array — no index gymnastics required.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["[1, 2, 3]"] --> B["for (const n of arr)"]
    B --> C["n = 1"]
    B --> D["n = 2"]
    B --> E["n = 3"]
```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: Classic for
parts.description: for (init; condition; update) { body } — initialises a counter, checks a condition each pass, and updates after the body.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: while
parts.description: while (condition) { body } — runs the body as long as the condition is truthy. Use when you do not know the count up front.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: do-while
parts.description: do { body } while (condition); — runs the body once first, then checks the condition. Handy for prompt-then-validate flows.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: for-of
parts.description: for (const x of iterable) { body } — yields each element of an array, string, Map, Set, or any other iterable directly.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: break
parts.description: break exits the nearest loop immediately. Pair it with a found-condition to stop searching as soon as you find a match.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: continue
parts.description: continue skips to the next iteration. Useful for filtering inside a loop without nesting another if.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Avoid infinite loops
parts.description: Every loop needs a path to ending. Make sure the condition becomes false (for / while) or the iterable runs out (for-of).

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Array methods often beat loops
parts.description: For transforming or filtering, map and filter are more declarative than a for loop. Reach for them when the goal is a new array.

analogy.subject: Loops compared to a metronome
analogy.comparison: A loop is a metronome that ticks until you stop it. for loops set the tempo (the counter) and total beats (the condition). while loops tick until you say 'enough'. for-of loops walk through a playlist of items, one at a time, no counter needed.

mapping.from: Number of beats decided in advance
One beat, then check if to continue

example.title: Example 1: A classic counter
example.explanation: Initialise i to 0, run while i < 3, increment after each pass. Prints 'tick 0', 'tick 1', 'tick 2'.

example.title: Example 2: while until done
example.explanation: Loops while n is positive, prints 10, 7, 4, 1, then exits when n becomes -2. Useful when iteration count is not known up front.

example.title: Example 3: for-of over an array
example.explanation: for-of binds each element directly to name — no indexing, no length check. The cleanest way to walk an array.

realWorldStory.storyText: Spotify's Daily Mix builder walks each candidate track with a for-of loop and uses continue to skip songs already heard that week. Once it has gathered enough tracks, it breaks out of the loop early instead of scanning the entire catalog. That single break shaves measurable milliseconds off every playlist build — multiplied by hundreds of millions of users, it is a meaningful infrastructure win.

keyTakeaways: Classic for loops shine when you know the iteration count or need fine control over the counter.

lessons.title: Logical Operators in Depth
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Use &&, ||, !, and ??, (2) Predict the result of short-circuit evaluation, (3) Apply logical-assignment operators (&&=, ||=, ??=).

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on JavaScript's logical operators and how short-circuit evaluation makes them powerful.
Why it matters: Logical operators compared to circuit gates — knowing them unlocks one-line guards and defaults.
Core terms you will use: `logical AND`, `logical OR`, `logical NOT`, `nullish coalescing`, `short-circuit evaluation`, `logical-assignment operators`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `const name = input ?? 'guest';`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: Basic && and ||" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the OR-vs-?? gotcha shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You can choose between || and ?? based on whether 0 and '' should fall through.

```mermaid
    A["Logical Operator"] --> B["&& returns first falsy"]
    A --> C["|| returns first truthy"]
    A --> D["?? falls back only for null/undefined"]
    A --> E["! flips a boolean"]
```

hooklines.text: && and || do not return booleans — they return one of their operands.

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: && (AND)
parts.description: Evaluates left to right. Returns the first falsy operand, or the last operand if all are truthy.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: || (OR)
parts.description: Evaluates left to right. Returns the first truthy operand, or the last operand if all are falsy.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: ! (NOT)
parts.description: Flips a value to its boolean opposite. !'' is true, !'hi' is false. Double-NOT !! coerces any value to its boolean form.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: ?? (Nullish coalescing)
parts.description: Returns the right side ONLY when the left is null or undefined. Preserves 0, '', and false as real values.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Short-circuit
parts.description: Operators stop evaluating once the result is known. true || expensive() never calls expensive.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Guard idiom
parts.description: user && user.email — read user.email only if user is truthy. Replaces a tiny if statement.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Default idiom
parts.description: name || 'Guest' and name ?? 'Guest' both supply a default; pick ?? unless you want 0/''/false to fall back too.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Logical-assignment operators
parts.description: a ||= b is shorthand for a = a || b. Equivalent shortcuts exist for && and ??.

analogy.subject: Logical operators compared to circuit gates
analogy.comparison: AND is a chain of locks — every link must open. OR is a row of doors — any one open is enough. ?? is a back-up generator that only kicks in when the main power is actually out, not just dimmed.

quiz.explanation: && returns the last operand when all earlier operands are truthy. true is truthy, so the result is 'yes'.

quiz.question: What does 0 || 'fallback' return?

quiz.question: What is 0 ?? 'fallback'?
quiz.explanation: ?? only falls back for null or undefined. 0 is a real value and is returned as-is.

quiz.explanation: !'hello' is false; !false is true. !! is the idiom for coercing any value to its boolean form.

quiz.explanation: ??= assigns only when a is null or undefined — the same semantics as ??.

quiz.explanation: Short-circuit — stopping evaluation as soon as the answer is known — is the engine behind every logical-operator idiom.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How TC39 added ?? to fix a port-zero bug
realWorldStory.storyText: For years, JavaScript developers used || to supply defaults. But teams running services on port 0 (a valid 'pick any port' value) kept getting silently overridden to 3000. The TC39 committee shipped the ?? operator in ES2020 precisely to draw a line between 'no value' (null/undefined) and 'a value that happens to be falsy' (0/''/false). Today, ?? is the recommended default-picking operator in every major JavaScript style guide.

keyTakeaways: && returns the first falsy operand or the last operand; || returns the first truthy operand or the last operand.
?? falls back only when the left is null or undefined. Use it whenever 0, '', or false are legal values.
!! coerces any value to a real boolean. ! flips just once.
Short-circuit evaluation makes guard (user && user.email) and default (name ?? 'Guest') idioms possible.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Using || for defaults when the input might legitimately be 0 or '' — those collapse to the fallback.
💡 Pro Tip: Enable the ESLint rule `prefer-nullish-coalescing` so the linter nudges you toward ?? automatically.

lessons.title: Truthy and Falsy Values
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) List every falsy value in JavaScript, (2) Predict whether a value will enter an if block, (3) Coerce any value into its boolean form safely.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on the exactly-seven falsy values and why everything else is truthy.
Why it matters: Truthiness compared to a traffic gate — knowing the rules unlocks safe conditional logic.
Core terms you will use: `truthy`, `falsy`, `Boolean conversion`, `falsy seven`, `empty array trap`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `if (value) { ... }`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: The falsy seven" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the empty-array-is-truthy bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You can recite the seven falsy values without thinking.

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: The falsy seven
parts.description: false, 0, -0, 0n (bigint zero), '' (empty string), null, undefined, NaN. That is the entire list.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Everything else is truthy
parts.description: Non-empty strings, non-zero numbers, all objects, all arrays (even []), all functions, Infinity, -Infinity, dates, regexes — all truthy.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Boolean conversion
parts.description: Boolean(value) returns true for truthy values, false for falsy. The same coercion happens automatically inside if, while, &&, ||, !

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: The !! idiom
parts.description: Doubled NOT coerces any value to its boolean form: !!'hello' is true, !!0 is false. Shorter than Boolean(value).

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Empty array surprise
parts.description: [] is truthy. To test 'has items', check array.length, not array. The same goes for objects vs Object.keys(obj).length.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: String '0' vs number 0
parts.description: The string '0' is truthy (non-empty string). The number 0 is falsy. Coercion bugs love this difference.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Guard clauses
parts.description: Early returns based on truthiness: if (!value) return;  is a clean way to dismiss bad input at the top.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Default values
parts.description: value || 'default' relies on truthiness. Switch to value ?? 'default' when 0, '', and false should be allowed.

analogy.subject: Truthiness compared to a traffic gate
analogy.comparison: At a gate, exactly seven categories of vehicles are turned away (the falsy seven). Everyone else drives through. Knowing the seven means you never have to inspect every visitor — just check the no-fly list.

example.title: Example 1: The falsy seven

realWorldStory.storyTitle: Why ESLint flags `if (array)`
realWorldStory.storyText: After enough bugs from developers writing `if (results)` to test for non-empty arrays, ESLint added a rule that flags any array-truthiness check as suspicious. keyTakeaways: There are exactly seven falsy values: false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy.
Empty arrays and empty objects are TRUTHY — check .length or Object.keys() to know if they have content.
Boolean(value) and !!value both convert any value to its boolean form. !! is the shorter idiom.
array.filter(Boolean) is the canonical one-liner to remove every falsy value from an array.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Checking `if (results)` to test for non-empty arrays — every array is truthy.
💡 Pro Tip: When a value can legitimately be 0, '', or false, never rely on truthiness — compare explicitly.

realWorldStory.storyText: Webpack's module resolver walks a tree of module dependencies looking for circular references. Labeled breaks let it do that without a 'found' boolean cluttering the logic — the abort is right where the cycle is detected, and the rest of the code reads top-to-bottom.

lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Pick the right iteration style for arrays, strings, Maps, and plain objects, (2) Explain why for-in is rarely the right choice on arrays, (3) Recognise when forEach is unsuitable.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on the three modern ways to iterate and when each shines.
Why it matters: Iteration choices compared to choosing a vehicle — knowing each one's terrain unlocks correct loops.
Core terms you will use: `for-in`, `for-of`, `forEach`, `enumerable property`, `iterable`, `Object.keys`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `for (const value of items)`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: for-of on an array" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the for-in-on-arrays bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You pick for-of for arrays and Object.entries for plain objects without thinking.

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: for-of
parts.description: Iterates VALUES from any iterable: arrays, strings, Maps, Sets, generators. The everyday loop for sequences.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: for-in
parts.description: Iterates the enumerable KEYS of any object. Including inherited keys. Rarely the right tool for arrays.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: forEach
parts.description: Array method that calls a callback per element. Clean for short transformations, but cannot break or properly handle await.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Iterating arrays — pick for-of
parts.description: for-of yields values in order; you can break and continue; you can await inside. for-in on arrays can yield extra inherited keys.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Iterating plain objects
parts.description: Use Object.keys, Object.values, or Object.entries combined with for-of. They give you a clean, owned-keys-only iteration.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Iterating strings
parts.description: for-of yields each character (handling surrogate pairs correctly). for-in would give indices — almost never what you want.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Maps and Sets
parts.description: for (const [k, v] of map) and for (const v of set) — clean access without manual .entries() calls.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: forEach pitfalls
parts.description: No break, no await semantics that work with awaiting inside, no return value to chain. Reach for it when none of those matter.

analogy.subject: Iteration styles compared to vehicles for terrain
analogy.comparison: for-of is a sedan — comfortable on any iterable terrain. for-in is a bicycle made for object-key roads, useless off-road on arrays. forEach is a single-speed scooter: easy and breezy, but you cannot pull a brake mid-trip.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How TypeScript flagged the for-in bug forever
realWorldStory.storyText: Microsoft's TypeScript team added a strict warning when developers wrote `for (const i in array)` because the keys come out as strings — leading to silent string concatenation when paired with arithmetic. After the warning shipped, internal reports of 'mysterious string output in number contexts' fell sharply. The lesson: for-of is what almost everyone meant when they wrote for-in.

keyTakeaways: for-of yields VALUES from any iterable — arrays, strings, Maps, Sets. Supports break and await.
for-in yields KEYS from any object, including inherited enumerable ones. Rarely the right tool for arrays.
forEach is a clean array callback but cannot break, cannot await sequentially, and returns undefined.
For plain objects, combine Object.keys/values/entries with for-of for safe, owned-only iteration.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Using for-in on an array — you get the indices as strings, often with surprising inherited props.
💡 Pro Tip: When you might want early exit or await, default to for-of from the start — switching later is painful.

lessons.title: Error Handling with try-catch
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Wrap risky code in try-catch, (2) Throw and catch Error objects, (3) Use finally for cleanup that must always run.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on JavaScript's try/catch/finally and the Error class hierarchy.
Why it matters: Error handling compared to seat belts — knowing them unlocks robust code that survives bad inputs.
Core terms you will use: `try`, `catch`, `finally`, `throw`, `Error`, `error propagation`, `error boundaries`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `try { ... } catch (err) { ... }`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: Catching a thrown error" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the over-catching bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You only wrap operations that can realistically fail and let the rest propagate.

```mermaid
    B -- yes --> C["catch (err) { ... }"]
    B -- no --> D["Skip catch"]

```

hooklines.text: try-catch lets you intercept errors at the layer where you can do something about them.


hooklines.text: finally is the cleanup that runs no matter what — even on early return.
