```mermaid
    A --> C["catch"]
    B --> D["finally"]
    C --> D
```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: try
parts.description: Wraps the code that may throw. Any error inside transfers control to the matching catch.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: catch
parts.description: Receives the thrown error as its parameter. Inspect err.message, err.name, and the stack to decide what to do.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: throw
parts.description: Raises an error. Always throw an Error instance (not a string) so you get a stack trace and named type.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Error class
parts.description: Standard error type with name, message, and stack. Subclasses include TypeError, RangeError, SyntaxError, ReferenceError.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Custom errors
parts.description: class ValidationError extends Error {} — gives your domain-specific failures a name that catch blocks can match on.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: finally
parts.description: Runs after try (and after catch, if used) regardless of outcome — even on early returns. Perfect for closing resources.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Rethrow when unsure
parts.description: If catch cannot handle the error meaningfully, rethrow with `throw err;` so the upper layer can decide.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Catch only what you handle
parts.description: Wrapping every line in try/catch hides bugs. Catch at the boundary where you can either recover or report meaningfully.

analogy.subject: Error handling compared to seat belts
analogy.comparison: Try is the car ride. Catch is the seat belt that engages when something violent happens. Finally is the cleanup the airbag does no matter how the ride ended. Throwing without an Error is like driving without a license — possible, but you lose all the safety information.

example.title: Example 1: Catching a thrown error

example.title: Example 5: Custom error class

quiz.question: Which keyword starts a block that may throw?
quiz.explanation: JavaScript uses try { ... } to wrap risky code. Errors inside transfer control to catch.

quiz.question: What does catch receive?
options: The thrown error as a single argument
quiz.explanation: catch (err) binds the thrown value to err. Modern syntax also allows catch with no binding when you do not need the error.

quiz.question: Should you throw a string like throw 'failed'?
options: No — throw an Error instance so you get a stack trace and named type
quiz.explanation: throw new Error('failed') gives a stack trace, a name, and is properly handled by tools. Plain strings are legal but lose all that context.

quiz.question: When does finally run?
options: Only when an error was caught
Only when no error was caught
After try (and catch if it ran) — regardless of outcome, including early returns
quiz.explanation: finally is the cleanup that always fires — even when try returns or catch returns. Use it for closing resources.

quiz.question: What is the name of the error thrown by null.foo?
quiz.explanation: Accessing a property of null produces a TypeError: Cannot read properties of null.

quiz.question: Why would you create a custom Error subclass?
options: Because Error itself cannot be thrown
So catch blocks can match on its class (instanceof) and you can attach domain fields
To make errors render in the DOM
quiz.explanation: class ValidationError extends Error {} lets specific catch blocks recognise the failure class and gives you space for fields like the offending value.

quiz.question: What does 'rethrow' mean?
options: Throwing a different error to confuse the caller
Throwing the same error you caught back up the stack so a higher layer can handle it
Catching the error a second time
Logging an error to the console
quiz.explanation: If catch cannot meaningfully handle an error, rethrow with `throw err` so the next layer up sees it.

quiz.question: Why is wrapping every line in try-catch usually a bad idea?
options: It is too verbose for the parser
It hides bugs and consumes errors the caller might want to know about
It is forbidden in strict mode
quiz.explanation: Defensive over-catching turns real bugs into silent no-ops. Catch only where you can recover or report meaningfully.

quiz.question: Which Error subclass is thrown by a malformed JSON.parse input?
quiz.explanation: JSON.parse throws SyntaxError when the input is not valid JSON.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Error Handling with try-catch"?
quiz.explanation: Error propagation — letting an error bubble up until the right layer catches it — is the central new idea.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How Sentry helps teams catch the right errors
realWorldStory.storyText: Sentry's golden rule for crash reporting is: catch errors only at the boundary where you can recover, and let everything else bubble up to the top-level error handler. Teams that wrap every function in try-catch see Sentry dashboards go silent — and bugs ship to production unnoticed. The discipline of 'catch narrow, log everything else' is what makes their dashboards trustworthy.

keyTakeaways: try wraps code that may throw; catch handles the error; finally is cleanup that always runs.
throw new Error('message') is the canonical way to signal failure — never throw plain strings.
Catch where you can do something meaningful — handle, retry, or report. Otherwise let the error propagate.
Custom Error subclasses let catch blocks match on instanceof and attach domain-specific fields.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Swallowing errors with an empty catch block — bugs become invisible and dashboards stay green while users suffer.
💡 Pro Tip: Pair finally with resource acquisition (locks, files, sockets) so they release no matter how the function exits.

modules.title: Arrays
modules.description: Master JavaScript's everyday data structure: create, mutate, iterate, transform, and search arrays with the methods every JS engineer reaches for daily.

points: This module covers Arrays across 8 focused lessons, building from creating arrays to advanced search, sort, and reduce patterns.
You will start with array basics — the foundation that every later lesson quietly relies on.
By the end you will be comfortable with the vocabulary used everywhere in JavaScript: `length`, `push/pop`, `shift/unshift`, `splice`, `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `find`, `sort`.
The lessons progress as: 1) Array Basics; 2) Adding/Removing; 3) forEach; 4) map; 5) filter; 6) reduce; 7) Searching; 8) Sorting. Each one builds on the last, so work through them in order.
Methods you will meet here: `push`, `pop`, `shift`, `unshift`, `splice`, `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `forEach`, `find`, `findIndex`, `includes`, `indexOf`, `sort`, `reverse`.
Each lesson exposes one realistic beginner trap (e.g. "sort() mutates and uses lexicographic order by default") and shows the fix.
Every lesson ships with a live "Try it" exercise, a graded mini challenge, drag-and-drop sorting, card-matching pairs, and a bug-hunt fix-it task.
After completing the final lesson on "Sorting and Reversing", you will have a working mental model for arrays that powers every modern data-pipeline pattern in JavaScript.

lessons.title: Array Basics: Creation and Access
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Create arrays with literal syntax and the Array constructor, (2) Read and write elements by index, (3) Use length, last-element tricks, and recognise arrays as objects.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on creating arrays, reading elements, and the quirky truth that arrays are objects.
Why it matters: Arrays compared to a numbered locker bank — knowing the access pattern unlocks every data-manipulation task.
Core terms you will use: `array literal`, `index`, `length`, `Array constructor`, `array-like`, `at()`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `const items = ['a', 'b', 'c']; items[0]`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: Literal array" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the sparse-array bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You know that arrays are objects whose keys happen to be integer strings.

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: Array literal
parts.description: Comma-separated values inside square brackets: ['a', 'b', 'c']. The everyday way to create an array.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Index access
parts.description: items[0] is the first element; items[items.length - 1] is the last. Indexing past the end returns undefined.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: length
parts.description: A live property. arr.length always tracks the highest index + 1. Setting it manually can grow or truncate the array.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: at()
parts.description: items.at(-1) gives the last element without arithmetic. Cleaner than items[items.length - 1].

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Array constructor (gotcha)
parts.description: new Array(3) creates a length-3 sparse array (NOT [3]). Use Array.of(3) for a single-element array.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Array.from
parts.description: Turns array-like or iterable values into real arrays. Array.from('abc') yields ['a','b','c'].

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Trailing commas
parts.description: ['a', 'b',] is valid. The trailing comma keeps diffs clean when you later add items.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Arrays are objects
parts.description: typeof [] is 'object'. Array.isArray is the precise check. Keys are integer strings under the hood.

analogy.subject: Arrays compared to a numbered locker bank
analogy.comparison: Each locker is identified by a number starting from 0. You can open any locker by number, drop something in, take something out, or count how many are in use. The locker bank does not care what is inside — strings, numbers, objects, even other arrays.

mapping.to: Arrays can hold any value type

example.title: Example 1: Literal array
example.code:
const names = ['Ada', 'Mei', 'Diego'];
console.log(names[0], names[2]);
example.explanation: Square-bracket literal creates the array. Indexing reads each slot. Output: Ada Diego.

example.title: Example 2: length tells the count
example.explanation: length is 4. The last element is at index length - 1. Output: 4 then 40.

example.title: Example 3: at() for negative indexing
example.explanation: at(-1) returns the LAST element; at(-2) the second-from-last. Cleaner than length-based math.

example.title: Example 4: Mixed types and nested arrays
example.explanation: Arrays can hold any value. Index into nested arrays or objects to reach deeper. Output: 3 and Ada.

example.title: Example 5: Array constructor gotcha
example.explanation: new Array(3) is a sparse length-3 array. Array.of(3) is [3]. Array.from(iterable) turns iterables into arrays. Knowing the difference avoids a classic confusion.

quiz.question: What is the value of ['a', 'b', 'c'][1]?
quiz.explanation: Arrays are zero-indexed. Index 1 is the second element, 'b'.

quiz.question: Which check tells an array apart from a plain object?
quiz.explanation: Array.isArray is the safe, cross-realm check. typeof gives 'object' for both arrays and plain objects.

quiz.question: What is arr.length after const arr = ['a', 'b', 'c']?
quiz.explanation: length is the highest index + 1. For three elements at indices 0-2, length is 3.

quiz.question: What does arr.at(-1) return for ['x', 'y', 'z']?
quiz.explanation: at(-1) returns the last element. Negative indices count from the end.

quiz.question: What does new Array(3) produce?
options: A sparse length-3 array with no defined elements
quiz.explanation: new Array(n) for a single integer n creates a sparse array of length n. Avoid this surprise by using Array.of(3) or [3].

quiz.question: What does Array.isArray([1, 2, 3]) return?
quiz.explanation: Array.isArray returns true for any array (regardless of length or contents).

quiz.question: What happens when you read an index past the end? const a = ['x']; console.log(a[5]);
quiz.explanation: Reading beyond the highest index returns undefined — the same as reading a missing object property.

quiz.question: Which is the cleanest way to get the last element of an array?
options: Both arr[arr.length-1] and arr.at(-1) work; at(-1) is cleaner
quiz.explanation: Both work; at(-1) avoids arithmetic and reads more naturally. pop() would mutate the array.

quiz.question: Can arrays hold mixed value types?
options: No — all elements must be the same type
Yes — any value type can sit in any slot
quiz.explanation: JavaScript arrays are heterogeneous. Strings, numbers, booleans, objects, even other arrays can coexist.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Array Basics"?
quiz.explanation: Index access — reading and writing by integer position — is the foundational array idea.

bugHunt.title: Find and fix the bug
bugHunt.instruction: A developer expects [5] but gets a sparse array of length 5. Fix the snippet.
bugHunt.bug: new Array(5) treats a single integer argument as a length, not a value. Use Array.of(5) or the literal [5] to get a one-element array containing 5.
bugHunt.hint: new Array(n) is special-cased for one integer argument. Use Array.of.

useCaseCards.useCase: Stores cart line items in an array so the checkout flow can iterate, total, and apply discounts in O(n).
Holds image URLs in an array indexed by display order so the lightbox can move forward or backward by integer index.
Pulls the last seven days of metrics with arr.at(-7) through arr.at(-1), no length arithmetic needed.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How Twitter avoids one-element-array bugs
realWorldStory.storyText: Twitter's frontend codebase explicitly bans `new Array(...)` because of a famous incident where a developer wrote `new Array(2)` expecting [2] and shipped a sparse array to production. The linter rule that flags any call to the Array constructor — pointing developers to Array.of and literal syntax — has been part of their style guide ever since.

keyTakeaways: Arrays are zero-indexed, ordered collections. Use the literal syntax [a, b, c] in 99% of cases.
length is the highest index + 1. Use arr.at(-1) for the last element to avoid arithmetic mistakes.
Arrays are objects — typeof says 'object'; use Array.isArray to distinguish them precisely.
new Array(n) for a single integer n produces a sparse array of length n. Prefer Array.of or literals.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Reading an out-of-bounds index expecting an error — you get undefined silently.
💡 Pro Tip: When iterating, default to for-of or array methods (map/filter/reduce) over classic for loops.

lessons.title: Adding and Removing Elements
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Add and remove elements at either end with push/pop/shift/unshift, (2) Use splice to insert or remove at any index, (3) Choose between mutating and non-mutating alternatives.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on the methods that change array length: push, pop, shift, unshift, splice.
Why it matters: Mutation compared to writing in pen vs pencil — knowing which methods change the array unlocks predictable code.
Core terms you will use: `push`, `pop`, `shift`, `unshift`, `splice`, `mutating method`, `non-mutating alternative`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `arr.push(item)`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: push and pop" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the silent-mutation bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You know which methods return the array, which return the removed element, and which return a new array.

hooklineimage.alt: Four operations on the ends of an array

hooklines.text: push/pop work at the tail. unshift/shift work at the head.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["head"] --> B["unshift adds, shift removes"]
    C["tail"] --> D["push adds, pop removes"]
```

hooklines.text: splice is the swiss-army knife: insert, delete, replace at any index.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["splice(start, deleteCount, ...newItems)"] --> B["Remove deleteCount items at start"]
    A --> C["Insert newItems in their place"]
    A --> D["Returns the removed items as an array"]
```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: push
parts.description: Adds one or more items to the end. Returns the new length. Mutates the array.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: pop
parts.description: Removes the last item and returns it. Returns undefined if empty. Mutates.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: shift
parts.description: Removes the first item and returns it. Slow on big arrays — every other element shifts left.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: unshift
parts.description: Adds items to the beginning. Returns the new length. Also slow on big arrays — existing items shift right.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: splice (insert)
parts.description: arr.splice(2, 0, 'x') inserts 'x' at index 2 without removing anything. deleteCount of 0 means 'pure insert'.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: splice (remove)
parts.description: arr.splice(2, 1) removes one item at index 2. Returns the removed item(s) as an array.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: splice (replace)
parts.description: arr.splice(1, 2, 'a', 'b') removes 2 items starting at index 1 and inserts 'a' and 'b' in their place. One call, full edit.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Non-mutating alternatives
parts.description: Modern non-mutating versions: toSpliced, with, toSorted, toReversed. They return a new array instead of mutating.

analogy.subject: Array mutation compared to writing in pen vs pencil
analogy.comparison: push and pop are like erasing or adding at the right margin of a notebook page. shift and unshift force you to rewrite the whole line because everything moves left. splice is grabbing scissors — you cut out a chunk and tape in a new one. Non-mutating versions are photocopies you scribble on so the original stays clean.

mapping.from: Rewriting the line for a new prefix

example.title: Example 1: push and pop
example.explanation: push appends; pop removes the last and returns it. Output: [1,2,3], 3, [1,2].

example.title: Example 2: unshift and shift
example.explanation: FIFO queue: push to enqueue, shift to dequeue. Output: 'a' then ['b'].

example.title: Example 3: splice to insert
example.explanation: splice(2, 0, 'c') inserts 'c' at index 2 without removing anything. Output: ['a','b','c','d'].

example.title: Example 4: splice to remove
example.explanation: splice(1, 2) removes 2 items at index 1. removed is ['b','c']; arr becomes ['a','d'].

example.title: Example 5: toSpliced is non-mutating
example.explanation: arr is unchanged; copy is ['a','c']. toSpliced is the immutable version of splice — handy when you do not want to mutate the input.

flowchart.title: Which add/remove method should I use?

interactiveExercise.title: Try It Yourself
interactiveExercise.instruction: Start with const arr = ['Mon', 'Wed', 'Fri']. Insert 'Tue' at index 1 and 'Thu' at index 3 using splice. Then push 'Sat' onto the end. Print the array after each step.
interactiveExercise.expectebehavior: Final array logs ['Mon','Tue','Wed','Thu','Fri','Sat'].

quiz.question: What does arr.push(value) return?
options: The new length of the array
quiz.explanation: push returns the new length — useful for chained logic. It mutates the array as a side effect.

quiz.question: What does arr.pop() return?
quiz.explanation: pop removes the last item and returns it. Returns undefined when the array was empty.

quiz.question: Which two methods turn an array into a FIFO queue?
quiz.explanation: Enqueue with push (append to tail) and dequeue with shift (remove from head). That is the classic queue contract.

quiz.question: What does splice(2, 0, 'x') do?
options: Inserts 'x' at index 2 without removing any items
Returns a new array of length 2
quiz.explanation: splice(start, deleteCount, ...items): deleteCount=0 means pure insert at start.

quiz.question: What does arr.splice(1, 2) return?
options: A new array containing the removed items
quiz.explanation: splice returns the removed items as an array. In this call, it returns the two items it just removed.

quiz.question: Why is shift typically slower than pop on large arrays?
options: It is implemented in CPU-bound C++
shift requires every remaining element to move left by one index
quiz.explanation: Removing from the head means every other element shifts left to fill the gap — O(n). pop is O(1).

quiz.question: Which is the non-mutating alternative to splice?
quiz.explanation: toSpliced is the immutable counterpart introduced in ES2023. It returns a new array; the original stays unchanged.

quiz.question: What does this return? ['a', 'b', 'c'].splice(0, 2, 'X', 'Y');
quiz.explanation: splice returns the removed elements (['a','b']). The array itself becomes ['X','Y','c'].

quiz.question: Which method is BEST for adding many items to the end?
options: All produce identical performance, choose any
quiz.explanation: arr.push(...newItems) is concise and faster than calling push in a loop. splice could work but is less idiomatic.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Adding and Removing Elements"?
quiz.explanation: Mutating methods — the ones that change the array in place — are the lesson's central idea, especially in contrast to non-mutating alternatives.

// 1. The engine reads start=1, deleteCount=2, insertions ['X','Y']
// 5. The array length is adjusted accordingly
// 3. Two items starting at index 1 are removed and remembered
// 6. The removed items are returned
// 2. The engine prepares the gap at index 1

cards.content: Adds item(s) at the end, returns new length
Removes and returns the last item
Removes and returns the first item
Insert, delete, or replace at any index
Non-mutating version that returns a new array

bugHunt.title: Find and fix the bug
bugHunt.instruction: A developer expects const newArr = arr.push('x') to be the new array. Instead newArr is a number. Fix the snippet.
bugHunt.bug: push returns the new LENGTH, not the array. Either use the existing arr variable (which was mutated) or build a new array with the spread operator.
bugHunt.hint: push returns the new length. To get a new array without mutation, use [...arr, item].

miniChallenge.title: Mini Challenge — Add/Remove
miniChallenge.prompt: Given const queue = ['a','b','c'], pull the head with shift, do something with it, and push it back to the end. Repeat twice. Print the queue after each round.
hints: shift returns the removed element, which you can push back to rotate.

useCaseCards.useCase: Implements a FIFO queue with push to enqueue jobs and shift to dequeue them in worker code.
Uses push for every action recorded and pop to implement Ctrl-Z, getting the classic stack data structure for free.
Builds new arrays with [...arr, item] instead of push when updating state, so React detects the change and re-renders.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How Redux Toolkit picks immutable methods
realWorldStory.storyText: Redux Toolkit's createSlice uses Immer under the hood to LOOK like you are mutating with arr.push, but it actually produces a new array. The reason: detecting state changes by reference is a thousand times faster than deep-comparing every item. Knowing which methods mutate lets you write reducers that work with React, Redux, and any framework that relies on referential equality.

keyTakeaways: push/pop work at the end (fast); unshift/shift work at the beginning (slower, O(n)).
splice(start, deleteCount, ...items) is the swiss-army knife for inserts, deletes, and replaces.
All five (push, pop, shift, unshift, splice) mutate the original array.
For non-mutating versions, use spread [...arr, x] or modern toSpliced / with / toSorted / toReversed.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Expecting arr.push(x) to return the array — it returns the new length.
💡 Pro Tip: In framework code (React, Vue), prefer non-mutating alternatives so change detection works correctly.

lessons.title: Iterating with forEach
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Call forEach with a callback, (2) Use the (element, index, array) parameters, (3) Recognise when forEach is the wrong tool.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on Array.prototype.forEach — the easy way to run a function per element.
Why it matters: forEach compared to a conveyor belt — knowing it unlocks expressive per-item processing.
Core terms you will use: `forEach`, `callback`, `element-index-array signature`, `void return`, `no early exit`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `arr.forEach((item, i) => console.log(i, item))`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: Print each" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the await-inside-forEach bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You reach for forEach when you only need a side effect — and for-of when you need anything more.

hooklineimage.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["arr.forEach(cb)"] --> B["cb(item0)"]
    A --> C["cb(item1)"]
    A --> D["cb(item2)"]
    A --> E["returns undefined"]
```
hooklineimage.alt: forEach calls the callback once per element

hooklines.text: forEach is for side effects — printing, drawing, dispatching. It returns nothing.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["[1,2,3]"] --> B["forEach(n => log(n))"]
    B --> C["logs 1, 2, 3"]
```
image.alt: forEach runs the callback per item

hooklines.text: forEach cannot break or return a value — when you need either, switch tools.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Need break or return?"] --> B{"Use forEach?"}
    B -- no --> C["for-of, map, find, some, every"]
```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: Basic call
parts.description: arr.forEach(callback). The callback runs once per element, in order, synchronously.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Callback parameters
parts.description: (item, index, array) — most code only uses item; index is handy for diagnostics; the whole array is rarely needed.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Return value
parts.description: forEach itself returns undefined. The callback's return value is ignored. Use map if you want to build a new array.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: No early exit
parts.description: You cannot break out of forEach. return inside the callback only skips the current iteration.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: forEach and await
parts.description: Awaiting inside forEach does not pause the iteration — the next callback fires immediately. Use for-of with await for serial async.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Sparse arrays
parts.description: forEach skips holes (sparse array slots). It does NOT visit indices that were never assigned.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: thisArg
parts.description: arr.forEach(cb, thisArg) binds this inside the callback. Rarely needed with arrow functions but useful for legacy method binding.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: When NOT to use
parts.description: Use map when you want a new array, filter when you want a subset, find when you want one element, some/every when you want a boolean.

analogy.subject: forEach compared to a conveyor belt with a station
analogy.comparison: Imagine a conveyor carrying boxes past one station. forEach is the station worker who does a job on each box — labels it, stamps it, hands it off — but produces no new line of products. The conveyor cannot be stopped midway and no record of work is returned.

example.title: Example 1: Print each
example.code: ['a', 'b', 'c'].forEach(item => console.log(item));
example.explanation: The callback runs three times. forEach itself returns undefined.

example.title: Example 2: Use the index
example.code: ['x', 'y', 'z'].forEach((item, i) => console.log(i, '->', item));
example.explanation: The second parameter is the index. Output: 0 -> x, 1 -> y, 2 -> z.

example.title: Example 3: Side-effect dispatch
example.code:
const buttons = document.querySelectorAll('button');
Array.from(buttons).forEach(btn => btn.addEventListener('click', handleClick));
example.explanation: Attach the same listener to every button. The work is purely side-effect; no new array needed.

example.title: Example 4: return inside forEach
example.explanation: return skips ONE iteration. Output: 1, 2, 4. To stop entirely, you would need a different loop.

example.title: Example 5: forEach + await trap
example.explanation: forEach with async callbacks fires every async function immediately. If you need sequential awaits, use for-of.

flowchart.title: forEach or something else?
flowchart.code:
flowchart TD
    A["Iterate an array"] --> B{"Need a new array?"}
    B -- yes --> C["map"]
    B -- subset --> D["filter"]
    B -- single element --> E["find"]
    B -- boolean --> F["some / every"]
    B -- side effects only --> G["forEach"]
    G --> H{"Need to break or await?"}
    H -- yes --> I["for-of instead"]

interactiveExercise.instruction: Given users = [{name:'Ada',score:92},{name:'Mei',score:85},{name:'Diego',score:78}], use forEach to print each user as 'index. name (score)'.
interactiveExercise.expectebehavior: Three lines: '1. Ada (92)', '2. Mei (85)', '3. Diego (78)'.

quiz.question: What does arr.forEach(cb) return?
quiz.explanation: forEach is run for side effects. It always returns undefined.

quiz.question: What are the parameters passed to the forEach callback?
quiz.explanation: The callback receives the element, its index, and the entire array — in that order.

quiz.question: If you need to stop iterating after finding a match, which is the cleanest array method?
options: find or some — both short-circuit on first match
quiz.explanation: find returns the element on first match; some returns a boolean. Both stop scanning early — forEach cannot.

quiz.question: What does return inside a forEach callback do?
options: Skips the rest of the current iteration only
quiz.explanation: return acts like continue — it ends the current callback invocation but the next one still runs.

quiz.question: Which iteration form correctly awaits sequentially?
options: for (const item of arr) { await save(item); }

realWorldStory.storyTitle: When Airbnb removed forEach from their hot paths
realWorldStory.storyText: Airbnb's listings page ran forEach on the search results, then ran map, then ran forEach again — three separate passes. keyTakeaways: forEach calls a callback once per element. It always returns undefined.
Callback signature is (element, index, array). Use the index when you need positional info.
You cannot break out of forEach; return inside the callback only skips one iteration.

⚠️ Common Mistake: Using forEach to build a new array. Reach for map instead.

lessons.title: Transforming with map
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Call map to produce a new array of transformed values, (2) Use the (element, index, array) callback signature, (3) Chain map with other array methods.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on Array.prototype.map — the canonical 1-to-1 transformer.
Why it matters: map compared to a factory machine — knowing it unlocks declarative data transformations.
Core terms you will use: `map`, `transformation`, `1-to-1`, `new array`, `callback signature`, `chaining`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `arr.map(item => item.id)`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: Doubling numbers" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the using-map-for-side-effects bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You instinctively use map for transformations and forEach for side effects.

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: Basic call
parts.description: arr.map(callback). The callback runs once per element; the returned value becomes the element of the new array.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Same length out
parts.description: map always produces an array of the SAME length as the input. One-in, one-out.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Callback signature
parts.description: (element, index, array) — same as forEach. Most callbacks use only element.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Non-mutating
parts.description: map produces a new array; the original is left alone. This makes it safe in React, Redux, and any framework that relies on reference equality.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Return value matters
parts.description: If your callback does not return a value, every element of the new array is undefined. That is the most common map mistake.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Chaining
parts.description: map returns an array, so .filter, .map, .reduce all chain off the result. arr.map(toX).filter(isY) reads top to bottom.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: flatMap
parts.description: When your callback returns an array, flatMap flattens one level: arr.flatMap(x => [x, x*2]) doubles the length.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: When NOT to use
parts.description: Pure side effects (logging) -> forEach. Pulling one item out -> find. Filtering -> filter. Aggregating into one value -> reduce.

analogy.subject: map compared to a factory machine
analogy.comparison: map is a machine on a production line: each raw input goes in, a transformed product comes out, and the input/output count is identical. The input bin (original array) is untouched; the output bin (new array) holds the transformed copies.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How Notion's blocks render with map
realWorldStory.storyText: Notion's document model is an array of blocks (paragraphs, headings, images). The editor renders the whole page with a single map call that turns each block into the corresponding React component. Because map produces a new array on every state change, React can diff cheaply and update only the blocks that actually changed.

keyTakeaways: map is the 1-to-1 transformer: same length in, same length out, each element replaced by the callback's return value.
map does NOT mutate — the original array stays the same.
Forgetting `return` inside a braced arrow callback is the #1 map bug. Either drop the braces or add return.
Chain map with filter and reduce for declarative pipelines: data.filter(active).map(toDTO).reduce(byId, {})

lessons.title: Filtering with filter
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Use filter to keep only the elements that pass a predicate, (2) Chain filter with map and reduce, (3) Recognise common predicate idioms.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on Array.prototype.filter — the predicate-driven subset builder.
Why it matters: filter compared to a sieve — knowing it unlocks clean conditional selection.
Core terms you will use: `filter`, `predicate`, `truthy callback`, `non-mutating`, `subset`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `arr.filter(x => x.active)`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: Even numbers only" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the truthy-trap bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You reach for filter when the goal is a smaller-or-equal-length subset of the original.

hooklines.text: filter keeps elements where the predicate returns a truthy value.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["item"] --> B{"predicate?"}
    B -- truthy --> C["keep"]
    B -- falsy --> D["drop"]
```

hooklines.text: filter(Boolean) is the one-line idiom for removing every falsy value.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["[0,1,'',null,'a']"] --> B["filter(Boolean)"]
    B --> C["[1,'a']"]
```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: Basic call
parts.description: arr.filter(predicate). Each element is passed to the predicate; the element is kept if the return value is truthy.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Truthy decides
parts.description: Anything truthy keeps the element. Returning 1, 'hi', or true all qualify. Falsy (0, '', null, undefined, NaN, false) drops it.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Length shrinks or stays
parts.description: filter returns a new array of length <= original. It cannot grow the array.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Non-mutating
parts.description: Like map, filter never modifies the original array. The new array is independent.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Boolean as predicate
parts.description: arr.filter(Boolean) drops every falsy value in one line — a famous idiom for cleaning data.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Chaining
parts.description: filter then map is the canonical pipeline: keep what matters, then transform. The reverse works too if filtering after transformation is easier.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: vs find
parts.description: Need ONE element matching a condition? Use find — it stops at the first match. Need every matching element? Use filter.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Edge cases
parts.description: filter with no callback returns a TypeError. The callback is required, even for filter(Boolean) — pass Boolean as the value.

analogy.subject: filter compared to a sieve
analogy.comparison: filter is a sieve held over your data. The predicate is the mesh size. Items small enough to fall through stay in the receiving bowl; the rest are caught and discarded. The original pile is unchanged.

example.title: Example 1: Even numbers only
example.code:
const evens = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].filter(n => n % 2 === 0);
console.log(evens);
example.explanation: Predicate returns true for even numbers. Output: [2, 4, 6].

example.title: Example 2: Adults from a user list
example.explanation: Keep only objects whose age is at least 18. Output is an array of two user objects.

example.title: Example 3: filter(Boolean) idiom
example.code:
const cleaned = [0, 1, '', 'a', null, NaN, false, 'b'].filter(Boolean);
console.log(cleaned);
example.explanation: Boolean is the predicate. It coerces each value to a boolean. Output: [1, 'a', 'b'].

example.title: Example 4: Filter then map
example.explanation: Two steps: keep adults, then extract names. Output: ['Ada', 'Diego'].

example.title: Example 5: Filter with index
example.code:
const dropFirst = ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'].filter((_, i) => i !== 0);
console.log(dropFirst);
example.explanation: Use the second parameter to filter by index. Output: ['b', 'c', 'd'].

options: No — it returns a new array
quiz.explanation: filter is non-mutating, like map. The original array stays untouched.

quiz.explanation: find stops at the first element that satisfies the predicate. filter scans the whole array.

quiz.question: What is the callback signature for filter?

quiz.question: Which call removes only undefined entries?

Output length is <= input length. filter never grows the array.

lessons.title: Reducing with reduce
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Use reduce with an accumulator and initial value, (2) Build sums, products, and lookup objects, (3) Recognise when reduce is overkill.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on Array.prototype.reduce — the universal aggregator.
Why it matters: reduce compared to a snowball rolling downhill — knowing it unlocks turning many values into one.
Core terms you will use: `reduce`, `accumulator`, `initial value`, `reducer function`, `aggregation`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `arr.reduce((acc, x) => acc + x, 0)`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: Sum" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the missing-initial-value bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You can pick the right initial value for any reducer.

hooklines.text: reduce turns many values into one — sum, product, lookup, anything.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["[a,b,c,d]"] --> B["reducer"]
    B --> C["final value"]
```
image.alt: Reduce collapses an array to one value

hooklines.text: Always pass an initial value — it defines the starting state and the accumulator's type.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["reducer signature"] --> B["(acc, item) => newAcc"]
    C["initial value"] --> A
```

highlight.code: const sum = arr.reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0);

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: Signature
parts.description: arr.reduce(reducer, initial). reducer is (acc, current, index, array) => newAcc.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Initial value
parts.description: The starting accumulator. Pass 0 for sums, 1 for products, [] for arrays, {} for objects. Always pass it explicitly.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Accumulator threads through
parts.description: Each iteration: the reducer receives the running accumulator and the next element, and returns the NEW accumulator.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Final value
parts.description: After every element has been processed, reduce returns the final accumulator. That is your aggregate.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: No initial value
parts.description: If you skip the initial value, reduce uses arr[0] as the starting accumulator and iterates from arr[1]. On an empty array this throws TypeError. Avoid the surprise — always pass an initial.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Build lookup objects
parts.description: reduce can also produce an object: items.reduce((map, item) => ({ ...map, [item.id]: item }), {}). For large arrays prefer a mutating Object.assign for speed.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: reduceRight
parts.description: Same as reduce but iterates from right to left. Useful for composing functions or reversing a string.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: When reduce is overkill
parts.description: Pure sums or counts can be expressed with map + .length or for-of + variable. Reach for reduce when you genuinely need a custom accumulator shape.

analogy.subject: reduce compared to a snowball rolling downhill
analogy.comparison: Reduce starts with a small snowball (the initial value). Each element it passes adds to the snowball, making a new, bigger snowball that continues down the slope. By the bottom you have one giant snowball — the aggregate result.

example.title: Example 1: Sum
example.code:
const total = [1, 2, 3, 4].reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0);
console.log(total);

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How Redux state updates work
realWorldStory.storyText: Redux's core algorithm is one reducer function applied repeatedly: store.reduce((state, action) => reducer(state, action)). The accumulator is your entire app state; the array is every action ever dispatched. That single insight — reduce is just folding state — is what makes Redux time-travel debugging possible.

keyTakeaways: reduce aggregates an array into one value (number, object, anything).
Reducer signature: (accumulator, current) => newAccumulator. Always return the new accumulator.

lessons.title: Searching: find, findIndex, includes, indexOf
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Pick the right search method for primitives and objects, (2) Understand each method's return value, (3) Avoid the NaN-with-indexOf trap.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on the four most common array-search methods and when to reach for each.
Why it matters: Searching compared to looking up a contact — knowing each tool unlocks fast O(n) lookups.
Core terms you will use: `find`, `findIndex`, `includes`, `indexOf`, `lastIndexOf`, `predicate`, `NaN trap`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `users.find(u => u.id === 42)`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: indexOf on primitives" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the NaN-indexOf bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You pick find for objects and includes for primitives without thinking.

```mermaid
    B -- yes --> C["includes / indexOf"]
    B -- object --> D["find / findIndex with predicate"]
    A --> E{"Need position?"}
    E -- yes --> F["findIndex / indexOf"]
    E -- no --> G["find / includes"]
```


parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: indexOf
parts.description: Returns the position of a primitive value (using ===), or -1 if not found. Fast for strings and numbers; useless for object equality.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: includes
parts.description: Returns true/false for primitive membership. More readable than indexOf >= 0. Correctly handles NaN, unlike indexOf.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: find
parts.description: Takes a predicate. Returns the FIRST element where the predicate is truthy, or undefined.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: findIndex
parts.description: Same as find but returns the index of the first match, or -1 if not found.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: lastIndexOf
parts.description: Like indexOf but starts from the end. Returns the position of the LAST occurrence.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: findLast / findLastIndex
parts.description: ES2023 additions. Same predicate idea, but searching from the end.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: NaN trap
parts.description: indexOf uses === which says NaN !== NaN. So indexOf(NaN) always returns -1. Use includes(NaN), which works correctly.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Early exit benefits
parts.description: All four stop scanning at the first match (or first negative result). Faster than filter when you only need one.

analogy.subject: Searching compared to looking up a contact
analogy.comparison: indexOf is asking 'is the number stored under this exact value?' includes is asking 'do I have this number at all?'. find is more like asking 'whose name starts with M?' — it returns the whole person, not the slot number.

quiz.question: What does indexOf return if the value is not found?
quiz.explanation: indexOf returns -1 when the value is absent. Always check against -1 before using the result.

quiz.question: What does find return if no element matches?
quiz.explanation: find returns undefined when no element satisfies the predicate. Compare with === undefined or use optional chaining downstream.

quiz.question: Which is the cleanest way to test 'array contains value' for a primitive?
quiz.explanation: includes is the readable boolean. The others work but are less direct.

quiz.question: What does [1, NaN, 3].indexOf(NaN) return?
quiz.explanation: indexOf uses ===, and NaN !== NaN. So it returns -1. Use includes(NaN) instead, which handles NaN correctly.

quiz.question: Which method should you use to find an OBJECT by a property?
quiz.explanation: indexOf and includes do reference equality on objects, which usually fails. Use find with a predicate for property-based matching.

quiz.question: What does findIndex return when no match exists?
quiz.explanation: findIndex returns -1 — same convention as indexOf — when the predicate never matches.

quiz.question: Do find and findIndex short-circuit on the first match?
options: No, they always scan the full array
Yes, they return as soon as the predicate is truthy
quiz.explanation: Both stop scanning at the first truthy result. That makes them faster than filter when you only need one element.

quiz.question: What does lastIndexOf do differently from indexOf?
options: Searches from the end and returns the position of the LAST match
quiz.explanation: lastIndexOf walks the array right-to-left and returns the index of the last occurrence, or -1.

quiz.question: Which method was added in ES2023 for predicate-based reverse search?
quiz.explanation: findLast (and findLastIndex) are ES2023 additions that search from the end with a predicate.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Searching"?
quiz.explanation: Predicate-based search — using a function to define 'match' — is what distinguishes find/findIndex from indexOf/includes.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How VS Code resolves commands
realWorldStory.storyText: When you type into VS Code's command palette, the editor uses find to scan a registry of commands looking for the first id that matches your filter. Because find short-circuits, queries feel instant even with thousands of registered commands. The team rejected filter precisely because filter would scan every entry — wasted work when you only need one match.

keyTakeaways: indexOf and includes match primitives by ===. They short-circuit at the first match.
find and findIndex take a predicate function. Use them for objects or any criteria-based search.
All four short-circuit — much faster than filter when you only need one match.
indexOf cannot find NaN. includes can.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Using indexOf on object arrays — reference equality almost never matches.
💡 Pro Tip: When the same lookup happens many times, build a Map once instead of searching the array repeatedly.

lessons.title: Sorting and Reversing
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Sort with a compare function, (2) Recognise the default lexicographic-sort gotcha, (3) Use toSorted and toReversed for non-mutating versions.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on Array.prototype.sort, reverse, and their non-mutating counterparts.
Why it matters: Sorting compared to organising a shelf — knowing the compare function unlocks correct order.
Core terms you will use: `sort`, `reverse`, `compare function`, `stable sort`, `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `lexicographic`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `arr.sort((a, b) => a - b)`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: Default sort surprise" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the default-lexicographic-sort bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You always pass a compare function for numeric or custom sort.

hooklineimage.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["arr.sort()"] --> B["Lexicographic by default!"]
    A --> C["Mutates the array"]
    D["arr.sort((a,b) => a-b)"] --> E["Numeric ascending"]
    F["arr.toSorted()"] --> G["Returns NEW sorted array"]
```

hooklines.text: The default sort is LEXICOGRAPHIC — '10' comes before '2' as strings.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["[10, 2, 30].sort()"] --> B["[10, 2, 30]"]
    C["...interpreted as strings"] --> D["'10','2','30' alphabetical"]
```

hooklines.text: A compare function turns sort into a proper ordering — for numbers, dates, anything.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["(a, b) => a - b"] --> B["Ascending numeric"]
    C["(a, b) => b - a"] --> D["Descending numeric"]
```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: Default sort is lexicographic
parts.description: arr.sort() converts every element to a string and sorts alphabetically. [10, 2, 30].sort() yields [10, 2, 30] (interpreted as strings).

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Compare function shape
parts.description: (a, b) => negative means a comes first, positive means b first, 0 means equal. (a, b) => a - b is the textbook numeric ascending.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Descending
parts.description: (a, b) => b - a sorts numbers descending. The same idea applies to any custom order.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Sort by object property
parts.description: users.sort((a, b) => a.age - b.age) sorts by numeric property. Use localeCompare for strings: (a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name).

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: sort mutates
parts.description: Array.prototype.sort changes the original array in place AND returns it. To avoid mutation, copy first with [...arr] or use toSorted.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Stable sort
parts.description: Since ES2019, sort is stable — equal elements retain their original relative order. Useful when sorting by multiple keys with successive sorts.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: reverse
parts.description: Reverses the array in place. To get a reversed copy without mutating, use [...arr].reverse() or toReversed.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Modern non-mutating versions
parts.description: toSorted and toReversed (ES2023) return new arrays, leaving the original untouched. Prefer them in framework code.

analogy.subject: Sorting compared to a librarian organising a shelf
analogy.comparison: Default sort is a librarian who only reads letters — she sorts every book by spine label as if it were a word. To sort by year or weight, you must give her a comparison rule (the compare function). She rearranges the actual shelf (mutation). A photocopier (toSorted) lets you arrange a fresh copy without disturbing the original.

example.title: Example 1: Default sort surprise
example.code:
const nums = [10, 2, 30, 1];
console.log(nums.sort());
example.explanation: Outputs [1, 10, 2, 30] — lexicographic! '10' starts with '1', so it comes before '2'.

example.title: Example 2: Numeric ascending
example.code:
const nums = [10, 2, 30, 1];
console.log(nums.sort((a, b) => a - b));
example.explanation: With a compare function, sort is numeric. Output: [1, 2, 10, 30].

example.title: Example 3: Sort objects by property
example.explanation: Sorts users by age ascending. Output: ['Mei', 'Diego', 'Ada'].

example.title: Example 4: Strings with localeCompare
example.explanation: localeCompare gives proper case-insensitive ordering with locale awareness. Output: ['Apple', 'banana', 'cherry'].

example.title: Example 5: Non-mutating with toSorted
example.explanation: nums is unchanged; sorted is [1, 2, 3]. Use toSorted in framework code to avoid mutating state.

flowchart.code:
flowchart TD
    A["Need to sort"] --> B{"Numbers or objects?"}
    B -- yes --> C["Provide compare function (a,b) => a-b"]
    B -- strings --> D["localeCompare for locale-aware"]
    A --> E{"Mutate original?"}
    E -- yes --> F["sort / reverse"]
    E -- no --> G["toSorted / toReversed (ES2023)"]

quiz.question: What does arr.sort() do by default?
quiz.explanation: Without a compare function, sort coerces elements to strings and sorts lexicographically. This is why [10, 2] becomes [10, 2] (as strings).

quiz.question: Which compare function sorts numbers ASCENDING?
quiz.explanation: (a, b) => a - b: negative means a comes first. The result is ascending numeric order.

quiz.question: Does sort mutate the array?
options: No, it returns a new array
Yes, it sorts in place and also returns the array
Only when a compare function is provided
quiz.explanation: sort mutates. To preserve the original, copy first with [...arr] or use toSorted.

quiz.question: What does (a, b) => b - a produce for numbers?
quiz.explanation: Reversing the operands flips the order. Positive when a > b, so a sorts AFTER b — descending.

quiz.question: What is a 'stable' sort?
options: A sort that does not throw
Equal elements keep their original relative order
A sort that runs in O(n log n)
A sort that returns a new array
quiz.explanation: Stable means ties are preserved. Since ES2019, Array.prototype.sort is required to be stable.

quiz.question: Which is the non-mutating version of sort?
quiz.explanation: toSorted (ES2023) returns a new sorted array, leaving the original untouched. [...arr].sort() also works.

quiz.question: Which is the right way to sort strings case-insensitively in a locale-aware way?
quiz.explanation: localeCompare with the sensitivity option handles case, diacritics, and locale-specific rules correctly.

quiz.question: What does arr.reverse() do?
options: Mutates the array in place and returns it reversed
quiz.explanation: reverse mutates the array. For an immutable copy, use [...arr].reverse() or toReversed.

quiz.question: Why must the compare function return a NUMBER, not a boolean?
options: It is a personal style choice
sort relies on the sign of the number to order elements; booleans coerce to 0 or 1, giving wrong order
Boolean returns trigger a deprecation warning
quiz.explanation: sort uses negative/positive/zero to order. Returning a > b (a boolean) collapses to 0 or 1 and produces incorrect sorts.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Sorting and Reversing"?
quiz.explanation: The compare function is what makes sort actually work for non-string data.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How TC39 made sort stable everywhere
realWorldStory.storyText: For years, Array.prototype.sort could be stable or unstable depending on the engine. V8 (Chrome) used an unstable QuickSort below a length threshold, while Firefox's SpiderMonkey was stable. TC39 standardised stability in ES2019, and engines converged. The takeaway: when sorting by multiple keys with successive sorts, you can now rely on the second sort preserving the order from the first.

keyTakeaways: Default sort is LEXICOGRAPHIC — always pass a compare function for non-string data.
Compare function returns a number: negative (a first), positive (b first), zero (equal).
sort and reverse MUTATE the array. Use toSorted / toReversed / [...arr].sort() for non-mutating copies.
Stable sort means equal elements retain their original order — relied on for multi-key sorts.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Calling arr.sort() on numbers and getting alphabetical order. Pass (a, b) => a - b.
💡 Pro Tip: In React / Redux code, default to toSorted to avoid sneaky state mutations.

modules.title: Objects
modules.description: Master JavaScript's universal key-value structure: define properties and methods, destructure and spread cleanly, and reach for safe optional chaining when paths can be missing.

points: This module covers Objects across 8 focused lessons, building from literal properties to spread, destructuring, optional chaining, and JSON.
You will start with object basics — the foundation every later lesson quietly relies on.

By the end you will be comfortable with the vocabulary used everywhere in JavaScript: `property`, `method`, `bracket notation`, `destructuring`, `spread`, `optional chaining`, `Object.entries`, `JSON`.
The lessons progress as: 1) Basics; 2) Dot vs Bracket; 3) Destructuring; 4) Spread; 5) Optional Chaining + ??; 6) Iteration; 7) Object.assign / freeze; 8) JSON. Each builds on the last.
Methods you will meet here: `Object.keys`, `Object.values`, `Object.entries`, `Object.assign`, `Object.freeze`, `JSON.stringify`, `JSON.parse`.
Each lesson exposes one realistic beginner trap (e.g. "const obj is not frozen — properties can still mutate") and shows the fix.
Every lesson ships with a live "Try it" exercise, a graded mini challenge, drag-and-drop sorting, card-matching pairs, and a bug-hunt fix-it task.
After completing the final lesson on "JSON", you will have a working mental model for objects that drives every API integration in JavaScript.

lessons.title: Object Basics: Properties and Methods
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Create objects with the literal syntax, (2) Read, add, update, and delete properties, (3) Define methods using shorthand syntax.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on plain objects — keys, values, methods.
Why it matters: Objects compared to filing cabinets — knowing the basics unlocks every API payload and form.
Core terms you will use: `object literal`, `property`, `method`, `key`, `value`, `delete operator`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `const user = { name: 'Ada', greet() {} };`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: A simple object" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the const-doesn't-freeze bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You know that const locks the binding, not the object contents.

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: Object literal
parts.description: Curly braces with comma-separated key: value pairs. The everyday way to create an object.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Reading a property
parts.description: obj.name (dot) and obj['name'] (bracket). Both read the same property; bracket lets you use dynamic keys.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Adding / updating
parts.description: obj.age = 30 adds or updates the age property. JavaScript objects are dynamic — you can add properties any time.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: delete
parts.description: delete obj.age removes the property entirely. Subsequent reads return undefined.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Method shorthand
parts.description: { greet() { ... } } is shorthand for { greet: function () { ... } }. Cleaner and idiomatic.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Shorthand property
parts.description: { name } is shorthand for { name: name } when the key and variable name match. Removes repetition.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Computed keys
parts.description: { [keyVar]: value } evaluates keyVar at runtime. Useful for dynamic property names.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Keys are strings
parts.description: All non-symbol keys become strings under the hood. { 1: 'a' } stores key '1', not the number 1.

analogy.subject: Objects compared to filing cabinets
analogy.comparison: An object is a filing cabinet of labelled folders. Each folder (property) holds one document (value). You can add, update, or remove folders at any time. Some folders hold pictures of doable actions (methods).

quiz.question: Which syntax creates an object literal?
quiz.explanation: Object literals use curly braces around comma-separated key: value pairs.

quiz.question: What does obj.missing return when missing is not a property?
quiz.explanation: Reading a non-existent property returns undefined — no error is thrown.

quiz.question: Which operator removes a property?
quiz.explanation: delete obj.key removes the property entirely from the object.

quiz.question: What does { greet() {} } expand to in long form?
options: Both arrow and regular function are valid expansions
quiz.explanation: Method shorthand expands to a regular function expression. Arrows would lose their own this — important difference.

quiz.question: What does { name } evaluate to if a variable name holds 'Ada'?
quiz.explanation: Shorthand property: { name } means { name: name }. The variable's value becomes the property value.

quiz.question: Are object keys stored as strings or other types?
options: All non-symbol keys are coerced to strings
quiz.explanation: Non-symbol keys become strings. { 1: 'a' } stores key '1'. Symbols are an exception.

quiz.question: Does const prevent mutating object properties?
options: Yes — const locks the entire object
No — const locks the binding; the object contents are still mutable
quiz.explanation: const stops reassignment of the variable. Adding, updating, deleting properties on the object remains legal.

quiz.question: What is this inside a method?
options: The object the method was called on
quiz.explanation: For method calls obj.method(), this refers to obj. Arrow functions inherit this lexically — different behaviour.

quiz.question: How do you set a property with a dynamic key?
quiz.explanation: Bracket notation evaluates the expression and uses the result as the key. obj[expr] is the standard form.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Object Basics"?
quiz.explanation: Property — a named slot in an object — is the foundational concept this lesson introduces.

useCaseCards.useCase: Builds response bodies as plain objects so the JSON serialiser can convert them with one call to JSON.stringify.
Stores environment-specific settings as a single config object with method shorthand for derived values.
Models form state as one object so the whole form can be reset by replacing the binding in a single assignment.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: Why JSON took over the API world
realWorldStory.storyText: When Douglas Crockford specified JSON in 2001, he chose object literal syntax for one reason: every JavaScript developer already knew it. Within five years, REST APIs replaced XML payloads with JSON, and 'I built an object and stringified it' became the de-facto contract for inter-service communication. Object literals are the lingua franca of the modern web.

keyTakeaways: Object literals are curly-braced collections of key: value pairs. Keys are strings (or symbols); values can be anything.
Access properties with obj.key (dot) or obj[expr] (bracket for dynamic keys).
Add or update by assignment; remove with the delete operator. Reading a missing property returns undefined.
Method shorthand { greet() {} } and shorthand properties { name } make object literals concise.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Assuming const freezes the object — it locks the binding only. Use Object.freeze for real immutability.
💡 Pro Tip: Reach for shorthand whenever variable names match keys — fewer typos and cleaner diffs.

lessons.title: Dot vs Bracket Notation
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Choose between dot and bracket access, (2) Use bracket notation for keys with spaces, hyphens, or dynamic names, (3) Read computed keys at object creation time.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on the two ways to read and write object properties.
Why it matters: Dot vs bracket compared to a fixed-key vs combination lock — knowing both unlocks dynamic access.
Core terms you will use: `dot notation`, `bracket notation`, `dynamic key`, `valid identifier`, `computed key`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `obj[keyVar]`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: Dot when key is fixed" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the dot-on-special-keys bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You reach for brackets the moment the key is in a variable or contains anything beyond letters, digits, $ and _.

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: Dot notation
parts.description: obj.key — the key is hard-coded and must be a valid identifier (letters, digits, $, _, no leading digit).

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Bracket notation
parts.description: obj['key'] — the value inside [] is any expression that evaluates to a string. The string becomes the key.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Keys with special characters
parts.description: Any key containing spaces, hyphens, or punctuation must use brackets: obj['user-id'], obj['first name'].

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Dynamic keys
parts.description: When the key lives in a variable, use brackets: obj[keyVar]. Dot interprets keyVar as a LITERAL property called 'keyVar'.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Computed properties
parts.description: { [keyVar]: value } during creation. Same idea — the expression computes the key.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Chained access
parts.description: obj.user.profile.name reads down a chain. Each segment can be dot or bracket independently.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Numeric keys
parts.description: Numbers as keys must use brackets (or strings): obj[1] or obj['1']. They are stored as strings under the hood.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Methods are properties
parts.description: obj.greet() and obj['greet']() both invoke the same method. Brackets are useful when the method name is dynamic.

analogy.subject: Dot vs bracket compared to fixed-label vs combination locks
analogy.comparison: Dot notation is a pre-labeled drawer: you read the label and use the matching key. Bracket notation is a combination lock — you can spin the dial to any combination at runtime, including ones the label-maker forgot.

quiz.question: Which is valid? obj.user-id
options: Yes — it reads the user-id property
No — JavaScript parses it as obj.user minus id
quiz.explanation: The hyphen is a subtraction operator in this context. Use brackets: obj['user-id'].

quiz.question: What does obj[key] do when key is the string 'name'?
options: Reads the property whose name is the value of key — i.e. 'name'
quiz.explanation: Brackets evaluate the expression. key holds 'name', so the lookup is for property 'name'.

quiz.question: Which is the correct shape of a computed key in an object literal?
quiz.explanation: Wrap the expression in [] to compute the key at object-creation time.

quiz.question: Can dot notation read a key called '1'?
options: No — leading digits are invalid identifiers
Only if the property is a function
quiz.explanation: Identifiers cannot start with a digit. Use obj[1] or obj['1'].

quiz.question: Are object keys case-sensitive?
quiz.explanation: JavaScript object keys are case-sensitive. Treat 'Name' and 'name' as distinct.

quiz.question: What does obj['greet']() do?
options: Reads a property whose value is the string 'greet'
Invokes the method whose key is 'greet'
quiz.explanation: Brackets resolve the property; the trailing () invokes it. Equivalent to obj.greet().

quiz.question: Which access works for the key 'first name'?
quiz.explanation: Keys with spaces require brackets and quotes around the string.

quiz.question: Which is BEST when the key comes from user input?
quiz.explanation: Brackets evaluate the expression at runtime. eval is dangerous and unnecessary.

quiz.question: Inside an object literal, what does { [a + b]: 'hi' } do?
options: Computes the key by evaluating a + b at runtime
quiz.explanation: Brackets in literals are computed-property syntax. The expression is evaluated and the result becomes the key.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Dot vs Bracket"?
quiz.explanation: Dynamic key access via brackets is the central new capability covered.

bugHunt.instruction: A developer tries dot access on a hyphenated key. Fix it.

const config = { 'api-key': 'abc' };

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How i18n libraries route translations
realWorldStory.storyText: Every i18n library — from i18next to FormatJS — relies on bracket access to fetch translations: messages[locale][key]. The locale is unknown at build time, the key is often dynamic, and both can contain dots themselves. Bracket notation is what makes runtime locale switching possible without code generation.

keyTakeaways: Dot access works only when the key is a hard-coded valid identifier.
Bracket access takes any string expression — variables, computed values, keys with hyphens or spaces.
{ [expr]: value } is the computed-property syntax inside an object literal.
All non-symbol keys are stored as strings, so obj[1] and obj['1'] access the same slot.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Writing obj.user-id and getting NaN because JavaScript parses it as subtraction.
💡 Pro Tip: Whenever a key is dynamic OR contains a non-identifier character, brackets are the answer.

lessons.title: Object Destructuring
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Destructure values out of an object, (2) Rename, default, and nest destructuring patterns, (3) Use destructuring in function parameters.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on object destructuring — extracting multiple values in one statement.
Why it matters: Destructuring compared to unpacking a parcel — knowing it unlocks compact data extraction.
Core terms you will use: `destructuring`, `rename`, `default value`, `nested destructuring`, `parameter destructuring`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `const { name, age = 0 } = user;`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: Basic extraction" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the undefined-default trap shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You destructure function parameters by default for option-bag APIs.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["{ name: 'Ada', age: 30 }"] --> B["const { name, age } = ..."]
    B --> C["name = 'Ada'"]
    B --> D["age = 30"]
```

hooklines.text: Destructuring lets you name many variables in one assignment.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["const user = { name, age, country }"] --> B["const { name, country } = user"]
```

hooklines.text: Rename, default, and nest — all in the same pattern.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["const { name: n, age = 0 } = user"] --> B["n = name"]
    A --> C["age = 0 if missing"]
```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: Basic extraction
parts.description: const { a, b } = obj; pulls out two properties into variables of the same name.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Rename
parts.description: const { a: alpha } = obj; pulls out a but binds it to the variable alpha.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Default values
parts.description: const { a = 1 } = obj; uses 1 when obj.a is undefined. Does NOT trigger for null or 0.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Combining rename + default
parts.description: const { a: alpha = 1 } = obj; alpha is the variable; 1 is its default when obj.a is undefined.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Nested destructuring
parts.description: const { user: { name } } = data; reaches into a nested object directly. Watch for missing intermediate objects.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Rest in destructuring
parts.description: const { a, ...rest } = obj; takes a, then collects everything else into rest as a new object.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Parameter destructuring
parts.description: function f({ a, b = 0 }) {} declares the function signature with destructuring. Caller passes one object; you bind named fields.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Defaults trigger only on undefined
parts.description: { a = 5 } gives a=5 ONLY when obj.a is undefined. null, 0, '' are kept as-is.

analogy.subject: Destructuring compared to unpacking a labeled parcel
analogy.comparison: Imagine unpacking a parcel where every item is labeled. Destructuring lets you place each labeled item onto its own shelf in one motion. Default values are the spare item you keep handy if something is missing; renames are sticker labels you slap on top.

example.title: Example 2: Rename and default

example.title: Example 4: Rest collects the leftover
example.explanation: host is extracted; rest is a new object with the rest. Output: 'localhost' and { port: 3000, debug: true }.

example.title: Example 5: Function parameter destructuring
example.explanation: Caller passes an object; the function pulls fields directly. Default supports the missing-last case. Output: 'Ada' and 'Mei Tanaka'.

quiz.question: What does const { a, b } = obj do?
options: Creates a new object with a and b
Creates two variables a and b from obj's properties
quiz.explanation: Object destructuring binds new variables with the same names as the keys being extracted.

quiz.question: What does const { a: x } = { a: 1 } produce?
options: Both a and x are bound to 1
quiz.explanation: Rename syntax: { a: x } means 'pull out a, bind it to the variable x'.

quiz.question: Defaults apply when the source value is...
quiz.explanation: Destructuring defaults trigger only for undefined. null, 0, '', false are preserved.

quiz.question: What does const { x: { y } } = obj require?
quiz.explanation: Nested destructuring assumes obj.x is an object. If obj.x is undefined, you get TypeError trying to destructure undefined.

quiz.question: What does const { a, ...rest } = { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 } yield?
quiz.explanation: Rest in object destructuring gathers remaining own enumerable properties into a NEW object.

quiz.question: How do you destructure in a function parameter?
quiz.explanation: Wrap the parameter list in curly braces — the caller passes an object and the function binds named fields.

quiz.question: What does this print? const { x = 5 } = { x: null }; console.log(x);
quiz.explanation: null is NOT undefined. The default does not apply; x is null.

quiz.question: Can you destructure from a function's return value?
options: No, only literals can be destructured
Only if the function is arrow
quiz.explanation: Any object expression on the right side can be destructured — including function return values.

quiz.question: Which is the cleanest way to grab id and name from response.data?
options: const id = response.data.id; const name = response.data.name;
Both 2 and 3 work; 3 is cleaner when response.data is what you want to dive into
quiz.explanation: Both options 2 and 3 are idiomatic. Option 3 dives one level deeper in a single statement.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Object Destructuring"?
quiz.explanation: Rename and default — the syntactic features that make destructuring powerful — are this lesson's key new tools.

// 5. The two new bindings are created in scope
// 3. The property a is read from obj
// 6. Execution continues with a and b available
// 2. The property b is read from obj (or undefined)
