realWorldStory.storyTitle: How React popularised props destructuring
realWorldStory.storyText: Pre-2016 React components received a single `props` argument and developers read `props.user`, `props.onSubmit`, and so on. Once destructuring landed in stable JavaScript, the community shifted to `({ user, onSubmit }) => …` almost overnight. Anyone reading a function now sees the contract in one glance — which is why it has become the default style guide rule.

keyTakeaways: Destructuring creates multiple bindings from one assignment: const { a, b } = obj.
Rename with { a: alpha }, default with { a = 1 }, and combine both with { a: alpha = 1 }.
Defaults trigger ONLY on undefined — null, 0, '', false are preserved.
Parameter destructuring is the modern way to accept options objects in a function.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Destructuring deep into a property that might be undefined — you get TypeError. Use optional chaining or guard upstream.
💡 Pro Tip: Whenever a function takes 3+ options, destructure with defaults in the parameter list — the signature becomes self-documenting.

lessons.title: The Spread Operator with Objects
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Clone an object with spread, (2) Merge two or more objects, (3) Override individual fields while keeping the rest.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on the ... spread operator applied to objects.
Why it matters: Spread compared to a photocopier — knowing it unlocks immutable updates.
Core terms you will use: `spread`, `shallow clone`, `merge`, `override`, `non-mutating update`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `const copy = { ...obj };`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: Shallow clone" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the shallow-clone bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You can update one field of an object without mutating the original.

hooklineimage.alt: Spread copies properties and lets you add more

hooklines.text: Spread is the cleanest way to update one field without touching the others.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["user"] --> B["{ ...user, age: 31 }"]
    B --> C["new object with age=31"]
```

hooklines.text: Later properties win — useful for defaults + overrides.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["{ ...defaults, ...overrides }"] --> B["overrides take precedence"]
```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: Shallow clone
parts.description: { ...obj } copies every own enumerable property of obj into a new object. Nested objects are NOT cloned — they are shared by reference.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Merge
parts.description: { ...a, ...b } combines a and b. Where keys overlap, the later spread wins.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Override one field
parts.description: { ...user, age: 31 } produces a new object with all of user's fields, but age replaced. Original user is untouched.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Defaults + overrides
parts.description: { ...defaults, ...userOptions } applies defaults first, then user options. User can override any default.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Add a computed key
parts.description: { ...obj, [keyVar]: value } combines spread with computed properties for dynamic updates.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Spread vs Object.assign
parts.description: { ...a, ...b } and Object.assign({}, a, b) do the same thing. Spread reads more naturally; assign mutates its first argument if you forget the empty object.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Spread is shallow
parts.description: Nested objects and arrays are still shared. Use structuredClone or a deep-clone helper when you need a truly independent copy.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Use in framework state updates
parts.description: React/Redux state must be replaced, not mutated. Spread is the canonical immutable-update idiom.

analogy.subject: Spread compared to a photocopier
analogy.comparison: Spread is a photocopier: it makes a copy of every page in your folder. If a page references another folder somewhere else (a nested object), the copy still points to that same original folder. The copy is independent for top-level pages only.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: Why React state updates use spread
realWorldStory.storyText: React's setState contract requires returning a NEW object so React's diff algorithm can detect the change in O(1). Spread became the canonical idiom for this exact reason: setState(prev => ({ ...prev, count: prev.count + 1 })) is short, clear, and immutable. Without spread, React state code would be twice as long.

keyTakeaways: Object spread { ...obj } copies every own enumerable property into a new object — a SHALLOW clone.
Later spreads win: { ...a, ...b } produces a merged object where b's values override a's.
Override one field with { ...obj, key: newValue } — the canonical immutable-update idiom.
Nested objects and arrays remain shared by reference. Use structuredClone for deep copies.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Mutating a nested value on a 'cloned' object and being surprised the original changed too.
💡 Pro Tip: In framework code, always reach for spread (or toSorted, toReversed, etc.) instead of mutating methods.

lessons.title: Optional Chaining and Nullish Coalescing
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Use ?. to safely access deep properties, (2) Apply ?? for value-preserving defaults, (3) Combine both for robust data access.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on ?. (optional chaining) and ?? (nullish coalescing).
Why it matters: ?. compared to a parachute mid-air — knowing it unlocks safe traversal through unreliable data.
Core terms you will use: `optional chaining`, `nullish coalescing`, `short-circuit`, `safe access`, `method call`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `user?.profile?.email ?? 'unknown'`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: Safe property access" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the over-chaining bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You combine ?. and ?? to express 'safe path with fallback' in one expression.

hooklineimage.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["user?.profile?.email"] --> B{"user is nullish?"}
    B -- yes --> C["undefined"]
    B -- no --> D{"profile is nullish?"}
    D -- yes --> C
    D -- no --> E["email"]
```
hooklineimage.alt: Short-circuit on first nullish in the chain

hooklines.text: ?. stops the moment it sees null or undefined — no TypeError, no nested if checks.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["user?.address"] --> B["undefined if user is null"]
    A --> C["address otherwise"]
```

hooklines.text: ?? supplies a fallback only for null and undefined — keeping 0, '' and false intact.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["value ?? 'default'"] --> B{"value nullish?"}
    B -- yes --> C["'default'"]
    B -- no --> D["value"]
```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: ?. (property)
parts.description: user?.profile reads profile if user is non-nullish; otherwise short-circuits to undefined.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: ?. (method call)
parts.description: user.greet?.() calls greet only if it exists. No TypeError if greet is undefined.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: ?.[] (dynamic key)
parts.description: config?.[envKey] reads a dynamic key safely. Brackets after the ?. token.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Chains short-circuit
parts.description: user?.profile?.email — the first nullish stops evaluation and the whole expression is undefined.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: ?? (nullish coalescing)
parts.description: Returns the left side unless it is null or undefined; then returns the right side. Preserves 0, '', false.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.description: Combined: user?.profile?.email ?? 'no email' — safe traversal AND a fallback in one line.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Not for assignment
parts.description: You cannot write user?.foo = 1. Optional chaining is read-only.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: vs ||
parts.description: || falls back on every falsy value (0, '', false). ?? falls back only on null/undefined. Prefer ?? for value-preserving defaults.

analogy.subject: Optional chaining compared to a parachute
analogy.comparison: Climbing a tower (property chain) without a parachute means any wobble (nullish value) throws you off the side (TypeError). ?. is the parachute — the moment you hit air (null/undefined), you float to safety (undefined) instead of crashing.

example.explanation: cfg.fr is undefined; the chain stops there. Output: undefined.

example.explanation: 0 is preserved (only null/undefined trigger ??). Output: 0, 8080, 8080.

console.log(user?.profile?.name ?? 'anonymous');
example.explanation: Safe traversal, then fallback only if the value is null/undefined. The empty string is NOT replaced. Output: ''.

options: ?? distinguishes 'no value' from 'falsy value', avoiding silent overrides of 0/''/false
quiz.explanation: ?? gives you precise semantics: fall back only when the value is literally null or undefined.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Optional Chaining and Nullish Coalescing"?

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How Next.js handles partial data
realWorldStory.storyText: Next.js's server-rendered pages frequently receive partial data — a missing user, a flag not set yet. The codebase uses ?. throughout to traverse deep paths, paired with ?? for sensible defaults. Without these two operators, the framework would need dozens of nested if checks per page render — code that nobody enjoys writing.

keyTakeaways: ?. short-circuits the moment it sees null or undefined and yields undefined.
?.() is safe method invocation; ?.[] is safe dynamic key access.
?? falls back only for null and undefined — preserving 0, '', and false.
Combine ?. and ?? to express 'safe traversal with fallback' in a single line.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Using || when 0/''/false are legal values — they get replaced silently.
💡 Pro Tip: When reading from an API response, lean on ?. everywhere. Server contracts evolve faster than your assumptions.

lessons.title: Iterating Objects: keys, values, entries
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Iterate own keys with Object.keys, (2) Iterate values with Object.values, (3) Iterate pairs with Object.entries for the cleanest object loops.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on the three Object methods that turn objects into iterable arrays.
Why it matters: Object iteration compared to indexing a card catalog — knowing the right tool unlocks clean lookups.
Core terms you will use: `Object.keys`, `Object.values`, `Object.entries`, `Object.fromEntries`, `own enumerable`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(obj))`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: Object.keys" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the for-in-vs-keys bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You reach for Object.entries + for-of as the default object loop.

hooklineimage.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["{ a: 1, b: 2 }"] --> B["Object.keys -> ['a','b']"]
    A --> C["Object.values -> [1, 2]"]
    A --> D["Object.entries -> [['a',1],['b',2]]"]
```

hooklines.text: Object.keys/values/entries are how you bridge from objects to array methods.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["object"] --> B["Object.entries"]
    B --> C["[[k,v],[k,v]]"]
    C --> D["map/filter/reduce"]
```

hooklines.text: Object.fromEntries reverses the transformation — array back to object.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["[['a',1],['b',2]]"] --> B["Object.fromEntries"]
    B --> C["{ a: 1, b: 2 }"]
```
image.alt: Array of pairs back to object

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: Object.keys
parts.description: Returns an array of own enumerable string keys. No inherited keys, no symbols.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Object.values
parts.description: Returns an array of own enumerable values, in the same order as Object.keys.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Object.entries
parts.description: Returns an array of [key, value] pairs. Perfect for for-of with destructuring.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: for-of + entries
parts.description: The canonical object loop: for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(obj)) { ... }. No inherited surprises.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Object.fromEntries
parts.description: Reverses the transformation. Given an array of [k, v] pairs (or a Map), build a new object.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Key order
parts.description: Integer-like keys come first in ascending order; string keys follow in insertion order; symbol keys last.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: vs for-in
parts.description: for-in walks the prototype chain. Object.keys does not. Prefer Object.keys for safety.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Round-trip with array methods
parts.description: Object.entries -> filter/map -> Object.fromEntries is a common one-liner for transforming objects.

analogy.subject: Object iteration compared to indexing a card catalog
analogy.comparison: Object.keys is asking 'just the call numbers'. Object.values is asking 'just the books'. Object.entries is asking 'each card with its call number AND book'. Once you have a list, you can sort, search, and transform with array tools.

quiz.question: Which is the cleanest way to iterate an object's key-value pairs?
quiz.explanation: Object.entries + for-of with destructuring is the canonical, safe form.

quiz.explanation: Object.keys returns OWN enumerable keys only. Inherited keys are excluded — safer than for-in.

quiz.question: What does Object.fromEntries do?

options: Object.keys returns own keys; for-in walks the prototype chain too
quiz.explanation: for-in can yield inherited keys, which is rarely what you want. Object.keys is the safer default.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Iterating Objects"?
quiz.explanation: Round-tripping objects via Object.entries / fromEntries is the most powerful new pattern introduced.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How URLSearchParams replaced manual loops
realWorldStory.storyText: Browsers added URLSearchParams precisely because every developer was writing the same Object.entries -> map -> join code by hand. Today, the canonical pattern is `new URLSearchParams(params).toString()` — but it works because URLSearchParams internally uses the same key-value iteration model that Object.entries exposes.

keyTakeaways: Object.keys, Object.values, and Object.entries are the bridges from objects to array methods.
for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(obj)) is the canonical object loop.
Object.fromEntries reverses the transformation — array back to object.
Prefer Object.keys over for-in: for-in walks the prototype chain and can yield inherited keys.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Iterating with for-in on objects with prototype chains and seeing unexpected inherited keys.
💡 Pro Tip: entries -> filter -> fromEntries is a one-liner for filtering object properties — keep it in your toolkit.

lessons.title: Object Methods: Object.assign and Object.freeze
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Merge objects with Object.assign, (2) Lock an object's properties with Object.freeze, (3) Recognise that freeze is shallow.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on Object.assign for merging and Object.freeze for immutability.
Why it matters: assign compared to a stamp, freeze compared to a lockbox — knowing both unlocks safe object handling.
Core terms you will use: `Object.assign`, `Object.freeze`, `Object.isFrozen`, `mutable target`, `shallow freeze`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `Object.assign(target, ...sources)`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: Object.assign basic" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the mutating-target bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You always pass {} as the first arg to Object.assign when you want a new object.

```mermaid
    B --> C["then src2 props"]
    C --> D["returns target"]
```

hooklines.text: Object.assign mutates the first argument — pass an empty {} to be safe.

```mermaid
flowchart LR

    C["Object.assign(a, b)"] --> D["a mutated"]
```
image.alt: Empty target gives a fresh object


parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: Object.assign signature
parts.description: Object.assign(target, source1, source2, ...) copies each source's own enumerable properties onto target and returns target.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Mutates the target
parts.description: The first argument is mutated in place. To avoid mutation, pass {} as the target.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Later sources win
parts.description: When sources have overlapping keys, the later one wins — same semantics as object spread.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: vs spread
parts.description: { ...a, ...b } and Object.assign({}, a, b) do the same thing. Spread is more idiomatic in modern code.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Object.freeze
parts.description: Object.freeze(obj) prevents adding, removing, or changing properties. Attempts silently fail in non-strict mode; throw in strict mode.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Shallow freeze
parts.description: Freeze locks the object's own properties only. Nested objects are still mutable — write a recursive helper for deep freeze.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Object.isFrozen
parts.description: Returns true if the object has been frozen. Useful for assertions in defensive code.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Object.seal
parts.description: Like freeze but properties can still be updated — only adding/removing is prevented. Less common.

analogy.subject: assign compared to a stamp, freeze compared to a lockbox
analogy.comparison: Object.assign is a rubber stamp: you press source properties onto the target. Object.freeze is a lockbox — once closed, the surface drawers cannot open or change, but a small box stored inside the lockbox can still be edited.

example.title: Example 1: Object.assign basic
example.explanation: Empty {} target gives a fresh merged object. a is untouched. Output: { x:1, y:2 } and { x:1 }.

example.title: Example 2: assign MUTATES the target
example.explanation: Skipping the empty target mutates a. Output: { x: 1, y: 2 }. Use this intentionally or not at all.

example.title: Example 3: Object.freeze blocks changes
example.explanation: The assignment is silently ignored in non-strict mode. Output: 'localhost'.

example.title: Example 4: Freeze is shallow
example.explanation: Freeze locked data itself, but data.user is a separate object — mutable. Output: 'Mei'.

example.title: Example 5: Object.isFrozen check
example.explanation: isFrozen detects whether freeze has been applied. Output: false then true.

quiz.question: What does Object.assign(a, b) do?
options: Returns a new merged object without changing a
Copies b's own enumerable properties onto a and returns a
Throws if a and b share keys
quiz.explanation: Object.assign mutates the target (first argument) and returns it.

quiz.question: How do you get a NEW merged object instead of mutating?
quiz.explanation: Pass {} as the target so the merge writes into a brand-new object.

quiz.question: Is Object.freeze deep?
options: No — only the immediate properties; nested objects stay mutable
Only when called with deep: true
quiz.explanation: Object.freeze is SHALLOW. Nested objects need their own freeze call (or a recursive helper).

quiz.question: What happens when you assign to a frozen property in NON-strict mode?
options: Silently fails — property keeps its old value
Property is added with new value
quiz.explanation: In non-strict mode the write is ignored silently. Strict mode throws TypeError, which is safer.

quiz.question: What does Object.isFrozen return for a never-frozen object?
quiz.explanation: isFrozen returns true only after Object.freeze has been applied (or for objects that are inherently sealed).

quiz.question: Which is roughly equivalent to { ...a, ...b }?
quiz.explanation: Both produce a new object with later sources winning. Spread is the modern idiom; assign is the older one.

quiz.question: What does Object.seal do that Object.freeze does not?
options: Allows new properties but blocks reassignment
Prevents adding/removing properties but ALLOWS updating existing ones
quiz.explanation: Object.seal locks the shape (no add/remove) but values can still be updated. Less restrictive than freeze.

quiz.question: Why pass {} as the first arg of Object.assign?
options: To avoid mutating any of the actual sources
quiz.explanation: Without an empty target, Object.assign mutates the first source. {} creates a throw-away target so the originals stay clean.

quiz.question: What does Object.assign return?
quiz.explanation: Return value IS the mutated target. Chaining is possible because of this.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Object.assign and Object.freeze"?
quiz.explanation: Shallow freeze — that freeze only locks the immediate properties — is the most surprising part of the lesson.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How Lodash's merge was eclipsed by spread
realWorldStory.storyText: For years, every JavaScript codebase pulled in Lodash for _.merge and _.assign. Once ES2015 shipped Object.assign and ES2018 added object spread, those imports vanished. The takeaway: the language now does in two characters (...) what a library used to do in 1 KB of code. Spread didn't kill Lodash — it just made one whole module obsolete.

keyTakeaways: Object.assign(target, ...sources) copies properties into target and returns it. Later sources override earlier ones.
Always pass {} as the first arg if you want a fresh object — otherwise the target is mutated.
Object.freeze blocks property changes at the top level. Nested objects remain mutable.
Object.isFrozen tells you whether an object has been frozen. Object.seal is a softer lock.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Forgetting the empty target on Object.assign and mutating the source by accident.
💡 Pro Tip: In strict mode, attempting to mutate a frozen object throws — flip strict mode on so bugs surface immediately.

lessons.title: JSON: Parsing and Stringifying
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Convert objects to JSON strings with JSON.stringify, (2) Parse JSON strings back into objects with JSON.parse, (3) Recognise the values JSON cannot represent.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on the JSON object's parse and stringify methods.
Why it matters: JSON compared to a shipping container — knowing the format unlocks every API integration.
Core terms you will use: `JSON.stringify`, `JSON.parse`, `replacer`, `reviver`, `pretty-print`, `unsupported types`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `const text = JSON.stringify(obj, null, 2);`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: stringify" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the undefined-disappears bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You know which JS values JSON drops on the floor and how to handle them.

hooklineimage.alt: Round-trip between objects and JSON text

hooklines.text: JSON is the wire format of the web. JS objects translate to it directly.

highlight.code:
const text = JSON.stringify(obj, null, 2);
const obj = JSON.parse(text);

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: JSON.stringify
parts.description: Turns a JavaScript value into a JSON string. Supports strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays, plain objects.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: JSON.parse
parts.description: Reverses the operation. Returns a fresh JavaScript value built from the JSON text.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Pretty-printing
parts.description: JSON.stringify(obj, null, 2) indents with 2 spaces — perfect for human-readable output.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Replacer
parts.description: Second arg of stringify can be a function or array of keys, controlling which values appear and how they are transformed.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Reviver
parts.description: Second arg of parse can transform values as they are parsed — useful for hydrating Date instances or BigInts.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Unsupported values
parts.description: undefined, functions, and symbols are dropped from objects and become null inside arrays. NaN and Infinity become null.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Date is stringified to ISO
parts.description: JSON.stringify(new Date()) gives an ISO string. JSON.parse keeps it as a string — use a reviver to rebuild a Date.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Common pitfalls
parts.description: Circular references throw TypeError. BigInts throw TypeError. Use structuredClone or a custom replacer for those cases.

analogy.subject: JSON compared to shipping containers
analogy.comparison: JSON is the standardised shipping container of the web — every port can load and unload it. Most goods fit (strings, numbers, lists), but some items (live animals, exotic equipment — read: functions, undefined, symbols) cannot be sealed inside. They have to stay home.

example.title: Example 1: stringify

example.title: Example 2: pretty-print
example.code:
const user = { name: 'Ada', age: 30 };
console.log(JSON.stringify(user, null, 2));
example.explanation: The third arg controls indentation. Output is a multi-line, human-readable JSON document.

example.title: Example 3: parse
example.explanation: Parse rebuilds a fresh object from the string. Output: 'Ada'.

example.title: Example 4: undefined disappears
example.code:
const data = { a: 1, b: undefined, c: function () {}, d: null };
console.log(JSON.stringify(data));
example.explanation: undefined and functions are dropped. null is preserved. Output: '{"a":1,"d":null}'.

example.title: Example 5: Round-trip clone (with caveats)
example.explanation: Quick deep clone, but Date instances become strings — use a reviver or structuredClone for full fidelity.

useCaseCards.useCase: Serialises every response with JSON.stringify and parses every request body with JSON.parse — the bread and butter of every HTTP service.
Persists complex state to localStorage by stringifying on save and parsing on load — round-trip in two lines.
Reads JSON config files with JSON.parse for both static checks and runtime hot reloads.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How localStorage became JSON's sidekick
realWorldStory.storyText: When browsers added localStorage, it only stored strings. Every web app immediately wrote the same wrapper: stringify on save, parse on load. The pattern was so universal that the React docs included it in the tutorial. Today, every Redux Persist, every saved-game state, every offline cache relies on JSON.stringify being the lingua franca of browser persistence.

keyTakeaways: JSON.stringify turns an object into a JSON string; JSON.parse rebuilds an object from one.
Pretty-print with JSON.stringify(obj, null, 2) — perfect for logs and saved files.
undefined, functions, and symbols are silently dropped from objects (become null in arrays).
Dates become ISO strings; circular references throw; BigInts throw.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Expecting JSON to round-trip Date instances — they come back as strings unless you use a reviver.
💡 Pro Tip: For deep clones with Dates, Maps, Sets, or cycles, use structuredClone instead of JSON tricks.

modules.title: DOM Manipulation
modules.description: Make HTML respond to JavaScript: select elements, change text and attributes, style on the fly, and create or remove nodes — the toolkit behind every interactive page.

points: This module covers DOM Manipulation across 8 focused lessons, from selecting elements to creating and removing them at runtime.
You will start with selectors — the foundation every later lesson relies on.

By the end you will be comfortable with the vocabulary used everywhere in JavaScript: `querySelector`, `textContent`, `classList`, `style`, `createElement`, `appendChild`, `closest`, `DOMContentLoaded`.
The lessons progress as: 1) Selecting; 2) Content; 3) Attributes/Classes; 4) Styles; 5) Creating; 6) Removing; 7) Traversal; 8) DOMContentLoaded. Each builds on the last.
APIs you will meet here: `document.querySelector`, `getElementById`, `textContent`, `innerHTML`, `setAttribute`, `classList`, `style`, `createElement`, `append`, `remove`, `closest`.
Each lesson exposes one realistic beginner trap (e.g. "innerHTML enables XSS if interpolating user content") and shows the fix.
Every lesson ships with a live "Try it" exercise, a graded mini challenge, drag-and-drop sorting, card-matching pairs, and a bug-hunt fix-it task.
After completing the final lesson on "DOMContentLoaded", you will have a working mental model for the DOM that drives every interactive UI in vanilla JavaScript.

lessons.title: Selecting DOM Elements
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Use querySelector and querySelectorAll for CSS-style selection, (2) Use getElementById for fast id lookups, (3) Recognise the difference between NodeList and HTMLCollection.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on the modern selector APIs every DOM operation starts with.
Why it matters: Selection compared to finding a book in a library — knowing the catalog unlocks every later manipulation.
Core terms you will use: `querySelector`, `querySelectorAll`, `getElementById`, `NodeList`, `HTMLCollection`, `CSS selector`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `document.querySelector('.btn')`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: getElementById" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the live-vs-static-collection bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You reach for querySelector for any modern selection task.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Need an element"] --> B{"Have an id?"}
    B -- yes --> C["getElementById"]
    B -- no --> D["querySelector / querySelectorAll"]
```

hooklines.text: querySelector accepts any CSS selector — id, class, attribute, descendant, you name it.

```mermaid
    C["getElementsByClassName"] --> D["Live HTMLCollection (auto-updates)"]
```

highlight.code:
const btn = document.querySelector('.btn');
const all = document.querySelectorAll('li');

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: querySelector
parts.description: Returns the FIRST element matching the CSS selector, or null. Accepts any selector you would use in CSS.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: querySelectorAll
parts.description: Returns a NodeList of ALL matching elements. The collection is static — it does not update if the DOM changes later.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: getElementById
parts.description: Fastest way to fetch by id. Returns the element or null. Skip the '#' prefix — getElementById('header'), not '#header'.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Selector scoping
parts.description: Call querySelector on any element to scope the search: card.querySelector('.btn') only looks inside card.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Returns null
parts.description: querySelector returns null when nothing matches. Guard with ?. or an explicit if before reading properties.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Iterating NodeList
parts.description: NodeList supports for-of and forEach. Convert with Array.from(list) if you need full array methods.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Live HTMLCollection trap
parts.description: getElementsByClassName and getElementsByTagName return LIVE collections. Adding or removing matching elements changes the collection during iteration.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Prefer query* in modern code
parts.description: querySelector/All cover every case with one consistent API. The older getElementsBy* APIs survive mainly for legacy code.

analogy.subject: Selection compared to finding a book in a library
analogy.comparison: getElementById is the call-number lookup — single book, instant. querySelector is the catalog search by author or subject — one matching book. querySelectorAll is the same search returning every match.

example.title: Example 1: getElementById
example.code:
const header = document.getElementById('header');
console.log(header.textContent);
example.explanation: Fastest by-id lookup. Returns null if no element has that id.

example.title: Example 2: querySelector with class
example.code:
const firstBtn = document.querySelector('.btn-primary');
firstBtn.textContent = 'Click me';
example.explanation: First matching element. Use class, attribute, descendant — any CSS selector works.

example.title: Example 3: querySelectorAll and iteration
example.code:
const items = document.querySelectorAll('li.todo');
items.forEach(it => console.log(it.textContent));
example.explanation: NodeList supports forEach directly. Walk every match without converting.

example.title: Example 4: Scoped selection
example.explanation: Calling querySelector on an element searches only inside that element. Useful inside reusable components.

example.title: Example 5: Defensive null check
example.code:
const maybe = document.querySelector('.missing');
console.log(maybe?.textContent ?? 'not found');
example.explanation: querySelector can return null. Optional chaining with ?. plus a fallback keeps your code robust.

    B -- yes --> C["getElementById"]
    B -- no --> D{"One match needed?"}
    D -- yes --> E["querySelector"]

    F --> G["forEach / for-of"]

quiz.question: What does document.querySelector('.x') return when no element matches?
quiz.explanation: querySelector returns null when no element matches. Always guard before reading properties.

quiz.question: What kind of collection does querySelectorAll return?
quiz.explanation: querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList — a snapshot at the time of the call.

quiz.question: What does getElementById('header') accept as its argument?
options: Just the id without the # prefix
quiz.explanation: getElementById takes the raw id string. No # prefix needed.

quiz.question: Which selectors does querySelector accept?
quiz.explanation: querySelector takes any CSS selector — '#id', '.class', 'tag[attr=value] > child:first-child', etc.

quiz.question: What is a 'live' collection?
options: One updated each time you read length, reflecting current DOM
A collection in a web worker
A streamed collection from the server
quiz.explanation: getElementsByClassName/TagName return LIVE collections — they auto-update as the DOM changes.

quiz.question: What is the cleanest way to iterate a NodeList?
quiz.explanation: Modern NodeList supports forEach directly. Array.from is needed for full array methods like map/filter.

quiz.question: Which is faster on a known id?
quiz.explanation: getElementById is the fastest lookup. Modern engines have made querySelector nearly as fast, but getElementById remains the textbook fastest.

quiz.question: What does card.querySelector('.btn') do differently from document.querySelector?
options: Throws if card has no .btn descendants
quiz.explanation: Calling querySelector on an element scopes the search to its descendants only.

quiz.question: Why guard with maybe?.textContent?
options: querySelector can return null; ?. avoids TypeError when reading properties
quiz.explanation: Without the guard, null.textContent throws. Optional chaining yields undefined instead.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How jQuery's $ inspired the browser
realWorldStory.storyText: Before 2010, selecting elements was painful — getElementById and getElementsByTagName were the main APIs. jQuery's $('#id .btn') felt magical. Within a few years, browsers adopted the same idea natively as querySelector and querySelectorAll, and jQuery's biggest selling point became unnecessary.

keyTakeaways: querySelector and querySelectorAll accept any CSS selector. They are the modern default.
getElementById remains the fastest lookup for a known id.
querySelectorAll returns a STATIC NodeList; getElementsByClassName returns a LIVE HTMLCollection.
Call querySelector on an element to scope the search to its descendants.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Passing a CSS selector to getElementById — only the raw id works.
💡 Pro Tip: Cache stable references at startup rather than re-querying inside hot loops.

lessons.title: Reading and Writing Content
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Read and write text with textContent, (2) Use innerHTML safely for trusted markup, (3) Update form inputs with .value.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on changing the text and markup inside DOM elements.
Why it matters: Content writing compared to refilling a page — knowing the right property unlocks safe updates.
Core terms you will use: `textContent`, `innerText`, `innerHTML`, `value`, `XSS`, `escape`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `el.textContent = 'Hello'`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: textContent" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the innerHTML-XSS bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You reach for textContent by default and reserve innerHTML for trusted strings.

hooklineimage.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Update an element"] --> B{"Setting text?"}
    B -- yes, plain text --> C["textContent"]
    B -- HTML markup --> D["innerHTML (safe input only)"]
    B -- form input --> E["value"]
```

hooklines.text: textContent is the safe default. innerHTML parses HTML — including malicious HTML.

image.html: ```mermaid flowchart LR A["textContent = 'hi'"] --> B["shows the literal tag text"] C["innerHTML = 'hi'"] --> D["renders bold 'hi'"] ```

hooklines.text: Form inputs use .value, not textContent — they store value, not innerHTML.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["input.value = 'Ada'"] --> B["Input now displays Ada"]
```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: textContent
parts.description: Read or write the combined text of an element and its descendants. HTML tags inside are treated as literal characters.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: innerText
parts.description: Similar to textContent but reflects RENDERED text (respects CSS visibility). Slower and quirkier — prefer textContent unless you need rendering awareness.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: innerHTML
parts.description: Read or write the HTML markup inside an element. Writing parses the string as HTML — powerful, but dangerous if the source is user input.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: XSS risk
parts.description: Setting innerHTML with user-controlled strings lets attackers inject <script> tags or event handlers. Escape or use textContent.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: value for inputs
parts.description: <input>, <textarea>, and <select> store their content in .value, NOT textContent. Set value to update.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Reading reflects state
parts.description: Reading textContent returns the current text, even after JavaScript modifications. Reading value returns the current user input.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: insertAdjacentText
parts.description: Inserts text relative to an element without replacing existing content. Useful for appending without rebuilding.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: When innerHTML is OK
parts.description: Trusted, server-generated markup or template-literal strings you fully control. Never user-supplied data.

analogy.subject: Content properties compared to writing tools
analogy.comparison: textContent is a marker — it lays down letters that everyone reads as text. innerHTML is a printing press — give it a template and it renders the formatted result. The printing press is fast but cannot tell user-supplied templates from a malicious one.

example.title: Example 1: textContent
example.code:
const h = document.querySelector('h1');
h.textContent = 'Hello, world';
example.explanation: Replaces the heading's text with a plain string. Tags in the new value would appear as literal text.

example.title: Example 2: innerHTML (trusted)
example.code: const card = document.querySelector('.card'); card.innerHTML = 'New entry';
example.explanation: Replaces the card's contents with parsed HTML. Use only when the string is controlled.

example.title: Example 3: Reading input value
example.explanation: Form inputs use .value. Both reading and writing happen through the same property.

example.title: Example 4: XSS-safe interpolation
example.explanation: textContent treats the value as plain text — the malicious markup is harmless. Output displays the literal characters.

example.title: Example 5: insertAdjacentText
example.code:
const log = document.querySelector('.log');
log.insertAdjacentText('beforeend', '\nNew entry');
example.explanation: Appends text without rebuilding the whole element. Useful for streaming logs or live updates.

flowchart.title: Picking the right content property

flowchart TD
    A["Update inside an element"] --> B{"Is it a form input?"}
    B -- yes --> C["Use .value"]
    B -- no --> D{"Plain text or HTML?"}
    D -- text --> E["textContent (safe)"]
    D -- trusted markup --> F["innerHTML"]
    D -- user-supplied --> E

quiz.question: Which property is safest for updating untrusted text?
quiz.explanation: textContent treats the value as literal text — no HTML parsing, no XSS risk.

quiz.question: What does setting innerHTML do?
options: Sets the text content as a string
Parses the value as HTML and replaces the inner markup
quiz.explanation: innerHTML PARSES the string as HTML. Trusted strings only — never user input directly.

quiz.question: Where do <input> elements store their current contents?
quiz.explanation: Form inputs use the .value property. textContent does not represent user input.

quiz.question: What is the XSS risk with innerHTML?
options: User-supplied HTML can include scripts or event attributes that execute
quiz.explanation: innerHTML executes scripts via attributes like onerror or src=javascript:. Always escape or use textContent.

quiz.question: Which is the difference between textContent and innerText?
options: innerText reflects rendered (visible) text and respects CSS; textContent reads all text regardless of styling
textContent is faster only on Chrome
quiz.explanation: innerText is rendering-aware (it hides display:none text and similar). textContent is the raw text content.

quiz.question: How do you append text without replacing existing content?
quiz.explanation: All three append text. insertAdjacentText is most precise; el.append is convenient; += works but rewrites the whole property.

quiz.question: When is innerHTML acceptable?
options: Only when the string is fully trusted (server-generated, hard-coded, or escaped)
quiz.explanation: innerHTML is fine for trusted markup. The danger is interpolating user input without escaping.

quiz.question: What does this print? el.textContent = 'hi'; console.log(el.textContent)
quiz.explanation: textContent treats the value as literal text — the tags appear verbatim.

quiz.question: Reading textContent returns...
options: The combined text content of the element and all descendants
quiz.explanation: textContent returns the joined text content from the element and every descendant.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Reading and Writing Content"?
quiz.explanation: XSS — the security risk that motivates textContent as the default — is the central idea.

Uses .value to drive controlled inputs, mirroring what React/Vue do under the hood for two-way binding.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How an XSS bug shut down MySpace in 2005
realWorldStory.storyText: The Samy worm spread by exploiting MySpace profiles that used innerHTML to render user-supplied bio text. Within 20 hours, more than a million accounts were affected. The fix industry-wide became: default to textContent, escape for innerHTML, and treat any 'just inline some HTML' approach as a security review trigger.

keyTakeaways: textContent reads and writes plain text — your safe default.
innerHTML parses the string as HTML — never use it directly on user input.
Form inputs use .value, not textContent.
innerText reflects rendered text; textContent reads everything. Prefer textContent unless rendering matters.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Interpolating user data into innerHTML — an XSS waiting to happen.
💡 Pro Tip: Build child elements with createElement + textContent for safe, structured updates.

lessons.title: Manipulating Attributes and Classes
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Read and set HTML attributes safely, (2) Toggle classes with classList, (3) Recognise the difference between attributes and properties.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on attribute and class manipulation — the bread and butter of interactive UI updates.
Why it matters: Class toggling compared to flipping a light switch — knowing classList unlocks effortless state-driven styling.
Core terms you will use: `getAttribute`, `setAttribute`, `removeAttribute`, `classList`, `dataset`, `attribute vs property`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `el.classList.toggle('active')`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: Reading an attribute" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the className-overwrite bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You use classList for any class change and dataset for any data-* attribute.

hooklineimage.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Need to change"] --> B{"What?"}
    B -- attribute --> C["getAttribute / setAttribute / removeAttribute"]
    B -- classes --> D["classList.add/remove/toggle/contains"]
    B -- data-* --> E["dataset.xKey"]
```
hooklineimage.alt: Routes to attribute and class APIs

hooklines.text: classList is purpose-built: add, remove, toggle, contains — no string concatenation.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["el.classList"] --> B["add('active')"]
    A --> C["remove('open')"]
    A --> D["toggle('hidden')"]
    A --> E["contains('selected')"]
```

hooklines.text: data-* attributes are exposed through dataset — camelCase converts to kebab-case automatically.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["data-user-id='42'"] --> B["el.dataset.userId"]
    B --> C["'42'"]
```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: getAttribute / setAttribute
parts.description: Read and write any HTML attribute by name. Values are strings.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: removeAttribute
parts.description: Removes the attribute entirely. Different from setting an empty value.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: hasAttribute
parts.description: Returns true if the attribute is present (regardless of its value). Useful for binary attributes like disabled.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: classList
parts.description: A DOMTokenList with add(), remove(), toggle(), contains(), replace() methods. Always use this for class manipulation.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: classList.toggle(name, force)
parts.description: Optional second argument forces add (true) or remove (false). Handy for state-driven UIs.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: className
parts.description: The legacy string property holding ALL classes. Setting it overwrites every existing class — usually a mistake.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: dataset
parts.description: Exposes data-* attributes as camelCase properties. data-user-id becomes el.dataset.userId.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Attribute vs property
parts.description: Most attributes have matching properties (e.g. input.value). For id/class, prefer the property; for custom or aria-*, use setAttribute.

analogy.subject: Attributes compared to labels and badges on a uniform
analogy.comparison: Attributes are like permanent labels stitched onto a uniform. Classes are removable badges you can pin, unpin, or flip. data-* attributes are personal-info cards tucked under the uniform — only you read them, but they belong to the wearer.

example.title: Example 1: Reading an attribute
example.explanation: getAttribute returns the raw string; the property version may resolve URLs. Both have their uses.

example.title: Example 2: Adding ARIA
example.explanation: ARIA attributes have no DOM property — setAttribute is the only way. Always strings.

example.title: Example 3: classList.toggle
example.explanation: Toggle flips a class on/off in one call. contains returns the current state.

example.title: Example 4: dataset
example.explanation: dataset exposes every data-* attribute. camelCase in JS maps to kebab-case in HTML.

example.title: Example 5: classList.toggle with force
example.explanation: Second argument forces add (true) or remove (false). Pair with an ARIA attribute for accessibility.

flowchart.title: Attribute or class?

interactiveExercise.title: Try It Yourself
interactiveExercise.instruction: Given a button.toggle-btn, attach a click handler that toggles the 'active' class on the button and logs whether it is currently active.
interactiveExercise.expectebehavior: Each click toggles the class and logs true/false alternately.

quiz.question: How do you toggle a CSS class on an element?
quiz.explanation: classList is the modern API for class manipulation. toggle adds the class if absent and removes it if present.

quiz.question: What does el.className = 'x' do?
options: Replaces ALL classes with just x — usually a bug
quiz.explanation: className is the legacy string property — assignment overwrites every existing class. Use classList instead.

quiz.question: How do you read a data-user-id attribute?
quiz.explanation: dataset converts data-user-id (kebab-case in HTML) to userId (camelCase in JS).

quiz.question: Which method removes an attribute entirely?
quiz.explanation: removeAttribute(name) removes the attribute from the element.

quiz.question: What does classList.toggle('x', false) do?
options: Toggles x as if force was absent
quiz.explanation: The second argument forces a specific state. false means remove (regardless of previous state).

quiz.question: How do you check whether an element has class 'open'?
options: Both 1 and 2 work, but classList.contains is correct
quiz.explanation: classList.contains is the proper API; className.includes also works but is fragile for substring keys like 'open' matching 'opened'.

quiz.question: What is the difference between getAttribute('id') and el.id?
options: Property reflects current state; attribute may reflect the original HTML string
quiz.explanation: Some attributes have matching properties that may differ subtly (e.g. checkbox.checked vs getAttribute('checked')). For id and class, property and attribute usually agree.

quiz.question: What does setAttribute('disabled', '') do to a button?
options: Disables it — presence of the attribute alone is enough for boolean attributes
quiz.explanation: For boolean attributes like disabled, presence matters — the value can be empty string and the button is still disabled.

quiz.question: Which is the safest way to flip a button between pressed and not?
quiz.explanation: Use classList plus an accessibility attribute. Avoid overwriting className or driving state via style alone.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Attributes and Classes"?
quiz.explanation: classList — the purpose-built class manipulation API — is the central new tool.

// 1. classList is accessed on the element
// 5. The new state (true/false) is returned
// 3. The class name is checked against the current list
// 6. CSS is reapplied on the next paint
// 2. If present, the class is removed

useCaseCards.useCase: Drives every visual state (hover, pressed, disabled) through classList toggles so CSS controls the look without inline styles.
Pairs every interactive state with the right aria-* attribute via setAttribute so assistive tech stays in sync with the visual state.
Uses data-* attributes to mark elements with metadata, then queries them later with [data-*] CSS attribute selectors.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How Bootstrap drives state with classes
realWorldStory.storyText: Bootstrap's modal, dropdown, and tab plugins all flip CSS classes via classList: .show, .active, .collapsed. Every visual change is one class toggle plus an ARIA attribute. That separation between JS-driven state and CSS-driven appearance is the reason Bootstrap themes can be restyled without touching a single line of JavaScript.

keyTakeaways: classList is the modern API for class manipulation: add, remove, toggle, contains, replace.
Avoid assigning className — it overwrites every existing class.
Use setAttribute/removeAttribute/hasAttribute for arbitrary HTML attributes, especially aria-*.
dataset exposes data-* attributes as camelCase properties.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Reaching for className when you mean classList.add — every other class disappears.
💡 Pro Tip: Pair every visual state class with the corresponding ARIA attribute for accessibility parity.

lessons.title: Inline Styles and CSS Variables
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Set inline styles with the style property, (2) Read computed styles, (3) Drive themes with CSS custom properties.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on changing CSS from JavaScript and tapping into CSS variables.
Why it matters: Styles compared to a control panel — knowing the right knobs unlocks animations and themes.
Core terms you will use: `style`, `kebab vs camelCase`, `getComputedStyle`, `CSS custom property`, `setProperty`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `el.style.backgroundColor = 'red'`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: Inline style set" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the camel-case-vs-kebab bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You drive themes with CSS variables and reach for setProperty when the name is dynamic.

hooklineimage.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Update look"] --> B{"Source of truth?"}
    B -- CSS class --> C["classList"]
    B -- ad-hoc visual --> D["el.style.x = value"]
    B -- design tokens --> E["setProperty('--token')"]
```

hooklines.text: el.style sets INLINE styles — they win over the stylesheet's normal rules.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["el.style.color='red'"] --> B["<div style='color: red'>"]
    B --> C["Inline beats class color"]
```
image.alt: Inline style wins over stylesheet rule

hooklines.text: CSS variables are the modern way to theme — set once on :root, read everywhere.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[":root { --accent: blue }"] --> B["document.documentElement.style.setProperty('--accent', 'red')"]
    B --> C["Every var(--accent) updates"]
```
image.alt: Setting a CSS variable cascades everywhere

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: el.style.* properties
parts.description: JS exposes CSS properties as camelCase on the style object: backgroundColor, fontSize, marginTop.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Inline wins
parts.description: Anything set on el.style becomes an inline style on the element, beating class rules by specificity.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: String values
parts.description: Values are strings, including units: '14px', '50%', '#f06'. Numbers without units are ignored for length-based properties.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: getComputedStyle
parts.description: Returns an object with the final resolved values from the cascade — including inherited ones. Read-only.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: removeProperty
parts.description: el.style.removeProperty('background-color') clears the inline style, letting the cascade take over again.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: CSS custom properties
parts.description: Variables defined with --name in CSS. Read with getComputedStyle(el).getPropertyValue('--name'); write with el.style.setProperty('--name', value).

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Drive themes
parts.description: Update CSS variables at the :root level once and every component using var(--token) updates instantly. The modern theming pattern.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: When to skip el.style
parts.description: For visual state, prefer classList + CSS. Use el.style for dynamic values (animation positions, colors derived at runtime).

analogy.subject: Inline styles compared to a control panel knob
analogy.comparison: Setting el.style is turning a single knob on the control panel — immediate, specific, hard to override. CSS variables are the master power supply — turn one knob and every dependent device updates at once.

example.title: Example 1: Inline style set
example.explanation: Two inline styles applied. They beat any matching class rule.

example.title: Example 2: kebab-case via setProperty
example.code:
const box = document.querySelector('.box');
box.style.setProperty('background-color', '#f06');
example.explanation: setProperty accepts the kebab-case CSS name directly. Useful when the property name is dynamic.

example.title: Example 3: getComputedStyle
example.explanation: Returns resolved values, including inherited and cascade-derived ones. Read-only.

example.title: Example 4: CSS variable read/write
example.explanation: Read with getPropertyValue; write with setProperty. Any var(--accent) reference updates immediately.

example.title: Example 5: Remove inline override
example.explanation: removeProperty clears the inline color. The stylesheet's rule (or inherited color) takes over again.

flowchart.title: Inline style or class?

interactiveExercise.expectebehavior: The element grows from 0% to 100% width.

quiz.question: How do you write background-color via el.style?
quiz.explanation: CSS kebab-case becomes JS camelCase. background-color -> backgroundColor.

quiz.question: Which API gives you final resolved style values?
quiz.explanation: getComputedStyle returns the resolved cascade — read-only.

quiz.question: How do you set a CSS variable from JavaScript?
quiz.explanation: setProperty accepts the variable name (including the leading --) and value.

quiz.question: Which CSS rule wins when there is both an inline style and a class rule?
quiz.explanation: Inline styles have higher specificity than class rules. Use them sparingly to avoid override headaches.

quiz.question: What does el.style.removeProperty('color') do?
options: Removes the inline color, letting the cascade decide
Throws if color was never set
quiz.explanation: removeProperty clears the inline style. The element falls back to whatever the cascade dictates.

quiz.question: What does this print? const styles = getComputedStyle(el); console.log(typeof styles.padding);
quiz.explanation: Computed styles are returned as strings, often with units ('12px').

quiz.question: Why might you reach for setProperty over el.style.color?
options: When the property name is dynamic (especially for CSS variables)
Setting via setProperty avoids inline styles
quiz.explanation: setProperty takes the property name as a string — handy for dynamic names or for setting custom properties starting with --.

quiz.question: Which best drives a theme switch (light/dark) across the app?
options: Toggle a class on :root and let CSS variables flow
quiz.explanation: Set a theme class on the root; CSS variables under that class define the palette; every component using var(--token) updates automatically.

lessons.title: Creating and Inserting Elements
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Create new elements with createElement, (2) Insert them with appendChild, append, prepend, or insertBefore, (3) Use insertAdjacentHTML for fast batched markup.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on building new DOM nodes and placing them in the tree.
Why it matters: Creating compared to assembling a Lego piece — knowing the inserter unlocks dynamic UIs.
Core terms you will use: `createElement`, `appendChild`, `append`, `prepend`, `insertBefore`, `insertAdjacentHTML`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `parent.append(child)`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: createElement" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the appendChild-single-arg bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You reach for append over appendChild when adding multiple children at once.



parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: createElement
parts.description: document.createElement('tag') creates a new detached element. Set properties before attaching.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Set properties
parts.description: Assign textContent, classList, dataset, attributes, event listeners — anything you can do on an existing element.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: appendChild
parts.description: parent.appendChild(node) adds the node as the last child. Returns the appended node. Takes ONE argument.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: append
parts.description: Modern alternative. Takes multiple children AND plain strings. parent.append(li1, li2, 'text node').

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: prepend
parts.description: Inserts at the beginning. Same multi-arg flexibility as append. parent.prepend(banner).

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: insertBefore
parts.description: parent.insertBefore(newNode, referenceNode) inserts newNode just before referenceNode. The classic API.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: insertAdjacentHTML
parts.description: Inserts a parsed HTML string at one of four positions: beforebegin, afterbegin, beforeend, afterend. Fast but XSS-risky with user data.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: DocumentFragment
parts.description: Build many nodes in a fragment, then insert once. Avoids layout thrashing when adding lots of children.

analogy.subject: Creating compared to assembling Lego
analogy.comparison: createElement is a Lego piece in your hand — yours to inspect and decorate. append snaps it onto an existing build. DocumentFragment is the building tray where you compose a complex sub-build before snapping it onto the main creation in one move.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How DocumentFragment made D3 fast
realWorldStory.storyText: Mike Bostock's D3 library generates thousands of SVG nodes for a single chart. Initial versions inserted nodes one at a time and caused noticeable jank. The library was rewritten to build everything inside a DocumentFragment and attach once — turning charts that took 200ms into ones that take 20ms. Same logic, one architectural change.

keyTakeaways: createElement makes a detached node. Decorate it before attaching.
append accepts multiple children (and strings). appendChild takes exactly one node.
prepend adds at the beginning. insertBefore inserts before a specific sibling.
DocumentFragment batches inserts into a single reflow.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Calling appendChild(a, b, c) and assuming all three are added — only `a` makes it in.
💡 Pro Tip: When rendering many nodes, build in a fragment first. The reflow cost is the same as appending one node.

lessons.title: Removing and Replacing Elements
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Remove a node with remove(), (2) Replace one element with another using replaceWith, (3) Recognise when removeChild and replaceChild are still useful.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on detaching nodes from the DOM cleanly.
Why it matters: Removal compared to taking pieces off a board — knowing the right API unlocks safe cleanup.
Core terms you will use: `remove`, `removeChild`, `replaceWith`, `replaceChild`, `detach`, `parentNode`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `el.remove()`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: el.remove()" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the iterate-then-remove bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You use el.remove() unless you specifically need the legacy parent.removeChild API.

```mermaid
    A --> E{"Replace?"}

```

hooklines.text: el.remove() is the one-line modern detach — no parent reference needed.

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: el.remove()
parts.description: Modern API. Removes the element from its parent in a single call.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: parent.removeChild(el)
parts.description: Legacy API. Requires a parent reference. Returns the removed node — useful when you want to keep using it.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: el.replaceWith(newEl)
parts.description: Replaces el with newEl (or multiple nodes/strings). Modern and concise.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: parent.replaceChild(newEl, oldEl)
parts.description: Legacy version. Note the argument order — new first, then old. Returns the old element.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Empty an element
parts.description: el.innerHTML = '' removes all children quickly. Or loop with while (el.firstChild) el.firstChild.remove() to preserve listeners.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Cleanup
parts.description: Removing an element from the DOM does NOT delete its event listeners automatically. Garbage collection handles them when no other reference remains.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Iterate then remove
parts.description: When removing items while iterating a live HTMLCollection, the collection shrinks mid-loop and you skip entries. Convert to an array first or iterate backwards.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: parentNode
parts.description: Every node has a parentNode property. Useful when you need to reach up before removing.

analogy.subject: Removing compared to taking pieces off a board
analogy.comparison: el.remove() is picking up your piece and pocketing it — clean and self-contained. removeChild is the older 'tell the board to release piece X' instruction. replaceWith is swapping one piece for another in a single motion.

example.title: Example 1: el.remove()
example.code:
const el = document.querySelector('.banner');
el.remove();
example.explanation: One line. No need to reach for parent. Listeners on the element are released when no other reference remains.

example.title: Example 2: parent.removeChild
example.explanation: Older API returns the removed node. Output: true. Use when you want to reattach later.

example.title: Example 3: replaceWith
example.explanation: Single call swap. replaceWith accepts multiple new children — even strings.

example.title: Example 4: Empty an element
example.explanation: Fast emptying. Replace with the while-firstChild loop if listeners on children must be preserved.

example.title: Example 5: Iterate-and-remove safely
example.code:
const items = Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('.todo.done'));
items.forEach(it => it.remove());
example.explanation: Convert the NodeList to an array first. Avoids mid-iteration surprises from live collections.

quiz.question: Which is the modern way to remove an element?
quiz.explanation: el.remove() is the modern API. parent.removeChild still works and returns the removed node.

quiz.question: What is the argument order for parent.replaceChild?
quiz.explanation: replaceChild(newEl, oldEl): the new one first, then the one to be replaced.

quiz.question: What does el.replaceWith(a, 'text', b) do?
options: Replaces el with a, then the text node, then b — in order
quiz.explanation: replaceWith accepts multiple nodes and strings — inserting all of them in place of the original.

quiz.question: Why might you choose removeChild over el.remove()?
options: It returns the removed node so you can store and reattach later
It is required in strict mode
quiz.explanation: removeChild returns the detached node. Keep a reference if you plan to reinsert it.

quiz.question: What is the fastest way to remove ALL children?
options: Both 2 and 3 work, with innerHTML='' being the canonical idiom
quiz.explanation: Both empty the element. innerHTML='' is the most common idiom. textContent='' is safer for non-HTML content.

quiz.question: Why is iterating a live HTMLCollection and removing items risky?
options: The collection auto-shrinks; the loop index skips items
remove() does not work in loops
quiz.explanation: Live collections update as you remove items. Convert to Array.from first or iterate from the end backwards.

quiz.question: What does removed.parentNode equal after el.remove()?
quiz.explanation: After removal, parentNode is null. The element is fully detached.

quiz.question: Does el.remove() also remove its event listeners?
options: Listeners are released when no other references remain and the node is garbage-collected
quiz.explanation: Removing from the DOM does not delete listeners. Once no JS code holds the node, garbage collection cleans up.

quiz.question: Which keeps event listeners on remaining children when emptying a list?
quiz.explanation: innerHTML='' rebuilds the DOM, breaking listener references. The while-firstChild loop detaches individually but preserves listeners on the remaining tree.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Removing and Replacing"?
quiz.explanation: The modern remove() / replaceWith APIs are the lesson's headline simplification.

bugHunt.instruction: A developer removes every .done todo, but only every OTHER one disappears. Fix the bug.
bugHunt.buggyCode:
const items = document.getElementsByClassName('todo done');
for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) items[i].remove();
bugHunt.bug: getElementsByClassName returns a LIVE collection. Removing items shrinks it mid-loop, so the index 'jumps' past every other entry. Convert to a static array first.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How the modern remove() simplified jQuery codebases
realWorldStory.storyText: For years, every codebase carried a one-liner: $(el).remove(). Native el.remove() arrived in 2014 and gradually replaced jQuery removal calls. Today, modern codebases drop the jQuery dependency entirely for DOM operations — saving 30+ KB of bundle size — precisely because APIs like remove(), append(), and toggle() are now native.

keyTakeaways: el.remove() is the modern detach — no parent reference needed.
parent.removeChild returns the removed node; useful when you want to reattach later.
el.replaceWith(newEl) is a single-call swap; accepts multiple new children too.
innerHTML='' is the canonical 'empty this element' idiom.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Iterating a live HTMLCollection and calling remove() — items get skipped.
💡 Pro Tip: When removing many items, snapshot with Array.from first so the loop sees a stable view.

lessons.title: Traversing the DOM Tree
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Walk up and down the DOM with parentNode/children, (2) Move sideways with siblings, (3) Use closest() to find the nearest matching ancestor.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on moving between related nodes — parents, children, siblings.
Why it matters: Traversal compared to walking branches of a tree — knowing the directions unlocks delegated event handlers.
Core terms you will use: `parentNode`, `children`, `firstElementChild`, `nextElementSibling`, `closest`, `contains`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `e.target.closest('.row')`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: parentNode" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the children-vs-childNodes bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You use closest() for event delegation by default.

```mermaid
    A --> C["children (elements)"]
    A --> D["previousElementSibling"]
    A --> E["nextElementSibling"]

```

text

hooklines.text: closest walks up the tree to find the nearest ancestor that matches a CSS selector.

```mermaid
flowchart TD

```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: parentNode
parts.description: The immediate parent. null if the node is detached or is the document.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: children
parts.description: Live HTMLCollection of ELEMENT children only — no text or comment nodes. Use for most layouts.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: childNodes
parts.description: NodeList of ALL child nodes including text nodes (whitespace counts!) and comments. Surprises beginners.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: firstElementChild / lastElementChild
parts.description: Shortcuts for children[0] and children[length-1]. Skip whitespace and comments.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: nextElementSibling / previousElementSibling
parts.description: Move sideways through sibling ELEMENTS — skipping text nodes.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: closest(selector)
parts.description: Walks up the tree (including the element itself) looking for the first ancestor matching the CSS selector. Returns null if none match.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: contains(other)
parts.description: Returns true if other is a descendant of this node (or equal to it). Useful for checking click-inside vs click-outside.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Delegation lifesaver
parts.description: Pair event delegation with closest: when a click bubbles up, e.target.closest('.row') gives you the row even if the click landed on an inner span.

analogy.subject: Traversal compared to walking a tree's branches
analogy.comparison: The DOM is a tree. Each node has a parent above, children below, and possibly siblings to either side. closest is climbing up the trunk looking for the first sign matching what you want; children is naming everyone hanging off this branch.

example.title: Example 1: parentNode
example.code:
const btn = document.querySelector('button');
console.log(btn.parentNode.tagName);
example.explanation: Walks one step up. parentNode is null only when the node is detached.

example.title: Example 2: children vs childNodes
example.explanation: children is 1 (the span); childNodes is 2 (the text node plus the span). The difference catches everyone once.

example.title: Example 3: siblings
example.code:
const first = document.querySelector('li');
console.log(first.nextElementSibling?.textContent);
example.explanation: Skips text/whitespace between siblings. Use ?. because the sibling may not exist.

example.title: Example 4: closest for delegation
example.explanation: One handler on document catches every click. closest finds the row even when the click hit a nested icon.

example.title: Example 5: contains for outside-click
example.explanation: contains is true if e.target is the menu or any of its descendants. A clean way to close popovers on outside click.

flowchart.title: Which traversal API?
flowchart.code:
flowchart TD
    A["Need to move from a node"] --> B{"Direction?"}
    B -- up --> C["parentNode or closest"]
    B -- down --> D["children / firstElementChild"]
    B -- sideways --> E["nextElementSibling / previousElementSibling"]
    A --> F{"Need ancestor matching selector?"}
    F -- yes --> G["closest"]

quiz.question: What does element.parentNode return?
options: The immediate parent of the element
quiz.explanation: parentNode is the immediate ancestor. null only if the node is detached or is the document itself.

quiz.question: What is the difference between children and childNodes?
options: children is ELEMENTS only; childNodes includes text and comment nodes
children is live, childNodes is static
quiz.explanation: children filters to elements; childNodes is everything (including whitespace text nodes).

quiz.question: What does element.closest('.row') return?
options: The nearest ancestor (including self) matching .row, or null
quiz.explanation: closest walks up starting from the element itself, looking for the first match.

quiz.question: Which API moves to the next ELEMENT sibling, skipping text nodes?
quiz.explanation: nextElementSibling skips text and comment nodes. nextSibling includes them, which trips beginners constantly.

quiz.question: What does parent.firstElementChild equal when parent has only text nodes?
options: null — there are no element children
quiz.explanation: firstElementChild ignores text and comment nodes. With no element children, it is null.

quiz.question: What does menu.contains(e.target) return when target is the menu itself?
quiz.explanation: contains returns true for descendants OR the node itself. Useful for outside-click checks.

quiz.question: Why use closest in event delegation?
options: It returns the meaningful element even when the click landed on a nested child

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How closest replaced jQuery's $().parents()
realWorldStory.storyText: jQuery's $(this).parents('.row').first() was the classic delegation pattern. Native closest() arrived in 2016 and did exactly the same thing in one call, on every element. Within a few years, every major codebase migrated to closest — saving an entire jQuery dependency and shrinking page weight noticeably.

keyTakeaways: parentNode walks one step up; closest('selector') walks up looking for a match.
children is element-only; childNodes includes text and comment nodes.
nextElementSibling / previousElementSibling skip whitespace; nextSibling / previousSibling do not.
