💡 Pro Tip: Pair contains(target) with click-outside-to-close popovers and dropdowns.

lessons.title: The DOMContentLoaded Event
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Run code after the HTML is parsed, (2) Recognise the difference between DOMContentLoaded and load, (3) Use defer or modules so scripts wait without an explicit event.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on running scripts at the right time during page load.
Why it matters: Timing compared to opening a shop at the right hour — knowing the events unlocks reliable startup.
Core terms you will use: `DOMContentLoaded`, `load`, `readyState`, `defer`, `module`, `async`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', init)`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: DOMContentLoaded" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the script-before-element bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You add defer to scripts in <head> and skip explicit DOMContentLoaded altogether.

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: DOMContentLoaded
parts.description: Fires when the HTML document is fully parsed — DOM tree built, scripts run. Images, stylesheets, and fonts may still be loading.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: load
parts.description: Fires when EVERYTHING — including images, stylesheets, iframes — has loaded. Much later than DOMContentLoaded.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Script placement
parts.description: Scripts in <head> run before the body parses. Scripts at the end of <body> run after most of the DOM is already there.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: defer attribute
parts.description: <script defer src='...'> downloads in parallel and runs only after parsing finishes — right before DOMContentLoaded. No event listener needed.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: async attribute
parts.description: <script async src='...'> runs as soon as it downloads — may race with parsing. Good for analytics; risky for code that touches the DOM.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: type='module'
parts.description: Module scripts are deferred by default. They run after parsing, in dependency order.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: document.readyState
parts.description: Read 'loading' (still parsing), 'interactive' (DOM ready), or 'complete' (everything loaded). Useful if you missed the event.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: When to use DOMContentLoaded
parts.description: Inline scripts in <head>, libraries that may be loaded before the DOM. Modern preference: ship code as defer or module.

analogy.subject: Page load compared to opening a shop
analogy.comparison: DOMContentLoaded is the moment the shop's interior is fully set up. load is when the awning, lights, and window displays have all been installed too. Customers can start browsing after the first; everything truly looks ready after the second.

example.explanation: Fires once images and stylesheets are loaded. Use for tasks that depend on layout (e.g. measuring images).

// Modules wait for parsing automatically — no defer needed.
example.explanation: Module scripts run after parsing by default. Modern apps use type=module and skip DOMContentLoaded entirely.

quiz.question: When does DOMContentLoaded fire?
options: When the HTML is fully parsed and the DOM tree is built
quiz.explanation: DOMContentLoaded fires after the HTML is parsed. Images, stylesheets, and fonts may still be loading.

quiz.question: What does <script defer> do?
options: Runs the script asynchronously, possibly before parsing finishes
Waits for parsing to finish before running the script
quiz.explanation: defer makes the script wait until parsing completes — running right before DOMContentLoaded.

quiz.question: Is <script type='module'> deferred by default?
quiz.explanation: Module scripts are deferred automatically. You do not need the defer attribute.

quiz.question: When does the load event fire?
options: When EVERYTHING is loaded — images, stylesheets, iframes
quiz.explanation: load is later than DOMContentLoaded. It waits for resources, not just markup.

quiz.question: Why might a script in <head> querying an element find nothing?
options: Parsing has not reached the element yet — the element does not exist in the DOM at script runtime
quiz.explanation: Inline <head> scripts run before the rest of the document parses. Move the script to the end of body, or use defer or DOMContentLoaded.

quiz.question: What does document.readyState equal once DOMContentLoaded fires?
quiz.explanation: readyState becomes 'interactive' at DOMContentLoaded and 'complete' at load.

quiz.question: What is the modern best practice for loading scripts?
quiz.explanation: defer or type=module lets you place the script in head without blocking parsing — and the DOM is ready when it runs.

quiz.question: Which is correct for a guard against missing the event?
options: Check readyState and run immediately if not 'loading'
Both 1 and 2 are valid — 2 handles late-loaded scripts
quiz.explanation: Both work. Reading readyState lets late-loaded scripts run immediately when the DOM is already ready.

quiz.question: What does <script async> do differently from defer?
options: async runs as soon as it loads, possibly during parsing; defer waits for parsing to finish
async is forbidden in modern browsers
quiz.explanation: async fires on download (parsing may still be running). defer waits until parsing completes.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "DOMContentLoaded"?
quiz.explanation: Script timing — knowing when your code runs relative to parsing — is the central new idea.

bugHunt.title: Find and fix the bug
bugHunt.instruction: An inline script in <head> tries to read a button but gets null. Fix it without moving the script.
bugHunt.buggyCode:
<head>
  <script>
    const btn = document.querySelector('button');
    btn.addEventListener('click', () => console.log('clicked'));
  </script>
</head>
bugHunt.bug: The script runs before the body has been parsed, so document.querySelector('button') returns null. Wrap the code in a DOMContentLoaded listener, or use defer on an external script.
bugHunt.fixedCode:
<head>
  <script>
    document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', () => {
      const btn = document.querySelector('button');
      btn.addEventListener('click', () => console.log('clicked'));
    });
  </script>
</head>
bugHunt.hint: DOMContentLoaded delays until the DOM is parsed.

useCaseCards.useCase: Bootstraps the app entry point with <script type='module' defer> in head, skipping explicit DOMContentLoaded entirely.
Loads analytics with <script async> so it fires as soon as it downloads without blocking the page render.
Uses window.addEventListener('load') to lazy-init image carousels that need final layout dimensions.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: Why defer replaced jQuery's $(document).ready
realWorldStory.storyText: For a decade, every jQuery script started with $(document).ready(function() { ... }) because no native equivalent existed cleanly cross-browser. Once browsers normalised DOMContentLoaded and the defer attribute landed, modern codebases dropped that wrapper entirely. The result: clearer code, smaller bundles, and one less jQuery dependency.

keyTakeaways: DOMContentLoaded fires when HTML parsing finishes — DOM is queryable, but images may still load.
load fires later, once images, stylesheets, and iframes finish loading.
<script defer> and <script type='module'> wait for parsing automatically — no DOMContentLoaded handler needed.
document.readyState lets you check the current phase ('loading', 'interactive', 'complete').
⚠️ Common Mistake: Inline script in <head> querying DOM elements that have not been parsed yet.
💡 Pro Tip: For modern apps, default to <script type='module' defer> in <head> — clean, fast, and DOM is ready when your code runs.

modules.title: Events
modules.description: Make pages respond to humans: listen for clicks, keys, and form submissions, understand bubbling, delegate efficiently, and prevent default browser behaviour when needed.

points: This module covers Events across 8 focused lessons, from registering listeners to mastering delegation.
You will start with addEventListener — the foundation every later lesson relies on.
By the end you will be comfortable with the vocabulary used everywhere in JavaScript: `addEventListener`, `event object`, `bubbling`, `capturing`, `delegation`, `preventDefault`, `stopPropagation`.
The lessons progress as: 1) addEventListener; 2) Event object; 3) Mouse events; 4) Keyboard events; 5) Form events; 6) Propagation; 7) Delegation; 8) preventDefault. Each builds on the last.
Events you will meet here: `click`, `dblclick`, `mousedown`, `keydown`, `keyup`, `submit`, `input`, `change`, `focus`, `blur`.
Each lesson exposes one realistic beginner trap (e.g. "using event.keyCode (deprecated) instead of event.key") and shows the fix.
Every lesson ships with a live "Try it" exercise, a graded mini challenge, drag-and-drop sorting, card-matching pairs, and a bug-hunt fix-it task.
After completing the final lesson on "preventDefault", you will have a working mental model for events that powers every interactive UI.

lessons.title: Event Listeners with addEventListener
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Register listeners with addEventListener, (2) Remove them with removeEventListener, (3) Use the options object (once, capture, signal).

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on attaching, configuring, and removing event listeners.
Why it matters: Listeners compared to subscribing to a newsletter — knowing the unsubscribe path unlocks tidy UI code.
Core terms you will use: `addEventListener`, `removeEventListener`, `event type`, `handler`, `options`, `once`, `capture`, `signal`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `el.addEventListener('click', handler)`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: A click listener" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the anonymous-handler-can't-be-removed bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You always pass a named handler so it can be unregistered later.

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: addEventListener
parts.description: el.addEventListener(type, handler) registers a function to run whenever the specified event fires on the element.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Multiple handlers
parts.description: You can register many handlers for the same event. They run in the order they were added.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: removeEventListener
parts.description: Requires the exact same function reference passed to addEventListener. Anonymous functions cannot be removed.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Options object
parts.description: Third argument can be { once: true, capture: false, passive: true, signal }. once auto-removes; capture flips the phase; signal lets an AbortController detach the listener.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: once
parts.description: The listener runs the first time, then is removed automatically. Great for 'load' or 'first interaction' events.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: capture
parts.description: Default is false (bubble). Setting capture:true runs the handler during the capture phase, before deeper handlers.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: passive
parts.description: Tells the browser the handler will not call preventDefault. Required for smooth scrolling on touchstart/wheel events.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: AbortSignal
parts.description: Pass { signal: controller.signal }. Calling controller.abort() removes the listener. Modern way to clean up many listeners at once.

analogy.subject: Listeners compared to newsletter subscriptions
analogy.comparison: Adding a listener is subscribing to a newsletter for a specific topic. removeEventListener is unsubscribing. The 'once' option is a 'send me just one email' subscription. AbortController is a master 'unsubscribe me from everything in this bundle' switch.

example.title: Example 1: A click listener
example.code:
const btn = document.querySelector('button');
btn.addEventListener('click', () => console.log('clicked'));
example.explanation: The handler runs every time the button is clicked.

example.title: Example 2: Named handler for removal
example.explanation: Use a named function so removeEventListener can find the same reference.

example.title: Example 3: once option
example.code: window.addEventListener('load', () => console.log('loaded'), { once: true });
example.explanation: The listener fires the first time, then auto-removes. Common for one-shot startup work.

example.title: Example 4: passive listener
example.explanation: Tells the browser the handler will not cancel default scroll, so scrolling stays smooth.

example.title: Example 5: AbortController cleanup
example.explanation: Both listeners share one controller. ctrl.abort() removes both — handy when unmounting a component.

flowchart.title: Choosing listener options

interactiveExercise.expectebehavior: Logs 'ready' once when the DOM is parsed.

quiz.question: How do you register a click listener on an element?
quiz.explanation: addEventListener is the modern, layered API. el.onclick = handler exists but only supports one handler.

quiz.question: Can you register multiple handlers for the same event?
quiz.explanation: addEventListener stacks handlers. Each one runs in the order it was added.

quiz.question: Why must removeEventListener receive the same function reference?
options: Equality is by identity — only the same function reference can be located
quiz.explanation: Inline anonymous functions cannot be removed because no reference was kept.

quiz.question: What does { once: true } do?
options: Listener runs once and is auto-removed
quiz.explanation: once is the auto-unsubscribe convenience option.

quiz.question: What is { capture: true } for?
options: Runs the handler during the capture phase (top-down) instead of bubble
quiz.explanation: capture switches phases. Almost all event handlers default to bubble; capture is for special targeting.

quiz.question: What does { passive: true } communicate?
options: The handler will not call preventDefault; browsers can optimise (e.g. smooth scrolling)
The handler runs in a worker
quiz.explanation: Telling the browser the handler will not block default lets it start scrolling instantly without waiting for JS.

quiz.question: How can you remove MANY listeners with one call?
options: Create an AbortController and pass its signal to every addEventListener; call abort() to detach all
quiz.explanation: AbortController + signal is the modern cleanup pattern — perfect for component unmount.

quiz.question: What is the default value of capture in the options object?
quiz.explanation: Default is false — listeners run in the bubble phase by default.

quiz.question: What happens if the same exact (type, handler, capture) triple is registered twice?
options: Both run, but only first is removable
quiz.explanation: Duplicate registrations with the same options are ignored — the listener exists only once.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Event Listeners with addEventListener"?
quiz.explanation: The options object (once, capture, passive, signal) is the lesson's most powerful new tool.

useCaseCards.useCase: Pairs every useEffect with an AbortController + signal so cleanup happens with one abort() call instead of dozens of removeEventListener calls.
Uses { once: true } so welcome toasts fire only the first time the user clicks anywhere.
Sets { passive: true } on scroll/touch handlers so the main thread does not stall the scrolling animation.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How Chrome forced the passive option
realWorldStory.storyText: In 2016 Chrome started warning that non-passive touch handlers were the #1 source of janky scrolling. The browser team made { passive: true } the new default for touchstart/touchmove on document and window — forcing libraries to opt in to passive explicitly. The visible result: every scroll on every page got noticeably smoother overnight.

keyTakeaways: addEventListener(type, handler, options) is the modern API. Multiple handlers per event are fine.
removeEventListener requires the SAME function reference — name your handlers.
Options: { once, capture, passive, signal }. signal + AbortController is the modern bulk-cleanup pattern.
passive:true lets the browser optimise scroll/touch; signal:abortController.signal makes detach trivial.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Registering an inline arrow and expecting to remove it — different reference every time.
💡 Pro Tip: Reach for AbortController in component code; one abort() replaces every removeEventListener call.

lessons.title: The Event Object
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Inspect event.target and event.currentTarget, (2) Read event.type and event.timeStamp, (3) Use event-specific properties (clientX, key, etc.).

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on the event object passed into every handler.
Why it matters: The event object compared to a receipt — knowing what's on it unlocks accurate interaction handling.
Core terms you will use: `event.target`, `event.currentTarget`, `event.type`, `event.timeStamp`, `event.detail`, `instanceof Event`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `function handler(event) { ... }`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: target vs currentTarget" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the target-vs-currentTarget bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You always reach for currentTarget when you want 'the element I bound the handler to'.

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: event.target
parts.description: The deepest element where the event was triggered. If you click on an icon inside a button, target is the icon.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: event.currentTarget
parts.description: The element on which THIS specific listener is attached. Useful when one handler covers many descendants.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: event.type
parts.description: String name of the event: 'click', 'keydown', 'submit'. Same string you passed to addEventListener.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: event.timeStamp
parts.description: High-resolution timestamp (ms since navigation start). Useful for measuring how long since something happened.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: event.bubbles / cancelable
parts.description: bubbles is true for most user events. cancelable indicates whether preventDefault has any effect.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Mouse-specific
parts.description: clientX/clientY (viewport), pageX/pageY (document), button (which mouse button), shiftKey/ctrlKey (modifiers).

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Keyboard-specific
parts.description: key ('a', 'Enter'), code ('KeyA', 'Enter'), shiftKey/ctrlKey/altKey/metaKey. Prefer key for character, code for physical position.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Custom events
parts.description: new CustomEvent('my-event', { detail: payload }) lets you dispatch your own. Listen for it like any built-in event.

analogy.subject: The event object compared to a delivery slip
analogy.comparison: When an event happens, the browser fills out a delivery slip and hands it to your handler. The slip notes who originally placed the order (target), who's currently signing for it (currentTarget), the kind of package (type), when it arrived (timeStamp), and any extras (coords, key, button).

example.title: Example 1: target vs currentTarget
example.explanation: Click anywhere inside .wrap. target is the deepest clicked element; currentTarget is always .wrap.

example.title: Example 2: event.type
example.explanation: One handler covers two event types. event.type tells you which one fired.

example.title: Example 3: Mouse coords
example.explanation: clientX/clientY are pixel coordinates relative to the viewport (the visible window).

example.title: Example 4: Keyboard key
example.explanation: event.key holds the printable character or a named key like Enter, Escape, ArrowLeft.

example.title: Example 5: Custom event
example.code:
el.addEventListener('greeting', e => console.log(e.detail));
el.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('greeting', { detail: { msg: 'hi' } }));
example.explanation: Listen for and dispatch your own events. event.detail carries the payload.

interactiveExercise.title: Try It Yourself

quiz.question: What does event.target refer to?
options: The element the listener was attached to
The deepest element where the event was triggered
quiz.explanation: target is the actual origin. It can differ from currentTarget when events bubble.

quiz.question: What is event.currentTarget?
options: The element the current listener was attached to
The same as event.target in delegation
quiz.explanation: currentTarget is whichever element the THIS handler was attached to.

quiz.question: What is event.type when you call el.addEventListener('click', ...)?
quiz.explanation: event.type is the exact event name string. Useful when one handler covers multiple types.

quiz.question: Which property holds the pressed key letter or named key?
quiz.explanation: event.key gives the printable character or named key. keyCode is deprecated.

quiz.question: Which property gives the X coordinate of a click relative to the viewport?
quiz.explanation: clientX/clientY are viewport-relative. pageX includes scroll offset; screenX is global to the monitor.

quiz.question: Which is true about event.bubbles?
options: true for most user events (click, input, keydown); false for some (focus, blur in old form)
quiz.explanation: Most events bubble. A handful (notably the focus/blur pair on some browsers) do not — use focusin/focusout if you need bubbling.

quiz.question: Which event allows preventDefault to take effect?
quiz.explanation: preventDefault works only when event.cancelable is true. Some events (resize, scroll) are non-cancelable.

quiz.question: How do you create a custom event with payload?
options: Both 2 and 3 work, but CustomEvent is the standard
quiz.explanation: Use CustomEvent with the detail option for payloads. Dispatch with el.dispatchEvent(...).

quiz.question: Why is event.timeStamp useful?
options: It is a high-resolution timestamp — useful for measuring durations between events
It is the date the page loaded
quiz.explanation: timeStamp is milliseconds since navigation start, with sub-millisecond precision.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "The Event Object"?
quiz.explanation: Distinguishing currentTarget from target is the lesson's most important concept.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How event.key replaced keyCode forever
realWorldStory.storyText: For years, every keyboard handler started with a switch on event.keyCode — numeric, browser-dependent, and impossible to remember. event.key (a string like 'Enter', 'a', 'ArrowLeft') landed across browsers around 2016 and became the standard immediately. Today keyCode is deprecated, but legacy codebases still carry tables of magic numbers.

keyTakeaways: event.target is where it started; event.currentTarget is where the handler is bound.
event.type, event.timeStamp, event.bubbles, event.cancelable are common to all events.
Mouse events expose clientX/Y; keyboard events expose key, code, and modifier booleans.
Custom events go through new CustomEvent + dispatchEvent with a detail payload.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Confusing target and currentTarget — especially in delegated handlers.
💡 Pro Tip: Reach for event.currentTarget by default; use event.target only when you genuinely care about the deepest element.

lessons.title: Common Mouse Events
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Handle click, dblclick, mousedown, mouseup, (2) Distinguish mouseenter/leave from mouseover/out, (3) Read mouse coordinates accurately.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on the family of mouse events and the differences between similar pairs.
Why it matters: Mouse events compared to a stenographer's keys — knowing the exact moment each fires unlocks precise UI feedback.
Core terms you will use: `click`, `dblclick`, `mousedown`, `mouseup`, `mousemove`, `mouseenter`, `mouseleave`, `mouseover`, `mouseout`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `el.addEventListener('click', handler)`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: click" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the mouseover-bubbles bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You reach for mouseenter/leave when you do not want re-fires on inner children.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["User press+release on element"] --> B["mousedown"]
    B --> C["mouseup"]
    C --> D["click"]
    D --> E["if quickly again: dblclick"]
```

hooklines.text: mousedown -> mouseup -> click. Fast second click triggers dblclick.

image.html:
```mermaid

    A["mousedown"] --> B["mouseup"]
    B --> C["click"]
    C --> D["(if quick) dblclick"]
```

hooklines.text: mouseenter does NOT bubble — perfect for one-time hover on a container.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["mouseover"] --> B["Fires on every child enter (bubbles)"]
    C["mouseenter"] --> D["Fires once when entering element (no bubble)"]
```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: click
parts.description: Fires after a complete press-and-release on the same element. The everyday button event.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: dblclick
parts.description: Fires after two quick clicks (browser-defined gap). Beware: click ALSO fires twice before dblclick — handle carefully.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: mousedown / mouseup
parts.description: Press down and release of any mouse button. Useful when you need to react before the full click completes.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: mousemove
parts.description: Fires continuously while the mouse moves. High frequency — throttle if doing expensive work.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: mouseenter / mouseleave
parts.description: Enter and leave the element. Does NOT bubble. Does not fire when moving between children — clean for hover effects.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: mouseover / mouseout
parts.description: Older counterparts. BUBBLES. Fires every time the pointer enters or leaves any descendant — surprising for hover states.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: event.button
parts.description: Numeric button code: 0 (primary/left), 1 (middle), 2 (secondary/right). For chord clicks check event.buttons (note the s).

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Right-click
parts.description: Listen for 'contextmenu' (not click) to handle right-clicks. Call preventDefault to suppress the native menu.

analogy.subject: Mouse events compared to a doorman
analogy.comparison: click is the doorman noticing a knock. mousedown/mouseup is them watching the hand press the knocker down, then lift it. mouseenter is when you cross the threshold; mouseover keeps repeating the announcement every time you step into another inner room.

example.title: Example 1: click
example.explanation: Fires after a complete press-release. clientX/Y give the location.

example.title: Example 2: dblclick + click careful
example.code:
el.addEventListener('click', () => console.log('single'));
el.addEventListener('dblclick', () => console.log('double'));
example.explanation: Double-clicking still triggers two single 'click' events before dblclick. Don't perform expensive work twice; debounce instead.

example.title: Example 3: Hover via mouseenter/mouseleave
example.code:
card.addEventListener('mouseenter', () => card.classList.add('hover'));
card.addEventListener('mouseleave', () => card.classList.remove('hover'));
example.explanation: Adds the hover class only when truly entering the card — moving between inner children does NOT re-fire.

example.title: Example 4: Drag with mousedown/move/up
example.explanation: Classic drag pattern: track state across mousedown -> mousemove -> mouseup.

example.title: Example 5: Right-click
example.explanation: contextmenu handles right-clicks. preventDefault stops the native browser menu.

quiz.question: Which event fires AFTER a complete press-and-release?
quiz.explanation: click fires once mousedown and mouseup have both completed on the same element.

quiz.question: Does mouseenter bubble?
options: No — it fires exactly once when the pointer enters the element
Only when modifier keys are held
quiz.explanation: mouseenter does NOT bubble. Compare mouseover, which does.

quiz.question: Which event would you use to capture every entry into a child element?
quiz.explanation: mouseover bubbles and fires repeatedly as the pointer moves between descendants.

quiz.question: Which event handles right-click?
quiz.explanation: Right-clicks trigger contextmenu. The click event does fire too, but contextmenu is the canonical right-click handler.

quiz.question: How do you suppress the native context menu?
options: Return false from a click handler
Call event.preventDefault inside the contextmenu handler
quiz.explanation: preventDefault on contextmenu suppresses the browser's native menu.

quiz.question: What does event.button equal for a primary (left) click?
quiz.explanation: button: 0=left, 1=middle, 2=right. event.buttons (with s) is a bitmask of all currently-pressed buttons.

quiz.question: What is the typical drag pattern?
options: mousedown sets state, mousemove updates while held, mouseup ends
quiz.explanation: Drag spans three events. Track 'dragging' state across them.

quiz.question: What is the relationship between click and dblclick?
options: click fires twice, then dblclick fires
Browsers vary, but generally only one
quiz.explanation: Two clicks fire individually, then dblclick. If you only want one of them, use a guard or debounce.

quiz.question: Which event fires continuously while the pointer moves?
quiz.explanation: mousemove fires many times per second. Throttle work inside the handler to keep the page responsive.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Common Mouse Events"?
quiz.explanation: The mouseenter-vs-mouseover distinction is what trips up most new developers.

bugHunt.title: Find and fix the bug
bugHunt.instruction: A hover effect uses mouseover/mouseout and flickers every time the cursor moves to a child element. Fix it.
bugHunt.buggyCode:
card.addEventListener('mouseover', () => card.classList.add('hover'));
card.addEventListener('mouseout', () => card.classList.remove('hover'));
bugHunt.bug: mouseover/mouseout bubble — every time the cursor enters a child, mouseout fires for the parent. Switch to mouseenter/mouseleave, which fire once per outer entry/exit.
bugHunt.fixedCode:
card.addEventListener('mouseenter', () => card.classList.add('hover'));
card.addEventListener('mouseleave', () => card.classList.remove('hover'));
bugHunt.hint: mouseenter/mouseleave do not bubble — perfect for outer-edge hover effects.

hints: Track 'start' state across the three events.

useCaseCards.useCase: Implements pan/drag with mousedown -> mousemove -> mouseup, tracking deltas to translate the canvas.
Uses contextmenu + preventDefault to provide a custom right-click toolbox.
Uses mouseenter/mouseleave to drive hover popovers that don't flicker when the cursor crosses inner labels.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: Why Figma uses mousedown for dragging
realWorldStory.storyText: Figma's canvas reacts to mousedown immediately — it does NOT wait for click — because click only fires AFTER the user lifts the mouse. Reacting to mousedown lets Figma feel instant: as soon as you begin pressing, drag-and-select feedback starts. Tiny event-choice; massive perceived speed.

keyTakeaways: Mouse event sequence: mousedown -> mouseup -> click. Quick second click adds dblclick.
mouseenter / mouseleave do NOT bubble — great for hover effects on containers.
mouseover / mouseout DO bubble — they fire as the pointer crosses every descendant.
Right-click uses contextmenu; suppress the browser menu with preventDefault.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Using mouseover for hover effects and getting flicker when the cursor crosses inner children.
💡 Pro Tip: For drag flows, attach mousemove and mouseup to document (not the dragged element) so motion outside the element still tracks.

lessons.title: Keyboard Events
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Handle keydown and keyup, (2) Read event.key vs event.code correctly, (3) Build keyboard shortcuts with modifiers.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on keyboard event handling — keydown, keyup, and the data they expose.
Why it matters: Keyboard events compared to Morse code — knowing each signal unlocks shortcuts and accessibility.
Core terms you will use: `keydown`, `keyup`, `keypress (deprecated)`, `event.key`, `event.code`, `modifier keys`, `event.repeat`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `if (e.key === 'Enter')`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: keydown" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the deprecated-keyCode bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You always use event.key for characters and event.code for physical positions.

hooklineimage.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["User presses a key"] --> B["keydown"]
    B --> C["if held: keydown repeat events"]
    C --> D["User releases: keyup"]
```

hooklines.text: event.key is the printed character. event.code is the physical key on the board.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["event.key"] --> B["'a' or 'Enter'"]
    C["event.code"] --> D["'KeyA' or 'Enter'"]
```

hooklines.text: Modifier keys are direct properties: event.ctrlKey, event.shiftKey, event.altKey, event.metaKey.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["e.ctrlKey + e.shiftKey + e.key"] --> B["Cmd+Shift+P shortcut"]
```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: keydown
parts.description: Fires when a key is pressed. Repeats while held, with event.repeat === true.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: keyup
parts.description: Fires when the key is released. Does not repeat.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: keypress (deprecated)
parts.description: Older event that fired for printable characters. Use keydown instead.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: event.key
parts.description: The character produced ('a') or named key ('Enter', 'ArrowLeft', 'Escape'). Affected by keyboard layout.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: event.code
parts.description: Physical key location ('KeyA', 'Digit1', 'Space'). Stable across layouts — use for WASD-style games.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Modifier keys
parts.description: event.ctrlKey, .shiftKey, .altKey, .metaKey are booleans. Combine to build shortcuts.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: event.repeat
parts.description: true when the key is being held down and the browser is firing repeated keydown events.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: preventDefault on keys
parts.description: Inside keydown, preventDefault can suppress the default browser action (e.g. Ctrl+S Save As).

analogy.subject: Keyboard events compared to a stenographer's keys
analogy.comparison: Pressing a key fires keydown; lifting fires keyup. event.key is the printed letter on your typewriter; event.code is the physical key position. The modifier keys are the function shifts that change which letter is typed.

example.title: Example 1: keydown
example.explanation: Logs every key as you press it. Repeats while held (with e.repeat === true).

example.title: Example 2: Enter submits
example.explanation: Detect Enter; preventDefault avoids inserting a newline in a form.

example.title: Example 3: Ctrl+S shortcut
example.explanation: Cmd on macOS uses metaKey; ctrl on others. Cover both. preventDefault stops the browser's Save As dialog.

example.title: Example 4: event.code for games
example.explanation: Use event.code so WASD works the same on QWERTY and AZERTY layouts.

example.title: Example 5: Ignoring repeats
example.explanation: Skip repeated keydowns so the handler fires only on the initial press.

quiz.question: Which event fires when a key is first pressed?
quiz.explanation: keydown fires the moment the key goes down. keyup is the release.

quiz.question: What does event.key give you?
options: The physical position of the key
The character or named key produced
quiz.explanation: event.key is 'a', 'Enter', 'ArrowUp', etc. Affected by keyboard layout and modifier keys.

quiz.question: Which property is best for WASD movement keys?
quiz.explanation: event.code identifies the physical key. WASD works regardless of layout.

quiz.question: Why avoid event.keyCode?
options: It is deprecated; numeric codes are inconsistent across browsers
quiz.explanation: keyCode is legacy and inconsistent. Use event.key or event.code.

quiz.question: How do you detect Cmd on macOS and Ctrl on others in one shortcut?
quiz.explanation: Mac users press metaKey for shortcuts; Windows/Linux use ctrlKey. Cover both.

quiz.question: What does event.repeat indicate?
options: Whether the user has pressed the key before
Whether this keydown is from holding the key down (auto-repeat)
Number of times key was pressed
quiz.explanation: event.repeat is true for the auto-repeat keydown events the browser fires when a key is held.

quiz.question: What does e.key equal for the Enter key?
quiz.explanation: Named keys use friendly strings. 'Enter' is the standard.

quiz.question: Which event fires when the user RELEASES a key?
quiz.explanation: keyup fires on release. It does not auto-repeat.

quiz.question: Why might you call preventDefault inside a keydown handler?
options: To suppress the browser's default action (e.g. Ctrl+S Save As) when you handle the shortcut yourself
quiz.explanation: Stops the browser from also doing its built-in action. Essential for custom shortcuts.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Keyboard Events"?
quiz.explanation: Distinguishing the produced character (key) from the physical position (code) is the lesson's key insight.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: Why Slack's keyboard layer uses event.code for games
realWorldStory.storyText: When Slack built keyboard navigation for its message list, the team first used event.key — and broke shortcuts for users on non-English keyboards. Switching to event.code for navigation keys (and keeping event.key for character typing) made the experience uniform across QWERTY, AZERTY, and Dvorak layouts.

keyTakeaways: keydown fires on press (auto-repeats); keyup fires on release. keypress is deprecated.
event.key is the character or named key; event.code is the physical position.
Modifier booleans (ctrlKey, shiftKey, altKey, metaKey) let you build shortcuts.
event.repeat distinguishes the initial press from auto-repeats while held.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Using event.keyCode === 13 — deprecated. Use event.key === 'Enter'.
💡 Pro Tip: Cover both metaKey and ctrlKey so shortcuts work on macOS and Windows/Linux alike.

lessons.title: Form Events: submit, input, change
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Handle form submit cleanly, (2) Distinguish input from change events, (3) Use focus and blur for UX hints.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on form-related events — submit, input, change, focus, blur.
Why it matters: Form events compared to a kitchen timer — knowing when each rings unlocks responsive forms.
Core terms you will use: `submit`, `input`, `change`, `focus`, `blur`, `FormData`, `preventDefault`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `form.addEventListener('submit', e => { e.preventDefault(); ... })`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: submit" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the submit-doesn't-preventDefault bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You wire submit to a single handler with preventDefault and pull values via FormData.



```mermaid
    C["change event"] --> D["after user commits"]
```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: submit
parts.description: Fires on the <form> element when the user submits (Enter in a text field or clicking a submit button). preventDefault stops the navigation/reload.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: FormData
parts.description: new FormData(form) builds a key/value map of the form fields. Iterate or use entries() / get(name).

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: input event
parts.description: Fires on EVERY change to the value — every keystroke, paste, autofill. Perfect for live validation.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: change event
parts.description: Fires when the user commits a value. For text inputs, on blur. For checkboxes/select, immediately on click/selection.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: focus / blur
parts.description: When an input gains or loses focus. Use for instructional UI (showing a hint) or commit logic.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: focusin / focusout
parts.description: Same as focus/blur but they BUBBLE. Useful when you want one handler at the form level.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Element.value
parts.description: Read or write the current value of any form control directly. Combine with input/change events for controlled behaviour.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Element.checked
parts.description: For checkboxes and radio buttons, .checked is the boolean state. Listen for change to react to toggles.

analogy.subject: Form events compared to kitchen timers
analogy.comparison: submit is the final 'meal ready' bell. input is the timer beeping every second as you adjust the heat. change is the moment you commit to a new dial setting. focus is putting your hand on a knob; blur is letting go.

example.title: Example 1: submit
example.explanation: Take over the form: preventDefault stops the browser reload, FormData gathers the values.

example.title: Example 2: Live validation with input

input.addEventListener('focus', () => hint.classList.add('show'));
input.addEventListener('blur', () => hint.classList.remove('show'));
example.explanation: Show a tooltip while the user is in the field; hide it when they leave.

example.title: Example 5: focusin at the form level

quiz.question: Which element does 'submit' typically fire on?
quiz.explanation: submit fires on the form. Always attach handlers there, not on the button.

quiz.question: What does preventDefault inside a submit handler do?

quiz.question: What is the difference between input and change for a text field?

quiz.explanation: Live updates need input. Commit-only logic uses change.

quiz.question: Which event bubbles?

quiz.question: Where do you read the current value of an <input>?

quiz.question: What is the cleanest way to handle a form WITHOUT page reload?

quiz.question: Why use input.setCustomValidity?

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Form Events"?

lessons.title: Event Propagation: Bubbling and Capturing
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Describe the capture and bubble phases, (2) Stop propagation when needed, (3) Choose the right phase for a listener.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on how events travel through the DOM tree.
Why it matters: Propagation compared to a ripple in water — knowing the path unlocks event delegation.
Core terms you will use: `capture phase`, `target phase`, `bubble phase`, `stopPropagation`, `stopImmediatePropagation`, `event path`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `addEventListener('click', h, { capture: true })`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: Bubble path" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the stopPropagation overuse bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You only call stopPropagation when you have a real reason — not as a reflex.

hooklineimage.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["window"] --> B["document"]
    B --> C["body"]
    C --> D["div"]
    D --> E["button (target)"]
    E --> D --> C --> B --> A
```

hooklines.text: Events ripple up by default. capture:true makes a listener fire on the way down instead.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Default: bubble (target -> root)"]
    B["capture:true: root -> target"]
```

hooklines.text: stopPropagation halts the journey. Use sparingly — it breaks delegation.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["target"] --> B["parent"]
    B -- stopPropagation --> C["event stops here"]
```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: Three phases
parts.description: Events flow from window down to the target (capture), arrive at the target (target phase), then bubble back up (bubble).

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Default = bubble
parts.description: addEventListener attaches in the BUBBLE phase by default. That's why event delegation naturally works.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Capture listener
parts.description: Pass { capture: true } (third argument) to register in the capture phase. Useful when you must run BEFORE descendants get a chance.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: stopPropagation
parts.description: Calling event.stopPropagation() prevents the event from continuing along its path. Other listeners on the SAME element still fire.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: stopImmediatePropagation
parts.description: More aggressive: stops propagation AND prevents any other listeners on the same element from running.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: event.composedPath
parts.description: Returns the full event path as an array — useful for inspecting where the event will travel.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Why bubbling matters
parts.description: Bubbling enables event delegation: one parent listener can handle many children. Without bubble, you'd need a listener per element.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Don't reflex-call stopPropagation
parts.description: Stopping events breaks code expecting to handle them upstream (analytics, modal close handlers). Use only when you have a clear reason.

analogy.subject: Propagation compared to a ripple in water
analogy.comparison: Drop a pebble in a pond at a leaf. The ripple first travels INWARD from the shore to the leaf (capture), then bounces outward from the leaf back to the shore (bubble). stopPropagation is putting a stick in the water — the ripple stops there.

example.title: Example 4: stopImmediatePropagation
example.explanation: Stops same-element listeners too. The second listener on btn never runs.

example.title: Example 5: event.composedPath

quiz.question: Which phase does addEventListener attach in by default?
quiz.explanation: Default is bubble. Pass { capture: true } for capture phase.

quiz.question: What does event.stopPropagation do?
options: Stops the event from continuing along its path
quiz.explanation: stopPropagation halts the journey through ancestors/descendants. Other listeners on the SAME element still fire.

quiz.question: When would you use { capture: true }?
options: Almost never — only when you must intercept BEFORE descendants get the event
When you want to stop bubbling
quiz.explanation: Capture is rare. Use when intercepting BEFORE inner handlers (e.g. global key shortcuts that override widget behaviour).

quiz.question: What does stopImmediatePropagation add over stopPropagation?
options: Also prevents other listeners on the SAME element from firing
quiz.explanation: stopImmediatePropagation halts both ancestors AND any later-registered listeners on the current element.

quiz.question: Why is bubbling important?
options: It enables event delegation: one parent listener handles many children
It is needed for capture to work
quiz.explanation: Without bubbling, you'd need a separate listener per child. Bubbling makes a single parent listener possible.

quiz.question: Does stopPropagation also call preventDefault?
quiz.explanation: They are independent. preventDefault stops the browser's default action; stopPropagation stops the event journey.

quiz.question: What does event.composedPath return?
options: The event's path through the DOM as an array
quiz.explanation: composedPath gives the array of nodes the event will visit. Useful for inspection and shadow DOM.

quiz.question: What is the order of events for a click on a deeply nested button?
options: Capture (window -> target), then target, then bubble (target -> window)
quiz.explanation: Capture (top-down) -> target -> bubble (bottom-up). Listeners run in their attached phase.

quiz.question: Which is the recommended attitude toward stopPropagation?
options: Use sparingly — it can break delegation and analytics
quiz.explanation: stopPropagation is a sharp tool. Reflex use creates bugs that are hard to diagnose later.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Event Propagation"?
quiz.explanation: The bubble phase is the path that powers event delegation — the lesson's foundational idea.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: Why React simulated bubbling
realWorldStory.storyText: Early React installed a single delegated click listener on document and dispatched synthetic events to components. That worked because of real DOM bubbling. When React 17 switched delegation to the root container, the same propagation model still applied — proving that bubbling is so fundamental that even SPA frameworks build on top of it.

keyTakeaways: Events travel through three phases: capture (down), target, bubble (up).
addEventListener attaches in the BUBBLE phase by default. Use { capture: true } to switch.
stopPropagation halts the journey; stopImmediatePropagation also halts same-element listeners.
Bubbling is what makes event delegation possible — one parent handler for many children.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Reflexive stopPropagation in every click handler — breaks modals, analytics, and delegation.
💡 Pro Tip: Use event.composedPath() to debug exactly where an event will travel.

lessons.title: Event Delegation
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Attach one listener to a parent and handle clicks on many children, (2) Use closest() to find the right delegate, (3) Handle dynamically added elements automatically.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on event delegation — one listener instead of many.
Why it matters: Delegation compared to one teller handling all customers — knowing the pattern unlocks scalable UI.
Core terms you will use: `delegation`, `event.target`, `closest`, `data attributes`, `dynamic children`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `parent.addEventListener('click', e => { const item = e.target.closest('.item'); ... })`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: Basic delegation" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the missing-closest-check bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You reach for delegation when adding listeners to lists or dynamic content.

```mermaid

    A["One listener on parent"] --> B["any child click bubbles up"]
    B --> C["e.target.closest('.item') gives the row"]
    C --> D["handler runs once per click"]
```

hooklines.text: One listener can handle a thousand children — that's event delegation.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["ul.addEventListener('click', handler)"] --> B["works for every <li>"]
```

hooklines.text: Dynamically added items get the same handler automatically — no re-binding needed.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["ul.append(newLi)"] --> B["works immediately — no new listener"]
```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: Why delegate
parts.description: Attaching a listener per child wastes memory and breaks for elements added later. One parent listener fixes both.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: How it works
parts.description: Events bubble from the target up. A parent listener catches every click on its descendants.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Find the meaningful element
parts.description: Use e.target.closest('.item') to find the nearest matching ancestor (or self). Returns null if none.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Guard the match
parts.description: Always check `if (!item) return;` before reading properties — the user may have clicked outside any item.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Read data attributes
parts.description: Store row ids as data-* on the element. The handler reads item.dataset.id without separate state.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Dynamic content
parts.description: Newly added children automatically inherit the parent's listener — no need to re-attach.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Choose the right root
parts.description: Attach to the nearest container that owns the items. Going too high (document) costs nothing but reduces scope clarity.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Limits
parts.description: Doesn't work for events that don't bubble (focus, blur). Use focusin/focusout for those — they bubble.

analogy.subject: Delegation compared to one bank teller for all customers
analogy.comparison: Without delegation, you'd hire a teller for every customer (one listener per row). Delegation hires ONE teller (one parent listener) who serves whoever steps to the counter. New customers (dynamic items) get the same service automatically.

example.title: Example 1: Basic delegation
example.explanation: One listener on the <ul> handles every <li> click. Works regardless of which inner span/icon got the click.

example.title: Example 2: Reading data attributes
example.explanation: Each row carries data-id. The handler reads it on whichever row was clicked.

example.title: Example 3: Multiple actions
example.explanation: Use data-action to switch behaviour without separate handlers per button.

example.title: Example 4: Dynamic content
example.explanation: Items added later automatically participate — no extra wiring needed.

example.title: Example 5: focusin for delegated focus
example.explanation: focus doesn't bubble, but focusin does — letting one form-level listener track every field.

quiz.question: What does event delegation rely on?
options: Event bubbling — the event bubbles up to the parent listener
quiz.explanation: Delegation works because events bubble. A parent listener sees clicks from any descendant.

quiz.question: Why use closest() inside a delegated handler?
options: It normalises e.target up to the meaningful container (e.g. .row), regardless of which inner span was clicked
quiz.explanation: Clicks often land on icons inside the row. closest walks up to the row itself.

quiz.question: What is the right guard pattern?
options: if (item) {...} - bail out early if the click missed any matching ancestor
quiz.explanation: Always check the result of closest before using it — clicks outside any item return null.

quiz.question: Why does delegation handle dynamically added items?
options: Because the parent listener catches events from children that may not have existed yet
Because closest() listens for new elements
quiz.explanation: The listener is on the parent. Any future child's events bubble to the same handler.

quiz.question: Which event needs focusin instead of focus for delegation?
quiz.explanation: focus doesn't bubble; focusin does. The same applies to blur vs focusout.

quiz.question: Which performance benefit does delegation give?
options: One listener instead of N — less memory and faster setup
quiz.explanation: A single listener costs a fraction of N separate listeners — especially important for large lists.

quiz.question: Which root is best for delegating a list?
options: The nearest container (the list itself or a specific section)
quiz.explanation: Closest meaningful container keeps the scope obvious and avoids surprising side effects.

quiz.question: What does closest('.item') do on a click that landed outside any .item?
quiz.explanation: closest returns null if no ancestor matches. Always guard before using the result.

quiz.question: Which is the best way to pass per-row metadata to a delegated handler?
options: data-* attributes on the row, read via dataset
quiz.explanation: data-* + dataset is the canonical pattern. The handler reads dataset.x from the matched row.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Event Delegation"?
quiz.explanation: The single-listener pattern is the heart of event delegation.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How GitHub's PR file tree scales
realWorldStory.storyText: GitHub's pull-request file tree can show thousands of changed files. Instead of attaching a click handler to each, the team delegates to the root tree element and uses closest('[data-file]'). Adding hundreds of dynamic files costs nothing — a single listener already handles every click.

keyTakeaways: Event delegation = one parent listener handles events from many descendants.
Use e.target.closest('.item') to walk up to the meaningful container, then guard with `if (!item) return`.
Delegated handlers handle dynamically added children for free — no re-binding.
For focus/blur, use focusin/focusout — they bubble.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Reading dataset directly off e.target — misses cases where the click landed on an inner element.
💡 Pro Tip: Combine data-action attributes with delegation to switch behaviour for many buttons from one handler.

lessons.title: Preventing Default Behavior
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Call event.preventDefault() to suppress built-in actions, (2) Recognise events that are NOT cancelable, (3) Pair preventDefault with custom handling for forms and anchors.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on stopping the browser's built-in reactions to events.
Why it matters: preventDefault compared to taking over the steering wheel — knowing when to call it unlocks custom UI.
Core terms you will use: `preventDefault`, `event.cancelable`, `event.defaultPrevented`, `anchor`, `submit`, `keydown shortcut`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `event.preventDefault()`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: Anchor preventDefault" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the passive-handler bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You always pair preventDefault with a clearly cancelable event.

hooklines.text: preventDefault tells the browser 'I'll handle this — don't do your default thing.'


parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: preventDefault
parts.description: Tells the browser to skip its built-in action for this event. Forms don't submit, anchors don't navigate, keys don't insert characters.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: event.cancelable
parts.description: Boolean: whether preventDefault has any effect. Most user events are cancelable; some (resize, scroll) are not.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: event.defaultPrevented
parts.description: Returns true if preventDefault has already been called on this event by another handler. Useful in chained scenarios.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Anchor defaults
parts.description: Click on <a href='...'> navigates. preventDefault keeps you on the same page — common for SPAs.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Form submit default
parts.description: Submitting a form navigates/reloads. preventDefault inside the submit handler keeps you on the page.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Keyboard shortcuts
parts.description: Stop the browser's default (Ctrl+S = Save As). Inside keydown, preventDefault is the canonical 'I handled this' marker.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Drag and drop
parts.description: Dropzones require preventDefault during dragover so the browser allows the drop. Forgetting this is the #1 drag-drop bug.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Passive constraint
parts.description: If you registered with { passive: true }, preventDefault is ignored. Browsers warn you in the console.

analogy.subject: preventDefault compared to grabbing the steering wheel
analogy.comparison: The browser drives the car by default. preventDefault is your hand grabbing the wheel: 'I'll steer this one.' If the event is non-cancelable, the wheel is locked — your grip does nothing. Passive listeners are a contract you signed that says 'I won't steer' — even if you try, the wheel doesn't move.

example.title: Example 1: Anchor preventDefault
example.explanation: Stops the browser from navigating. Your SPA router takes over.

example.title: Example 2: Form submit
example.explanation: Stops the page reload; you handle submission with fetch.

example.title: Example 3: Shortcut override
example.explanation: Override Cmd+P so your custom print dialog opens instead of the browser's.

example.title: Example 4: Drop zone setup
example.explanation: preventDefault on dragover is REQUIRED for drop to fire. Forgetting it is the most common drag-drop bug.

example.title: Example 5: Check cancelable first
example.explanation: scroll is NOT cancelable. preventDefault has no effect. event.cancelable lets you check before trying.

quiz.question: What does preventDefault do?
options: Stops the browser's default action for the event
quiz.explanation: preventDefault stops the browser's built-in reaction (navigate, submit, type character).

quiz.question: What does event.cancelable tell you?
options: Whether the event can be removed
Whether preventDefault has any effect on this event
Whether it is a custom event
quiz.explanation: Some events (scroll, resize) are not cancelable. preventDefault on those is a no-op.

quiz.question: Does preventDefault stop propagation?
quiz.explanation: preventDefault and stopPropagation do different things. preventDefault stops the default; stopPropagation stops the journey.

quiz.question: Why must you preventDefault on dragover for drop to fire?
options: By default the browser refuses the drop; preventDefault signals 'this zone accepts drops'
quiz.explanation: preventDefault on dragover is how you tell the browser 'this is a valid drop target'.

quiz.question: What happens if you call preventDefault inside a passive listener?
options: Nothing — the browser ignores it and warns in the console
quiz.explanation: Passive listeners promised they wouldn't preventDefault. The call is ignored and you get a console warning.

quiz.question: What is the most common preventDefault use case?

quiz.explanation: scroll is non-cancelable. preventDefault has no effect there.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Preventing Default Behavior"?
quiz.explanation: event.cancelable is the gate that decides whether preventDefault matters.

bugHunt.bug: Passive listeners promise NOT to call preventDefault. The call is ignored and the browser warns. Drop the passive option (or remove preventDefault if you want scroll to continue).

Implements drop zones with preventDefault on dragover so the browser allows the drop instead of refusing it.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: Why Gmail intercepts Cmd+S
realWorldStory.storyText: Gmail's compose window catches Cmd+S with preventDefault and triggers 'save draft' instead of the browser's Save As dialog. Without preventDefault, you'd download a half-finished HTML file every time. The pattern — keydown listener + preventDefault + custom action — powers every keyboard shortcut in productivity apps.

keyTakeaways: preventDefault stops the browser's built-in reaction (navigate, submit, type character, scroll to anchor).
Only cancelable events respond — check event.cancelable when in doubt.
stopPropagation and preventDefault solve different problems. Don't confuse them.
Dragover REQUIRES preventDefault to allow drop. The single most-forgotten requirement in drag-and-drop.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Calling preventDefault inside a { passive: true } listener — the call is ignored.
💡 Pro Tip: Pair preventDefault with a clearly cancelable event and a documented reason — gratuitous calls confuse readers.

modules.title: Asynchronous JavaScript
modules.description: Master the JS event loop: handle timers, network calls, and parallel work with callbacks, promises, and async/await — and learn the error-handling patterns each style needs.

points: This module covers Asynchronous JavaScript across 8 focused lessons, from the event loop to fetch and Promise.all.
You will start with the sync/async distinction — the foundation every later lesson relies on.
By the end you will be comfortable with the vocabulary used everywhere in JavaScript: `event loop`, `callback`, `Promise`, `async`, `await`, `fetch`, `Promise.all`, `setTimeout`.
The lessons progress as: 1) Sync vs Async; 2) Callbacks; 3) Promises; 4) async/await; 5) fetch; 6) Error handling; 7) Promise.all/race; 8) Timers. Each builds on the last.
APIs you will meet here: `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `Promise`, `fetch`, `Response`, `Promise.all`, `Promise.allSettled`, `Promise.race`.
Each lesson exposes one realistic beginner trap (e.g. "awaiting inside forEach runs in parallel, not serial") and shows the fix.
Every lesson ships with a live "Try it" exercise, a graded mini challenge, drag-and-drop sorting, card-matching pairs, and a bug-hunt fix-it task.
After completing the final lesson on "Timers", you will have a working mental model for async code that powers every modern API integration.

lessons.title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous Code
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Describe the difference between sync and async, (2) Explain the JS single-thread / event-loop model, (3) Recognise blocking vs non-blocking operations.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on the model that makes asynchronous JavaScript possible.
Why it matters: Sync/async compared to a single chef in a kitchen — knowing the queue unlocks responsive UIs.
Core terms you will use: `synchronous`, `asynchronous`, `event loop`, `task queue`, `microtask`, `single-thread`, `blocking`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `setTimeout(() => ..., 0)`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: Sync order" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the blocking-loop bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You can predict the output order of mixed sync/async logs.

hooklineimage.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["JS engine (single-thread)"] --> B["Call stack"]
    B --> C["Sync code runs here"]
    A --> D["Web APIs (timers, fetch)"]
    D --> E["Task queue"]
    E --> F["Event loop pulls into stack"]
```

hooklines.text: JavaScript has ONE thread for your code. Async work happens elsewhere; the event loop schedules callbacks.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Sync work"] --> B["Call stack"]
    C["Timers / Network"] --> D["Task queue"]
    D --> B
```

hooklines.text: Blocking the thread freezes the UI. Async APIs let the page breathe.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Heavy sync loop"] --> B["UI frozen"]
    C["setTimeout / fetch"] --> D["UI stays responsive"]
```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: Synchronous
parts.description: Code runs top-to-bottom on the call stack. Each statement finishes before the next starts.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Asynchronous
parts.description: Some operations (timers, fetch, IO) return immediately and complete later. Their callbacks run when the engine picks them up.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Single-threaded
parts.description: JS has only one main thread for your code. Two synchronous blocks cannot run truly in parallel.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Event loop
parts.description: Continuously checks: stack empty? If so, pull the next task from the queue and run it. Repeats forever.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Task queue
parts.description: Where setTimeout/setInterval callbacks, fetch responses, and DOM events line up.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Microtask queue
parts.description: Higher-priority queue used by Promises (.then) and queueMicrotask. Drained completely between tasks.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Blocking
parts.description: A long synchronous loop blocks the call stack. Animations, clicks, and rendering all wait. Avoid in the main thread.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Non-blocking
parts.description: Async APIs (timers, fetch, IndexedDB) hand work off to the platform and return immediately. The page stays responsive.

analogy.subject: Sync vs async compared to a single chef in a kitchen
analogy.comparison: JavaScript is one chef. Sync orders go in queue order and each is finished before the next begins. Async orders (waiting for water to boil) are handed off to a side burner; the chef takes the next order. When the water boils, the chef returns to finish that order.

example.title: Example 1: Sync order
example.explanation: Output: 1, 2, 3 — strictly in order, on the call stack.

example.title: Example 2: Async surprise
example.explanation: Output: 1, 3, 2. The setTimeout callback queues and runs AFTER the sync code completes.

example.title: Example 3: Microtask wins
example.explanation: Output: 1, 2, promise, timer. Microtasks (Promise.then) run before macrotasks (setTimeout).

example.title: Example 4: Blocking loop
example.explanation: The synchronous busy-wait blocks everything for 1 second — clicks, animations, even setTimeout don't fire.

example.title: Example 5: Non-blocking version
example.code:
console.log('start');
setTimeout(() => console.log('end'), 1000);
example.explanation: Same effect, but the page stays interactive for that second. setTimeout hands the wait to the platform.

flowchart.title: Sync or async?
flowchart.code:
flowchart TD

    B -- short --> C["Sync is fine"]
    B -- long (IO, timers, heavy compute) --> D["Use async APIs"]
    D --> E["Callbacks / Promises / async-await"]

interactiveExercise.title: Try It Yourself
interactiveExercise.instruction: Run console.log('1'); setTimeout(() => console.log('2'), 0); console.log('3'); and predict the output. Then verify in DevTools.
interactiveExercise.expectebehavior: Output order is 1, 3, 2.

quiz.question: How many threads does JavaScript use for your code?
quiz.explanation: JS is single-threaded for the main code. Web Workers run separately but cannot touch the DOM.

quiz.question: What is the output of console.log('1'); setTimeout(() => console.log('2'), 0); console.log('3');?
quiz.explanation: setTimeout queues the callback. Sync logs run first, the timer callback last.

quiz.question: Which runs first when both are queued: a Promise.then or a setTimeout(fn, 0)?
quiz.explanation: Microtasks (.then) drain before the next macrotask (setTimeout).

quiz.question: What is the event loop's job?
options: Push tasks from queues onto the call stack when the stack is empty
quiz.explanation: The event loop coordinates: stack empty? pull next task from the queue and run it.

quiz.question: What does 'blocking' mean in JS?
options: Long synchronous work that keeps the call stack busy — the page can't respond to anything else
quiz.explanation: Blocking is long sync work. While it runs, no other JS or browser work can happen on the page.

quiz.question: Why is async essential in the browser?
options: It is required by the spec
Keeps the UI responsive while waiting for IO (network, timers)
quiz.explanation: Without async, every fetch or timer would freeze the page until done.

quiz.question: What is the call stack?
options: The stack of in-progress function calls
quiz.explanation: The stack records currently-executing function frames. Each call pushes, each return pops.

quiz.question: Which is NOT an async operation in JS?
quiz.explanation: JSON.parse is synchronous — runs entirely on the call stack. The others hand work off to the platform.

quiz.question: When does the event loop pull from the task queue?
options: Whenever the call stack is empty
quiz.explanation: The loop pulls a task only when the stack is empty so it doesn't interleave.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Sync vs Async"?
quiz.explanation: The event loop is the mental model behind every async JS topic.

// 5. Execution finishes
// 3. '2' is logged second (sync)

// 2. 'promise' is logged from the microtask queue

dragandropp.instruction: Drag each operation into the right bucket.

cardmatching.instruction: Match each concept on the left with its description on the right.

bugHunt.bug: Busy-waiting blocks the thread — the UI stalls and clicks/animations halt. Use setTimeout to yield the thread.
bugHunt.fixedCode:

setTimeout(() => console.log('end'), 2000);
bugHunt.hint: Never busy-wait on the main thread.
