useCaseCards.useCase: Pushes long calculations to setTimeout or Web Workers so the page stays responsive during heavy work.
Receives WS messages as async tasks, processed without blocking the rendering loop.
Schedules React state updates via the microtask queue (Promises) so DOM updates batch efficiently.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How Node.js built a server on one thread
realWorldStory.storyText: When Ryan Dahl built Node.js in 2009, he bet on one core idea: a single-threaded event loop plus non-blocking IO. Other languages used a thread per request and ran out of memory. Node served thousands of connections from one process — because every IO call was async by default. That insight is still the foundation of modern server JS.

keyTakeaways: JavaScript runs your code on a single main thread.
Async APIs (timers, fetch, IO) hand work to the platform and queue a callback for later.
The event loop pulls queued tasks onto the call stack whenever the stack is empty.
Microtasks (Promise.then) have higher priority than macrotasks (setTimeout).
⚠️ Common Mistake: Busy-waiting on the main thread — freezes the entire UI.
💡 Pro Tip: Always reach for async APIs for IO or delays. The main thread is for rendering, not for waiting.

lessons.title: Callbacks and Callback Hell
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Write async code with callbacks, (2) Recognise the error-first convention, (3) Avoid the pyramid of doom with named callbacks or Promises.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on async callbacks — the original way to handle delayed work.
Why it matters: Callbacks compared to a 'call me when ready' note — knowing the pattern unlocks every async API older than ES2015.
Core terms you will use: `async callback`, `error-first callback`, `callback hell`, `pyramid of doom`, `named extraction`, `Promise alternative`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `setTimeout(fn, 1000)`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: setTimeout callback" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the parentheses-on-callback bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You spot a pyramid of doom and reach for promises or named functions.

hooklineimage.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Caller passes a callback"] --> B["Async work happens in background"]
    B --> C["Callback fires when done"]
```

hooklines.text: Pass a function in, get called back later — that's the original async pattern.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["setTimeout(fn, 1000)"] --> B["timer waits 1s"]
    B --> C["fn(args)"]
```

hooklines.text: Three nested callbacks is fine. Six is callback hell.

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: Async callback
parts.description: A function passed to an async API. The API calls it when the work completes.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Error-first convention
parts.description: Node-style: callback receives (err, data). Handle err first; use data only when err is falsy.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Single-call rule
parts.description: A well-designed callback fires exactly once per operation. Calling it twice is a bug.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Callback hell
parts.description: Deeply nested callbacks form a pyramid that's hard to read. Each level adds an indent and handler.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Named extraction
parts.description: Pull each callback into a named function. The pyramid flattens; stack traces improve.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Promises are the cure
parts.description: Promises let you chain async steps with .then. async/await reads like sync code. Both built on top of the callback idea.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: promisify
parts.description: Many legacy callback APIs have a 'promisified' alternative (e.g. fs.promises in Node) or can be wrapped manually.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Context
parts.description: Inside a callback, this is determined by how it's called. Arrow functions inherit this from where they were written — usually what you want.

analogy.subject: Callbacks compared to a 'call me back' note
analogy.comparison: You hand a doctor's office a note: 'please call me when results are in.' That's a callback. If you need three tests in sequence, each office promises to call the next — a chain. With six offices, you have six layered phone calls. Promises replace the note system with a structured calendar.

example.title: Example 1: setTimeout callback
example.explanation: Output: 'start', 'end', 'later'. The callback fires after 500ms, after the sync code completes.

example.title: Example 2: Error-first style
example.explanation: callback gets (err, data). Always check err first.

example.title: Example 3: A taste of callback hell
example.explanation: Three nested levels each repeating error checks. Manageable, but more steps becomes painful.

example.title: Example 4: Named extraction
example.explanation: Each callback becomes a named function. The pyramid flattens; stack traces improve. Still verbose, but readable.

example.title: Example 5: Promise rewrite preview
example.code:
loadUserAsync(1)
  .then(loadPostsAsync)
  .then(loadCommentsAsync)
  .then(console.log)
  .catch(console.error);
example.explanation: Same flow with Promises. Top-to-bottom reading, single .catch. Detailed in the next lesson.

flowchart.title: Callback or Promise?

interactiveExercise.title: Try It Yourself
interactiveExercise.instruction: Write loadAndPrint(id) that uses setTimeout to simulate async load (200ms) and calls a callback (err, data). Test it with id=7 (success) and id=0 (error).
interactiveExercise.expectebehavior: First call prints the object; second prints the error.

quiz.question: Which of these is an async callback?
quiz.explanation: setTimeout schedules its callback to run later. The other examples are synchronous.

quiz.question: What is the error-first callback convention?
quiz.explanation: err is the first argument so callers always handle it before using data.

quiz.question: What is callback hell?
options: Deeply nested callbacks forming an unreadable pyramid
quiz.explanation: Nested levels make the code hard to follow and the error handling repetitive.

quiz.question: What is the first fix when callbacks pile up?
options: Extract each callback into a named function
quiz.explanation: Named extraction flattens the pyramid. After that, Promises or async/await go further.

quiz.question: How many times should a well-designed callback fire per operation?
quiz.explanation: Single-call semantics is the contract — double-calls cause subtle bugs.

quiz.question: What does Node-style fs.readFile pass to its callback?
quiz.explanation: Classic error-first. err is null on success.

quiz.question: Why use setTimeout(fn, 0) instead of calling fn() immediately?
options: Defer fn until after the current sync work finishes (next event-loop tick)
quiz.explanation: setTimeout(fn, 0) queues fn so it runs after the current call stack clears.

quiz.question: Which call form passes the function rather than calling it?
quiz.explanation: Drop the parentheses to pass the reference. Calling immediately would queue undefined.

quiz.question: Why introduce Promises after callbacks?
options: Promises compose top-to-bottom and have one .catch — no per-step error handling
quiz.explanation: Promises flatten the pyramid into a chain with one centralised error handler.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Callbacks and Callback Hell"?
quiz.explanation: Recognising the pyramid of doom is the lesson's most actionable insight.

codelines: // 4. After the delay, the timer fires
// 1. setTimeout(fn, 500) is called
// 5. The event loop picks up the callback when the stack is empty
// 3. setTimeout returns immediately; sync code continues
// 6. The callback runs and finishes
// 2. The browser schedules a 500ms timer

dragandropp.instruction: Drag each callback into the right bucket.

Pulling inline callbacks into named functions

bugHunt.title: Find and fix the bug
bugHunt.instruction: A developer wants to delay a greeting by 1 second but it fires immediately. Fix it.
bugHunt.buggyCode:
function greet() { console.log('hi'); }
setTimeout(greet(), 1000);
bugHunt.bug: greet() runs immediately and passes its return value (undefined) to setTimeout. Pass the function REFERENCE — drop the parentheses.
bugHunt.fixedCode:
function greet() { console.log('hi'); }
setTimeout(greet, 1000);
bugHunt.hint: Pass the function, do not call it.

useCaseCards.useCase: Maintains older Node APIs (fs, dns, http) that still use error-first callbacks; wraps them in Promises when consumed by modern code.
Pairs DOM event listeners with named callbacks so removeEventListener can find the same reference for cleanup.
Offers both callback and Promise versions of every async method so legacy consumers can migrate gradually.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How async/await replaced callbacks in Node
realWorldStory.storyText: Node.js shipped in 2009 with error-first callbacks everywhere. Promise support landed in 2014, and async/await arrived in Node 7 (2016). Today, every new fs API has a fs.promises version, and old patterns like fs.readFile(path, (err, data) => …) are slowly retreating into legacy code. The pyramid that everyone wrote for a decade is finally gone.

keyTakeaways: Callbacks are functions passed to async APIs that get called when work finishes.
Node-style APIs use error-first callbacks: (err, data). Handle err first.
Three nested callbacks is fine; six is a pyramid of doom.
Promises and async/await replace the pyramid with linear top-to-bottom code.
⚠️ Common Mistake: setTimeout(fn(), 1000) — fires fn immediately; pass fn without parentheses.
💡 Pro Tip: When a third callback level appears, refactor to Promises or async/await.

lessons.title: Promises: then, catch, finally
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Build and consume Promises, (2) Chain .then with returned values or new promises, (3) Centralise errors with .catch and cleanup with .finally.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on Promises — the structured way to model async outcomes.
Why it matters: Promises compared to a tracked package — knowing the states unlocks reliable async flows.
Core terms you will use: `Promise`, `pending`, `fulfilled`, `rejected`, `.then`, `.catch`, `.finally`, `chaining`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `fetch(url).then(...)`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: A promise that resolves" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the missing-return bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You return from every .then so the next .then receives the right value.

hooklineimage.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Promise: pending"] --> B["fulfilled (value)"]
    A --> C["rejected (error)"]
    B --> D[".then receives value"]
    C --> E[".catch receives error"]
```

hooklines.text: A Promise is pending until it settles — fulfilled with a value or rejected with an error.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["pending"] --> B["fulfilled"]
    A --> C["rejected"]
```

hooklines.text: Chain .then to transform the value. One .catch at the end handles every error.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["fetch"] --> B[".then(res => res.json())"]
    B --> C[".then(data => render(data))"]
    C --> D[".catch(err => warn(err))"]
```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: Promise basics
parts.description: A Promise is an object representing the eventual result of an async operation. It's pending until it settles.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Create with new Promise
parts.description: new Promise((resolve, reject) => { ... }). Call resolve(value) or reject(error) inside to settle it.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: .then
parts.description: Runs when the promise fulfills. Receives the resolved value. Returns a NEW promise — that's why chaining works.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: .catch
parts.description: Runs when any promise in the chain rejects. Catches errors thrown inside .then handlers too.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: .finally
parts.description: Runs no matter what — success or failure. Perfect for cleanup like 'hide loading spinner'.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Return inside .then
parts.description: Whatever you return becomes the next .then's input. Returning a promise makes the chain wait for it.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Promise.resolve / Promise.reject
parts.description: Shortcut creators: Promise.resolve(value) gives an already-fulfilled promise; Promise.reject(err) gives a rejected one.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Microtask priority
parts.description: Promise callbacks run in the microtask queue — before any setTimeout callback queued earlier.

analogy.subject: Promises compared to package tracking
analogy.comparison: A Promise is your tracking number. It starts 'In transit' (pending). Eventually it's either 'Delivered' (fulfilled) or 'Lost' (rejected). .then is what you do when the package arrives; .catch is your insurance claim; .finally is the receipt you file no matter what.

example.title: Example 1: A promise that resolves
example.explanation: Promise resolves after 100ms. .then receives 'done' and logs it.

example.title: Example 2: Promise.resolve shortcut
example.code: Promise.resolve(42).then(n => console.log(n * 2));
example.explanation: Promise.resolve creates an already-fulfilled promise. Output: 84.

example.title: Example 3: Chaining
example.code:
Promise.resolve(2)
  .then(n => n + 1)
  .then(n => n * 10)
  .then(console.log);
example.explanation: Each .then's return becomes the next .then's input. Output: 30.

example.title: Example 4: catch and finally
example.code:
fetch('/api')
  .then(r => r.json())
  .then(data => render(data))
  .catch(err => console.error('Failed', err))
  .finally(() => hideSpinner());
example.explanation: One .catch handles any failure in the chain. .finally always runs.

example.title: Example 5: Returning a promise
example.explanation: Returning a promise from .then makes the chain WAIT for it. Output 'AB' after ~200ms.

flowchart.title: Reading a promise chain
flowchart.code:
flowchart TD
    A["Async source"] --> B[".then transform"]
    B --> C[".then more transform"]
    C --> D{"Error anywhere?"}
    D -- yes --> E[".catch handles it"]
    D -- no --> F[".finally cleanup"]

interactiveExercise.instruction: Build delay(ms, value) returning a Promise that resolves to value after ms. Chain three calls to log 'A', 'B', 'C' 100ms apart.

quiz.question: What are the three Promise states?
quiz.explanation: Pending until it settles. Settles to fulfilled (value) or rejected (error).

quiz.question: What does .then return?
options: A new Promise — that's why you can chain
quiz.explanation: Each .then returns a new Promise, enabling chains. Whatever you return becomes the next .then's value.

quiz.question: What does .catch handle?
options: Any rejection or thrown error in the chain above it
quiz.explanation: .catch is a centralised handler for rejections AND thrown errors in earlier .then handlers.

quiz.question: When does .finally run?
quiz.explanation: .finally runs on success and on failure. Perfect for cleanup (e.g. hiding spinners).

quiz.question: What does Promise.resolve(7) produce?
options: A pending promise that resolves to 7
quiz.explanation: Shortcut for an already-fulfilled promise — handy for normalising values to promises.

quiz.question: If a .then handler returns a Promise, what happens?
options: The next .then receives the Promise as-is
The chain waits for that promise; the next .then receives ITS value
quiz.explanation: Returning a promise from .then makes the chain wait for it to settle before continuing.

quiz.question: What does throwing inside a .then do?
options: Rejects the chain — caught by the next .catch
quiz.explanation: Throws are converted to rejections in promise chains. .catch handles them like explicit rejections.

quiz.question: Where do Promise callbacks run in the event loop?
quiz.explanation: Microtasks drain BEFORE the next macrotask, so a queued Promise.then runs before a setTimeout(fn, 0) queued at the same time.

quiz.question: Which .catch position catches ALL errors in the chain?
quiz.explanation: A .catch at the end captures every rejection/throw in the chain above it.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Promises"?
quiz.explanation: Chaining transforms with .then is what makes promises so powerful compared to nested callbacks.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How Promises killed callback nesting
realWorldStory.storyText: When ES2015 added native Promises, the JavaScript community rejoiced — the pyramid of doom finally had a structural cure. Within two years, every major library exposed Promise APIs, and Promise.then(... ).catch became the new normal. Today async/await sits on top of Promises — proof that the foundation matters as much as the syntax sugar.

keyTakeaways: A Promise has three states: pending, fulfilled, rejected.
.then chains; each .then returns a new Promise; whatever you return becomes the next handler's input.
.catch handles rejections AND thrown errors anywhere earlier in the chain.
.finally always runs — success or failure — perfect for cleanup.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Forgetting return inside a braced .then handler — the next step gets undefined.
💡 Pro Tip: Place one .catch at the chain's end to centralise error handling — far cleaner than per-step try/catch.

lessons.title: async/await Syntax
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Mark functions async and use await, (2) Read async code top-to-bottom like sync, (3) Avoid the await-in-forEach trap.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on async/await — syntactic sugar over Promises.
Why it matters: async/await compared to writing your async story top-to-bottom — knowing it unlocks the cleanest async style.
Core terms you will use: `async`, `await`, `async function`, `top-level await`, `async returns Promise`, `parallel vs serial`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `const data = await fetch(url).then(r => r.json())`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: A basic async function" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the await-inside-forEach bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You use try/catch inside async for error handling and reach for Promise.all for parallel awaits.

hooklineimage.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["async function f() {"] --> B["const x = await promise;"]
    B --> C["// use x like sync"]
    C --> D["return value -> auto-wrapped in Promise"]
```

hooklines.text: async/await makes promise chains read like sync code. Same engine; cleaner syntax.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[".then(r => r.json()).then(render)"] --> B["const data = await (await fetch()).json(); render(data);"]
```

hooklines.text: await pauses ONLY inside async functions. Outside one is a SyntaxError (or top-level await in modules).

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["async function"] --> B["await ok"]
    C["normal function"] --> D["await is SyntaxError"]
```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: async functions
parts.description: Prefix a function with async to make it return a Promise automatically. Any return value is auto-wrapped.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: await
parts.description: Inside an async function, await pauses until the promise settles, then continues with the resolved value.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Same engine as Promises
parts.description: async/await is sugar over Promises — same microtask scheduling, same .then mechanics under the hood.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: try/catch for errors
parts.description: Wrap await calls in try/catch to handle rejections. Cleaner than .catch attached to a chain.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Top-level await
parts.description: ES2022 modules allow await at module top level. Outside modules, await must live in an async function.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Serial awaiting
parts.description: for (const x of arr) await f(x) processes one at a time. Sequential, simple — but slow when independent.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Parallel with Promise.all
parts.description: await Promise.all(arr.map(f)) fires all calls at once and waits for all to settle. Much faster for independent work.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: forEach + async is wrong
parts.description: forEach ignores returned promises — your handler runs in parallel without awaits. Use for-of with await or Promise.all.

analogy.subject: async/await compared to reading a story top to bottom
analogy.comparison: Promise chains are a story where every page handed you a folded paper to read next (.then). async/await is the same story printed linearly — you read paragraph by paragraph. The plot is identical; the formatting is cleaner.

example.title: Example 1: A basic async function
example.explanation: async functions return a Promise. greet() resolves to 'hello'.

example.title: Example 2: await inside
example.explanation: Each await pauses until the promise settles, then continues. Reads top-to-bottom like sync.

example.title: Example 3: try/catch for errors
example.explanation: try/catch catches rejections from any awaited promise inside. Cleaner than .catch.

example.title: Example 4: Serial vs parallel
example.explanation: Serial waits for each call before starting the next. Parallel fires them all and waits for the slowest.

example.title: Example 5: forEach is wrong for awaits
example.explanation: forEach ignores the promise its callback returns. The function returns before the awaits settle. Use for-of.

quiz.question: What does an async function always return?
quiz.explanation: async functions wrap returned values in a Promise automatically.

quiz.question: Where can await appear?
options: Inside async functions (or top-level of an ES module)
quiz.explanation: await needs an async context. Outside one is a SyntaxError (modules allow top-level await).

quiz.question: What does await do?
options: Pauses the async function until the promise settles, then resumes with its value
quiz.explanation: Function execution pauses; the engine continues other work. When the promise settles, execution resumes.

quiz.question: How do you handle errors with await?
options: .catch chained at the end of the file
quiz.explanation: try/catch is the natural fit. Rejections come out as thrown errors.

quiz.question: Which form runs requests in parallel?
options: for (const id of ids) await load(id)
quiz.explanation: Promise.all fires every call at once. The for-of version is serial.

quiz.question: Why is awaiting inside forEach broken?
options: forEach ignores returned promises — every callback runs in parallel and the function exits before awaits settle
quiz.explanation: forEach doesn't await its callbacks. The async function continues immediately.

quiz.question: What does async function f() { return 7; } produce?
quiz.explanation: async wraps the return value in a Promise. The caller awaits or chains .then.

quiz.question: What is top-level await?
options: Awaiting at the top of an ES module without wrapping in async
quiz.explanation: ES2022 lets ES modules use await at the module top. Common in Deno and modern Node.

quiz.question: Which is the cleanest error pattern with async?
options: Both work, but try/catch is more natural inside async
quiz.explanation: Inside async, try/catch reads like sync code. .catch on the returned promise also works at the call site.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "async/await"?
quiz.explanation: Top-down readability is the headline benefit of async/await over promise chains.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How async/await came to JavaScript
realWorldStory.storyText: Microsoft introduced async/await in C# in 2012. TC39 ported the idea to JavaScript and shipped it in ES2017. Within two years, every major framework's docs were rewritten in async/await style. The pattern was so successful it has become the default — Promises remain the foundation, but writing chain-style .then is now considered legacy in most contexts.

keyTakeaways: async functions return a Promise automatically; values are wrapped, throws become rejections.
await pauses an async function until the promise settles, then resumes with the value.
Use try/catch around awaits for natural error handling inside async functions.
Promise.all + await is parallel; for-of + await is serial. Choose based on whether you need ordering.
⚠️ Common Mistake: forEach with async callbacks — awaits are ignored. Use for-of.
💡 Pro Tip: When you find a long Promise chain, rewrite as async/await — readers will thank you.

lessons.title: The fetch API
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Make GET requests with fetch, (2) Read JSON, text, and blob responses, (3) Send POST requests with a body.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on the browser's built-in fetch — the modern HTTP API.
Why it matters: fetch compared to a courier service — knowing the parts unlocks every API integration.
Core terms you will use: `fetch`, `Response`, `response.json`, `response.ok`, `headers`, `method`, `body`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `await fetch(url, options)`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: A simple GET" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the response.ok-bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You always check response.ok before parsing the body.

hooklineimage.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["fetch(url)"] --> B["Promise<Response>"]
    B --> C["response.json() / text() / blob()"]
    C --> D["Use parsed body"]
```

hooklines.text: fetch returns a Promise<Response>. You parse the body in a SECOND step.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["const r = await fetch(url)"] --> B["const data = await r.json()"]
```

hooklines.text: fetch does NOT reject on HTTP 4xx/5xx — check response.ok yourself.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["404"] --> B["Promise resolves"]
    B --> C["response.ok === false"]
```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: Basic GET
parts.description: fetch(url) issues a GET. Returns a Promise that resolves to a Response object representing the headers/status.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Parsing the body
parts.description: response.json(), .text(), or .blob() return Promises for the parsed body. The body is read once.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: response.ok
parts.description: Boolean: true for 2xx statuses. 4xx and 5xx still RESOLVE the promise — you must check ok yourself.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: response.status
parts.description: The numeric HTTP status (200, 404, 500). Use along with ok for nuanced handling.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Request options
parts.description: fetch(url, { method, headers, body, credentials, signal }). Defaults are sensible — GET, no body, omit cookies cross-origin.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Headers and JSON body
parts.description: Send JSON: method:'POST', headers:{'Content-Type':'application/json'}, body: JSON.stringify(data).

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: AbortSignal
parts.description: Pass an AbortController.signal to cancel a fetch (e.g. on component unmount or new query).

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Errors
parts.description: fetch only rejects on network failure or CORS issues. HTTP errors are NOT rejections — check ok.

analogy.subject: fetch compared to a courier service
analogy.comparison: fetch is the courier driving to a remote address. The first delivery is the envelope (Response) — you must open it (response.json) to see the contents. A 404 means 'address not found' but the courier still came back — it's your job to read the slip.

example.title: Example 1: A simple GET
example.explanation: fetch -> check ok -> parse json. The two-step body parse is what trips beginners.

example.title: Example 2: Text body
example.explanation: response.text() returns a string. Use for plain text or HTML.

example.title: Example 3: POST with JSON
example.explanation: POST with JSON body and the right Content-Type header. The server reads the JSON payload.

example.title: Example 4: Aborting
example.explanation: AbortController gives you a kill switch. Aborted fetches reject with AbortError.

example.title: Example 5: Checking status
example.explanation: Branch by status — 401 triggers login; other non-ok statuses throw.

flowchart.code:
flowchart TD

    B -- no --> C["Throw or branch on r.status"]
    B -- yes --> D{"Body format?"}

quiz.question: What does fetch return?
options: A Promise that resolves to a Response object
quiz.explanation: fetch returns Promise<Response>. You parse the body in a second await.

quiz.question: How do you get parsed JSON from a Response?
quiz.explanation: response.json() returns a Promise that resolves to the parsed object.

quiz.question: Does fetch reject on HTTP 404?
options: No — the promise resolves; check response.ok
quiz.explanation: HTTP errors RESOLVE the promise. Only network failures or CORS issues reject.

quiz.question: Which option sets the HTTP method to POST?
quiz.explanation: method is the property name.

quiz.question: How do you send a JSON body?
options: body: JSON.stringify({ a: 1 }) plus Content-Type header
quiz.explanation: Stringify the object and set Content-Type to application/json so the server parses correctly.

quiz.question: What is response.ok?
quiz.explanation: ok is true only for status codes 200-299.

quiz.question: Which API cancels an in-flight fetch?
quiz.explanation: Create an AbortController and pass its signal. Call controller.abort() to cancel.

quiz.question: Which body type is for binary downloads (images)?
quiz.explanation: blob() returns a Blob — handy for images, files, or arbitrary bytes.

quiz.question: Why do many wrappers add 'throw if !ok' helpers?
options: fetch doesn't auto-reject on HTTP errors — code that forgets to check ok ships silent bugs
quiz.explanation: It's so easy to forget the check that libraries like Axios/fetch-wrappers throw by default.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "fetch API"?
quiz.explanation: Checking response.ok is the single most common skipped step that causes silent bugs.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: Why every Axios alternative was 'just fetch'
realWorldStory.storyText: For years, Axios was the de-facto library for HTTP because XMLHttpRequest was painful. Once fetch became universal, libraries thinned out into 'fetch wrappers' that just add the throw-on-not-ok and timeout handling. Today, many projects ship with no HTTP library at all — fetch + a 10-line wrapper does the job.

keyTakeaways: fetch returns Promise<Response>. The body is parsed in a second step (await response.json()).
fetch does NOT reject on HTTP errors — always check response.ok.
POST JSON: method:'POST', Content-Type header, body: JSON.stringify(data).
AbortController + signal lets you cancel an in-flight fetch.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Skipping response.ok and parsing error responses as if they were data.
💡 Pro Tip: Build a small fetchOk helper that throws on !ok — reduces boilerplate across the app.

lessons.title: Error Handling in Async Code
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Catch rejections with try/catch and .catch, (2) Distinguish thrown errors from rejected promises, (3) Handle unhandled rejections globally.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on handling errors in promise chains and async functions.
Why it matters: Error handling compared to seatbelts in async code — knowing it unlocks robust apps.
Core terms you will use: `rejection`, `try/catch`, `.catch`, `unhandled rejection`, `re-throw`, `error boundary`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `try { await x } catch (err) { ... }`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: try/catch with await" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the missing-await bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You catch where you can recover and re-throw otherwise.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["async operation"] --> B{"settle?"}
    B -- success --> C["value"]
    B -- failure --> D["thrown / rejected"]
    D --> E["try/catch or .catch"]
```

hooklines.text: Inside async, await rejections show up as thrown errors — try/catch catches both.

hooklines.text: Unhandled rejections fire the 'unhandledrejection' window event — wire it up for monitoring.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Promise rejects with no .catch"] --> B["window 'unhandledrejection' event"]
```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: try/catch with await
parts.description: Wrap awaits in try/catch. Rejections become thrown errors inside the async function.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: .catch on promise chains
parts.description: promise.then().catch(handler) — works for chain-style code. Placed at the end catches all errors above.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: throw inside async
parts.description: Throwing inside an async function rejects the returned Promise. Equivalent to Promise.reject.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Re-throwing
parts.description: If catch can't handle the error meaningfully, re-throw so the caller can decide. catch { throw err; }

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Unhandled rejection
parts.description: If a Promise rejects with no handler, the runtime fires unhandledrejection (window or process). Wire to your monitoring.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Catch where you can recover
parts.description: Catch only where you can either fix it, retry, or report meaningfully. Otherwise let errors propagate.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Promise.reject
parts.description: Shortcut to create an already-rejected promise. Useful when an async function needs to bail out cleanly.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Awaiting forgotten
parts.description: If you don't await a promise, its rejection becomes an unhandled rejection. Always await promises that can fail.

analogy.subject: Async errors compared to insurance claims
analogy.comparison: A try/catch is your insurance: when something goes wrong (a thrown error, a rejected promise), the policy kicks in. Re-throwing is escalating to a higher policy. Unhandled rejections are uninsured losses — they get reported globally so you at least know they happened.

example.title: Example 1: try/catch with await
example.explanation: Any rejection or throw inside try is caught. Decide to recover or return a default.

example.title: Example 2: .catch on chains
example.code:
fetch('/api')
  .then(r => r.json())
  .then(data => render(data))
  .catch(err => console.error(err));
example.explanation: One .catch at the end handles every step's rejection. Cleaner than per-step error checks.

example.title: Example 3: Re-throw
example.explanation: Log locally but let the caller decide what to do. Re-throw with `throw err`.

example.title: Example 4: Global unhandledrejection
example.explanation: Catches any promise rejection with no handler. Wire it to your error monitoring service.

example.title: Example 5: Forgotten await
example.explanation: Forgetting await means p is a Promise object, not the value. Rejections become unhandled.

flowchart.title: Should I catch this error here?
flowchart.code:
flowchart TD
    A["Error in async code"] --> B{"Can I recover, retry, or default?"}
    B -- yes --> C["try/catch and handle"]
    B -- log only --> D["try/catch, log, re-throw"]
    B -- no --> E["Let it propagate"]
    E --> F["Global unhandledrejection catches the rest"]

quiz.question: How do rejected awaits surface inside an async function?
options: As thrown errors caught by try/catch
quiz.explanation: await rejects via throw — try/catch is the natural handler.

quiz.question: What does throw inside an async function do?
quiz.explanation: async wraps throws as Promise rejections.

quiz.question: Where should .catch be placed in a promise chain?
options: End of the chain — catches all earlier errors
quiz.explanation: One .catch at the end handles every preceding step's rejection.

quiz.question: What is an unhandled rejection?
options: A rejected promise with no .catch or try/catch
quiz.explanation: If a rejection has no handler, the runtime emits unhandledrejection. Wire it for visibility.

quiz.question: How do you re-throw inside a catch?
quiz.explanation: `throw err` re-raises the caught error to the next outer handler.

quiz.question: Which approach is best for 'log and continue'?
quiz.explanation: Catch, log meaningfully, and continue with a sensible default.

quiz.question: If you forget to await a promise, what happens to its rejection?

realWorldStory.storyTitle: How Node deprecated silent rejections
realWorldStory.storyText: Early Node didn't crash on unhandled rejections — they just disappeared. After many production incidents, Node started warning, then (Node 15+) crashes on unhandled rejections by default. Today every well-run Node service wires the 'unhandledRejection' process event into structured logging.

keyTakeaways: Inside async, await rejections show up as thrown errors — try/catch is the natural handler.
In promise chains, place one .catch at the end. It catches every preceding error.
Re-throw when you can't handle meaningfully — let the caller decide.
Unhandled rejections fire the unhandledrejection event. Wire it for visibility.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Forgetting await — the rejection becomes unhandled and silent.
💡 Pro Tip: Catch where you can recover; let everything else propagate to a centralised reporter.

lessons.title: Promise.all and Promise.race
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Run promises in parallel with Promise.all, (2) Use Promise.allSettled for resilient batches, (3) Pick winners with Promise.race / Promise.any.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on the Promise.* combinators that orchestrate multiple async calls.
Why it matters: Combinators compared to a relay race — knowing which one to pick unlocks fast and resilient async flows.
Core terms you will use: `Promise.all`, `Promise.allSettled`, `Promise.race`, `Promise.any`, `fail-fast`, `aggregate`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `await Promise.all([a, b, c])`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: Promise.all" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the all-fails-fast bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You pick allSettled when you want every result even if some fail.

hooklineimage.html:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["[p1, p2, p3]"] --> B["Promise.all (all succeed)"]
    A --> C["Promise.allSettled (every result)"]
    A --> D["Promise.race (first to settle)"]
    A --> E["Promise.any (first to fulfill)"]
```

hooklines.text: Promise.all is fail-fast: one rejection rejects the whole.

image.html:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["p1 ok, p2 reject, p3 ok"] --> B["Promise.all rejects with p2's error"]
```

hooklines.text: Promise.allSettled is resilient: returns an array of {status, value} or {status, reason}.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["[p1, p2, p3]"] --> B["allSettled"]
    B --> C["[{status:'fulfilled',value}, {status:'rejected',reason}, ...]"]
```

highlight.code: const [a, b, c] = await Promise.all([p1, p2, p3]);

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: Promise.all
parts.description: Takes an array of promises. Resolves with an array of values when ALL fulfill. Rejects on the FIRST rejection.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: Fail-fast
parts.description: Promise.all does not wait — the moment any input rejects, the combined promise rejects with that error.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: Promise.allSettled
parts.description: Waits for every promise to settle. Returns an array of { status, value } or { status, reason }. Never rejects.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: Promise.race
parts.description: Resolves or rejects with the first promise to SETTLE (whether fulfilled or rejected). Useful for timeouts.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: Promise.any
parts.description: Resolves with the first promise to FULFILL. Rejects only if all reject — with an AggregateError.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Order is preserved
parts.description: Promise.all/allSettled return results in INPUT ORDER, not settle order. The second result is always from the second promise.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Timeouts via race
parts.description: Race the real work against a timeout promise. Whichever settles first wins. Pair with AbortController for cleanup.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: Performance
parts.description: Combinators do NOT run promises — they wait on already-started ones. The async work begins the moment you create each promise.

analogy.subject: Promise combinators compared to a race
analogy.comparison: Promise.all is a team relay — everyone must finish for the team to win; one falls and the team loses. allSettled is a marathon roll call — every runner is recorded whether they finished or DNFed. race is a sprint — first across the line wins, even if they tripped. any is a marathon — first to actually finish wins; if nobody does, the day is lost.

example.title: Example 1: Promise.all
example.explanation: Fire both in parallel; wait for both. Destructure the result array.

example.title: Example 2: Fail-fast surprise
example.explanation: The first rejection rejects the whole. The other promises still run but their results are discarded.

example.title: Example 3: allSettled
example.explanation: Get every result, success or failure. Inspect status to branch.

example.title: Example 4: Timeout via race
example.explanation: Race the real work against a timeout. Whichever resolves first wins.

example.title: Example 5: Promise.any
example.explanation: Try multiple mirrors; the first successful response wins. AggregateError fires only when every promise fails.

    B -- and stop on first error --> C["Promise.all"]
    B -- continue regardless --> D["Promise.allSettled"]
    A --> E{"Want first to finish?"}
    E -- any settle --> F["Promise.race"]
    E -- first success --> G["Promise.any"]

quiz.question: What does Promise.all do?
options: Resolves with the first successful promise
Resolves with an array of all values when all fulfill; rejects on first rejection
quiz.explanation: all is fail-fast and preserves input order in the result array.

quiz.question: Which combinator never rejects?
quiz.explanation: allSettled always resolves with an array of {status, value/reason} objects.

quiz.question: What does Promise.race resolve with?
options: The first promise to SETTLE (success or failure)
quiz.explanation: race uses the first settled promise, whether it fulfilled or rejected.

quiz.question: What does Promise.any do?
options: Resolves with the first FULFILLED promise; rejects with AggregateError only if all reject
quiz.explanation: any wants a successful settle. Only when every input rejects does it fail.

quiz.question: What error type does Promise.any reject with when all fail?
quiz.explanation: AggregateError holds all rejection reasons in .errors.

quiz.question: Does Promise.all preserve input order in its result?
options: Yes — same order as the input array
quiz.explanation: all returns values in the same positions as the input promises.

quiz.question: When should you choose allSettled over all?
options: When you want every result even if some fail
When you only have one promise
quiz.explanation: allSettled is the resilient choice — useful for analytics, batch APIs, or anywhere partial success matters.

quiz.question: How is a timeout typically implemented?
options: Promise.race between the real work and a rejecting timer
quiz.explanation: race the real work against a timer that rejects after N ms. Whichever settles first wins.

quiz.question: Do Promise.* combinators start the work?
options: No — the work begins when each promise is created; combinators only observe
quiz.explanation: Promises are eager. Combinators wait on already-running work.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "Promise.all and Promise.race"?
quiz.explanation: Fail-fast — the defining behaviour of Promise.all — is the key idea.

bugHunt.instruction: A batch of API calls uses Promise.all. When one fails, the whole batch errors and the partial successes are lost. Fix it.

bugHunt.hint: Use allSettled when you want every result, even if some fail.

useCaseCards.useCase: Promise.all fires user + config + flag fetches together so page rendering waits for the slowest, not the sum.
Uses allSettled for batches of event submissions — failures are recorded but don't drop healthy events.
Promise.any pings all replicas; the fastest healthy region wins.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: Why allSettled exists
realWorldStory.storyText: For years, teams wrote workaround helpers because Promise.all crashed entire batches on single failures. allSettled landed in ES2020 specifically to remove that workaround. Today, batch APIs, analytics services, and partial-render scenarios reach for allSettled by default — saving teams from inventing the same pattern again and again.

keyTakeaways: Promise.all is parallel and fail-fast. Use when every call must succeed.
Promise.allSettled waits for every promise to settle; returns {status, value/reason} per slot. Resilient.
Promise.race resolves with the first promise to SETTLE — used for timeouts.
Promise.any resolves with the first to FULFILL — used for fallback mirrors. Aggregates errors on total failure.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Using Promise.all for a resilient batch and losing every result on the first failure.
💡 Pro Tip: Pair Promise.race with AbortController so a timeout also cancels the in-flight work.

lessons.title: setTimeout and setInterval
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: (1) Schedule code with setTimeout, (2) Repeat with setInterval and clear it, (3) Recognise the 4ms minimum and other timer quirks.

points: What this lesson teaches: This lesson focuses on the classic timer APIs.
Why it matters: Timers compared to an oven timer — knowing when they fire (and don't) unlocks scheduled work.
Core terms you will use: `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `clearTimeout`, `clearInterval`, `4ms minimum`, `requestAnimationFrame`.
Syntax to recognise on sight: `const id = setTimeout(fn, 1000); clearTimeout(id);`. Learn this shape so you spot it in any codebase.
Worked code: 5 progressive examples, starting from "Example 1: setTimeout" and getting more practical with each step.
Watch out for the drifting-interval bug shown in the bug-hunt activity — fixing it cements the underlying mental model.
The lesson keeps the focus narrow on its core idea so you finish with a sharp, transferable mental model.
Sign you have got it: You reach for setInterval cautiously and rAF for visual loops.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["setTimeout(fn, 1000)"] --> B["fires once after ~1s"]
    C["setInterval(fn, 1000)"] --> D["fires every ~1s"]
    D --> E["clearInterval(id) to stop"]
```

hooklines.text: setTimeout fires once. setInterval keeps firing until you clear it.

flowchart LR

    C["setInterval"] --> D["keeps firing"]
```

hooklines.text: Timers are minimum delays — heavy main thread work can push them later.

```

parts.label: Step 1
parts.name: setTimeout
parts.description: Schedules fn to run after at least ms. Returns an id for cancellation.

parts.label: Step 2
parts.name: clearTimeout
parts.description: Cancels a pending timeout via its id. No-op if already fired.

parts.label: Step 3
parts.name: setInterval
parts.description: Calls fn repeatedly at the given interval. Returns an id.

parts.label: Step 4
parts.name: clearInterval
parts.description: Stops a running interval. Always store the id when you create an interval.

parts.label: Step 5
parts.name: 4ms minimum
parts.description: Nested timeouts cap at 4ms after a few levels. Even setTimeout(fn, 0) waits at least that long.

parts.label: Step 6
parts.name: Drift
parts.description: Timers are minimum delays — actual fire may be later if the main thread is busy. Don't rely on exact timing.

parts.label: Step 7
parts.name: Animation loops
parts.description: For frame-by-frame animation, use requestAnimationFrame — synced to the display refresh rate.

parts.label: Step 8
parts.name: queueMicrotask
parts.description: Queues a microtask — runs before the next macrotask. Use when you need fast next-tick scheduling that's NOT a timer.

analogy.subject: Timers compared to an oven timer
analogy.comparison: setTimeout is setting the oven for one buzz. setInterval is a repeating chime every interval. clear* is canceling the buzz before it goes off. The cook (main thread) can be too busy to hear it on time — that's drift.

example.title: Example 1: setTimeout
example.explanation: Fires once after ~1000ms. Store the id so you can cancel if needed.

example.title: Example 2: setInterval
example.explanation: Logs 1-5, then stops. clearInterval ensures the timer doesn't keep firing.

example.title: Example 3: 4ms minimum
example.explanation: Despite the 0, the browser enforces a minimum (typically 4ms in deeply nested cases). Tasks queue and run in order.

example.title: Example 4: Drift-aware recursive setTimeout
example.explanation: Recursive setTimeout self-cancels on done. More predictable than setInterval for variable work.

example.title: Example 5: rAF for animation
example.explanation: Synced to display refresh (~60fps). Use rAF for smooth animations, not setInterval.

quiz.question: What does setTimeout return?
quiz.explanation: Store the id so clearTimeout can cancel before it fires.

quiz.question: How do you stop a setInterval?
quiz.explanation: clearInterval halts a repeating timer. Use the id returned by setInterval.

quiz.question: Why does setTimeout(fn, 0) not fire immediately?
options: Browsers enforce a minimum delay (often 4ms once nested) and the callback queues until the stack is empty
quiz.explanation: Timers are minimum delays; the spec mandates a 4ms floor after nested timeouts.

quiz.question: What is timer 'drift'?
options: Timer firing slightly later than requested due to main-thread work
Timers running in the wrong order
quiz.explanation: Timers are best-effort. Heavy main-thread work delays them.

quiz.question: Which is better for smooth visual animations?
quiz.explanation: rAF syncs to the display refresh — typically 60fps — and pauses when the tab is hidden.

quiz.question: What is queueMicrotask used for?
options: Schedules a microtask — runs before the next macrotask, useful for 'right after this turn'
quiz.explanation: queueMicrotask is microtask-level scheduling — same priority as Promise.then.

quiz.question: Which is more predictable for variable work?
options: Recursive setTimeout — schedules the next fire when the previous one finishes
quiz.explanation: Recursive setTimeout adapts to variable durations. setInterval can stack overlapping ticks if work is slow.

quiz.question: Can you pass arguments to the callback in setTimeout?
options: Yes — extra arguments after the delay are passed
quiz.explanation: setTimeout(fn, delay, arg1, arg2) — fn receives the trailing args.

quiz.question: What happens if you forget to clearInterval before the page navigates away?
options: On SPA navigation it can leak and keep running; on full-page navigation it's cleaned up by the browser
quiz.explanation: Full page navigation kills timers; SPA route changes do NOT — always clear intervals on component unmount.

quiz.question: Which of these is a core concept introduced in "setTimeout and setInterval"?
quiz.explanation: Timer drift — the reality that timers fire AT LEAST the requested delay — is the lesson's central insight.

bugHunt.title: Find and fix the bug
bugHunt.instruction: A developer uses setInterval(work, 1000) where work() takes 1500ms. Calls stack and the page slows. Fix with recursive setTimeout.
bugHunt.bug: setInterval queues a new call every 1000ms regardless of whether the previous one finished. Recursive setTimeout schedules the next call only AFTER the previous one completes.
bugHunt.hint: Recursive setTimeout self-paces; setInterval doesn't.

realWorldStory.storyTitle: Why rAF replaced setInterval for animation
realWorldStory.storyText: Early JS games used setInterval(render, 16) hoping for 60fps. The result: animations stuttered, batteries drained, and tabs kept running in the background. requestAnimationFrame landed around 2010 and tied frame work to the display's natural refresh — and paused entirely on hidden tabs. Today rAF is the only acceptable choice for visual animations on the web.

keyTakeaways: setTimeout(fn, ms) schedules fn ONCE; setInterval repeats. Both return an id for cancellation.
clearTimeout / clearInterval cancel a pending or running timer.
Timers are minimum delays — actual fire time can drift if the main thread is busy.
Use requestAnimationFrame for animations and queueMicrotask for 'right after this turn' scheduling.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Using setInterval for slow work — calls pile up if work takes longer than the interval.
💡 Pro Tip: Prefer recursive setTimeout over setInterval for self-pacing periodic work.
